title: $699M has gone to 'red flag' suppliers under federal Indigenous procurement strategy: study
body:
The federal government may be overestimating how much procurement spending ends up in Indigenous hands by 
hundreds of millions of dollars, a recent study finds.
The peer-reviewed research paper( https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07078552.2025.2598513 ), 
published in the journal Studies in Political Economy, found that up to $839 million in government spending under 
the Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business (PSIB) went to organizations that appear to have few Indigenous 
employees or limited capacity to carry out the work.
Of that total, the study found $699 million was awarded to "red flag" suppliers, or those that qualify as Indigenous 
under current federal rules but, according to the study, seem to offer little to no added value to a given government 
contract.
"It puts into question the effectiveness of PSIB in bringing dollars to Indigenous peoples," said Noah Fry, a 
postdoctoral fellow in political science at Dalhousie University and the study's author.
"They (the government) is going to come up with figures saying they've awarded billions of dollars to Indigenous 
peoples and firms, and the reality is a lot of those dollars aren't going to Indigenous peoples and firms."
The study, published online at the end of February, puts a dollar figure on an issue thrust into the spotlight during 
the ArriveCan scandal and the ensuing federal hearings and reports( https://ottawacitizen.com/news/a-scramble-
and-scrutiny-of-the-public-service-not-seen-in-more-than-20-years ) released in the aftermath.
ArriveCAN scandal raised questions about procurement
The PSIB is meant to increase the number of federal contracts awarded to Indigenous-owned and -operated 
businesses.
The strategy has been around in some form since 1996, but government spending under the PSIB has increased 
substantially since 2021, when then prime minister Justin Trudeau's government set a target that would see five 
per cent of total federal procurement spending go to Indigenous businesses.
"Under the Trudeau government, they ramped up the ambition of the strategy," Fry said. "It has been ramping up to 
include more and more departments."
Page 2 of 5
$699M has gone to 'red flag' suppliers under federal Indigenous procurement strategy: study
Progress toward the five per cent target is achieved through "set-asides," or restrictions on some federal contracts 
that limit competition to Indigenous suppliers. Suppliers are required to be at least 51 per cent Indigenous owned 
and conduct at least 33 per cent of the total value of work performed on the contract.
The approach came under scrutiny during the ArriveCAN scandal, a series of revelations over the mismanaged 
procurement process( https://ottawacitizen.com/opinion/boots-and-clarke-arrivecan-mess-should-drive-deeper-
reforms-in-government-contracting ) behind an app developed during the COVID-19 pandemic to help travellers 
share their vaccination status before entering the country.
The fallout led to scrutiny of Dalian Enterprises, an Indigenous IT firm awarded several set-asides for work on the 
app.
Dalian, which was part of a joint venture with a non-Indigenous firm, received nearly $8 million in federal 
procurement value while subcontracting the work to other non-Indigenous firms.
Several Indigenous organizations have voiced concerns both at parliamentary committees and in the media about 
potential abuses of the system.
Dawn Madahbee Leach, member of the First Nation Procurement Authority (FNPA) board, said Fry's study points to 
a "major problem."
Using two government datasets - the Indigenous Business Directory (IBD) and a government database for proactive 
disclosure of government contracts - Fry searched for businesses with a similar setup to Dalian.
'Red flag suppliers'
By combing the databases for organizations with "no evident added value to their work as suppliers beyond 
contract management," Fry flagged 44 distinct organizations representing 1,192 contracts worth up to $839 million.
The contracts he included date back to 2014, though most were awarded after 2021 when the "ambition" of the 
strategy started to grow, Fry said.
Fry labelled 26 of the 44 firms as "red flag suppliers" that "often have no products, limited internal capacity (i.e. 
staff) to deliver the contracts they receive, and vague company descriptions." Many of these firms were IT 
suppliers, Fry found.
While these firms illustrate government loopholes, Fry stressed that they work within legal parameters.
"Nothing in this research note suggests that these groups are conducting immoral or illicit work," Fry wrote.
In one example, the study cited Adirondack Information, which was listed as receiving contracts worth up to a total 
of $220 million and had just four employees, according to the IBD. The consulting firm had several contracts with a 
non-Indigenous businesses, according to the study.
Adirondack Information's website said that it was "a pre-approved vendor to the Federal Government [... that] has 
access to a variety of Aboriginal set-aside and non-Aboriginal procurement vehicles."
Adirondack Information did not respond to requests for comment.
In another example, Tato Recruiting - an Indigenous-owned IT professional services firm - was listed as the primary 
contractor for up to 33 contracts worth $42.9 million, despite having one staff member, according to the IBD.
According to the study, 30 of those contracts were joint ventures with S.i. Systems, a non-Indigenous IT company 
with a workforce large enough it lists 14 vice-presidents on its website.
"Contracts may not be going to Indigenous people at all because they don't have the in-house capacity to do those 
contracts," Fry said.
Page 3 of 5
$699M has gone to 'red flag' suppliers under federal Indigenous procurement strategy: study
Reached by the Ottawa Citizen for comment, president of Tato Recruiting John Beaupré said he is a proud First 
Nation entrepreneur and member of Timiskaming First Nation, with more than 15 years of experience in industry 
and strong ties to his community.
"I am aware of the study in question which has significant factual inaccuracies and many of its assertions are 
patently false. I will note that at no time was I ever contacted for comment or fact-checking prior to publication," he 
said.
"Tato Recruiting has already returned more than $200,000 to Indigenous communities through direct support and 
community initiatives, from supporting youth sports teams and friendship centers to funding academic 
scholarships."
Beaupré added that the majority of Tato Recruiting's team is Indigenous.
"Tato Recruiting has followed all rules and regulations of the Procurement for Indigenous Business Strategy 
(PSIB)... This has been confirmed through government audits, as well as most recently through an Indigenous 
Business Directory audit," he said.
Beaupré said the study is based on an "erroneous conception of how the industry operates," and that firms in the 
space provide significant value beyond contract management. Further, he said Tato is a "staffing firm" and not a 
recruiting agency, as the study suggested. The company, he said, conducts its own recruiting and in cases where it 
works with third parties, they are Indigenous partners.
An organization called Setaside Solutions was another example cited in Fry's research. The study said that the 
business management consultancy was named to five contracts worth up to a total of $519,043, and it had just 
three listed employees, according to its IBD registration.
Setaside Solutions did not respond to a request for comment.
Indigenous firms, suppliers not to blame, researcher says
Fry emphasized that nothing in his research suggested these Indigenous firms or suppliers are to blame.
Instead, he said, the federal government "has created a procurement landscape in which departments (and) 
procuring officers are incentivized to flag firms and suppliers as Indigenous without much consideration to whether 
those dollars are going to Indigenous people at all."
In an email, Indigenous Services Canada spokesperson Anispiragas Piragasanathar said safeguards are in place, 
such as ensuring businesses listed in the IBD are at least 51 per cent Indigenous-owned and have Indigenous 
partners who are actively involved in strategic and operational decision-making and receive financial benefits 
proportional to their ownership and role.
In 2025, the department strengthened the integrity of the directory by standardizing internal processes and audits, 
enhancing training materials and strengthening verification guidelines for staff, Piragasanathar said.
He also pointed to a federal government webpage( https://www.sac-isc.gc.ca/eng/1746637262900/1746637283564 
), which aims to "set the record straight, dispelling common misconceptions" about the PSIB and defends the 
strategy as an effective way to create fair and equitable opportunities for Indigenous businesses.
"PSIB reduces barriers, advances reconciliation, and supports the growth of Indigenous businesses," the website 
reads.
"In 2023-24, the Government of Canada awarded over $1.24 billion in contracts to Indigenous businesses, 
surpassing the 5% minimum target and representing 6.1% of all eligible government contracts, of which about 40% 
were awarded through set-aside opportunities specific to Indigenous businesses under the PSIB."
Page 4 of 5
$699M has gone to 'red flag' suppliers under federal Indigenous procurement strategy: study
Responding to a follow-up question, another spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada Jacinthe Goulet said 
the study "appears to make conclusions" that do not fully reflect policies and practices under the PSIB.
Goulet said most PSIB contracts are competitively tendered and awarded to firms delivering needed services.
"As well, business eligibility to be listed on the Indigenous Business Directory and/or capacity to participate in PSIB 
contracts cannot be judged solely from publicly available information," she said.
The government said it is working to transfer administration of the IBD to an Indigenous organization to allow 
Indigenous peoples to set their own criteria for which businesses qualify.
Indigenous organization says study points to 'major problem'
The task of developing an Indigenous-led national First Nations business directory will fall to the First Nation 
Procurement Authority (FNPA), established by the Assembly of First Nations.
Madahbee Leach is a board member.
"It concerns me that some opportunities may be taken by others who aren't experienced or are using non-
Indigenous suppliers to meet the need when we do have Indigenous suppliers able and ready and willing to take on 
some of these contracts," said Madahbee Leach, who has worked for nearly 40 years on financing Indigenous 
businesses.
"I think there's a lot of opportunities that legitimate Indigenous businesses are missing when we don't have the 
proper requirements in place."
Dawn Madahbee Leach, member of the First Nations Procurement Authority board.
Madahbee Leach said she favours a system that would verify whether applicants have the necessary credentials to 
carry out the work for the contract on offer.
"If it's a mechanic's garage, they have to have the mechanic's licence," she said. "We always have to make sure 
that the individual has the expertise and the credentials... We've brought that into the Indigenous business 
directory, too."
Madahbee Leach said any issues occurring in public contracting are likely found in the private sector, too.
"There's lost opportunity in the private sector as well," she said.
And Canada isn't the only place grappling with the problem, Fry said, listing Australia as another country with an 
Indigenous procurement target and similar loopholes.
"If you don't design the program right, then what's going to happen is you're going to have these firms who are 
effectively using the program to further the ends of those who have long been advantaged by public procurement 
anyway," he said.

title: 'Gabie Renaud' law would let Quebecers see police files on intimate partners
body:
Québec solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal hugs Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette, centre, after the 
government and Quebec Deputy premier and Minister of Internal Security Ian Lafrenière tabled legislation to 
protect women from intimate partner violence on Wednesday, May 13, 2026. The Canadian Press (Credit: Jacques 
Boissinot)
The new Fréchette government tabled a bill on Wednesday that would allow someone to find out from police if a 
current or former intimate partner has a documented history of violent or abusive behaviour.
The main purpose of the bill, introduced by Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière, is "to allow the 
communication of information concerning an intimate partner who could pose a risk to the safety of the person or 
the person's child."
It allows a victim to be informed of conditions attached to monitoring imposed as part of a release order, a probation 
order with supervision or a conditional prison sentence, and to know the area where the offender resides.
The bill is inspired by Clare's Law( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare%27s_Law ), implemented in the United 
Kingdom in 2014 and named for a woman killed by an ex-boyfriend known by police to be dangerous. Several 
Canadian provinces have since adopted similar laws.
In April, acoalition of women led by Québec solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal, called on the government to take 
concrete action to prevent future femicides( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/act-for-the-next-
woman-who-is-still-alive-coalition-calls-on-premier-frechette-to-address-rise-in-femicides/ ). Quebec Premier 
Christine Fréchette asked Lafrenière to present a Quebec version( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-
news/provincial-politics/analysis-frechette-tries-to-breathe-life-into-an-old-government-will-it-fly-with-voters/ ).
Jacques Boissinot / The Canadian PressQuébec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal hugs Quebec Premier 
Christine Fréchette, centre, after the government and Quebec deputy premier and Minister of Internal Security Ian 
Lafrenière tabled legislation to protect women from intimate partner violence on Wednesday, May 13, 2026.
Although anyone can experience intimate partner violence, victims are generally women, the government noted in 
its announcement: In 2024, 76 per cent were women. In 2025, Statistics Canada reported a sharp increase in 
femicide( https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/251202/dq251202a-eng.htm )by a former or current 
intimate partner: 81 in 2024, up from 53 in 2023. There have been 10 suspected femicides in Quebec since the 
beginning of 2026.
Page 2 of 4
'Gabie Renaud' law would let Quebecers see police files on intimate partners
The coalition had wanted the law named for Gabie Renaud, the 43-year-old victim of a suspected femicide who was 
found dead in her St-Jerôme apartment last September, the province's 12th suspected femicide that year. Jonathan 
Blanchet, who had at least six convictions related to conjugal violence, was arrested and charged with first-degree 
murder.
At a press conference following the tabling of the bill, Martine Biron, minister responsible for the status of women, 
said Gabie Renaud represents many women and "the law will not be personalized. There are so many victims."
But at an emotional press briefing held by women who had campaigned for the law, they called it the Gabie Renaud 
law.
Ghazal called "a Gabie Renaud law is truly a concrete and real way to assure that woman are protected" and that 
there is not another femicide.
"Behind the word femicide there is a woman, a mother, a sister, a daughter, a friend, an entire family - destroyed," 
said Gabie Renaud's sister, Rachel Renaud. "There are children who will grow up without their mother. There are 
birthdays that will never again be celebrated the same way. There are chairs which will alway be empty."
"We will remember her forever. And she's helping other women with a law with her name on," she said.
She said the law represents a possibility "of preventing, a possibility of protecting, a possibility of saving lives. ... 
The Gabie Renaud law will allow women to better know a partner's violent background and to make informed 
decisions for their safety."
She said she hoped the Coalition Avenir Québéc and opposition parties set aside partisan lines and the bill is 
passed into law before the National Assembly breaks for the summer "because the safety of women should never 
be a political issue."
Under the new law, information shared would involve intelligence gathered by police: 911 calls, complaints or police 
reports about violence, Lafrenière said at the press conference. A theft reported 20 years ago would not be 
included, but information about fraud involving intimate partners could be shared, he said. He said priority would be 
given to files referred by police or emergency shelters.
Once the information is provided to the person who requested it, that person will also be offered personalized 
support and directed to appropriate resources as needed, Lafrenière said: The goal is to provide all the necessary 
tools for people to make an informed decision about their relationship, not to be judgmental or to impose a decision 
on them, he said.
Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette acknowledged that giving someone information police have of an intimate 
partner's criminal antecedents violates that individual's right to privacy but, in this case, he said, it is justified.
The work of the S&;#151;reté du Québec will be to gather the relevant factual information, which will be sent in turn 
to women's organizations, Biron said.
"We will designate some organizations, which will do the analysis of the factual information and then meet with a 
potential victim and then do follow-up. The police work is centralized and it is factual work, but the analysis and 
meeting with the partner will be left to women's organizations."
The bill is intended as an additional mechanism to complement measures already in place to combat femicide and 
intimate partner violence in Quebec - "a supplementary tool," she said.
She said programs implemented to help victims of intimate partner violence have "saved many lives."
These measures include personnel specializing in conjugal and sexual violence being added to police forces and 
anti-proximity bracelets, and electronic geolocation devices used to prevent a person accused or convicted of an 
Page 3 of 4
'Gabie Renaud' law would let Quebecers see police files on intimate partners
offence related to conjugal violence or sexual abuse from approaching the victim; since 2021, 1,500 of these 
bracelets have been used.
Jolin-Barrette said there have been more than 100,000 free consultations with the Rebâtir line, a specialized legal 
advice service in Quebec for victims of sexual or domestic violence that provides up to four hours of free 
consultation with a lawyer for victims to discuss legal issues related to the violence they have experienced.
Rapid intervention units and crisis units to assist victims of conjugal violence have been introduced all over 
Quebec; funding has been increased to emergency shelters, 21 second-stage shelters have been opened, and 
emergency financial assistance has been provided to quickly relocate victims of sexual or conjugal violence who 
wish to leave a dangerous environment, said Biron.
But for all services available to victims, distressingly, she said none of the victims of the 10 suspected femicides in 
Quebec this year had reached out to organizations available to help victims of intimate partner violence.
Intimate partner violence is complicated, said Biron: It is known that, on average, a victim leaves a toxic relationship 
seven times before staying away for good, she said.
It is encouraging to note, however, that younger women are coming to emergency shelters and that the subject is 
being discussed among friends who pressure victims to leave, Biron said.
Said Jolin-Barrette: "If this new law prevents even one tragedy, it will be a victory."

communication of information concerning an intimate partner who could pose a risk to the safety of the person or 
the person's child."
It allows a victim to be informed of conditions attached to monitoring imposed as part of a release order, a probation 
order with supervision or a conditional prison sentence, and to know the area where the offender resides.
The bill is inspired by Clare's Law( https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clare%27s_Law ), implemented in the United 
Kingdom in 2014 and named for a woman killed by an ex-boyfriend known by police to be dangerous. Several 
Canadian provinces have since adopted similar laws.
In April, acoalition of women led by Québec solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal, called on the government to take 
concrete action to prevent future femicides( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/act-for-the-next-
woman-who-is-still-alive-coalition-calls-on-premier-frechette-to-address-rise-in-femicides/ ). Quebec Premier 
Christine Fréchette asked Lafrenière to present a Quebec version( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-
news/provincial-politics/analysis-frechette-tries-to-breathe-life-into-an-old-government-will-it-fly-with-voters/ ).
Jacques Boissinot / The Canadian PressQuébec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal hugs Quebec Premier 
Christine Fréchette, centre, after the government and Quebec deputy premier and Minister of Internal Security Ian 
Lafrenière tabled legislation to protect women from intimate partner violence on Wednesday, May 13, 2026.
Although anyone can experience intimate partner violence, victims are generally women, the government noted in 
its announcement: In 2024, 76 per cent were women. In 2025, Statistics Canada reported a sharp increase in 
femicide( https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/251202/dq251202a-eng.htm )by a former or current 
intimate partner: 81 in 2024, up from 53 in 2023. There have been 10 suspected femicides in Quebec since the 
beginning of 2026.
Page 2 of 4
'Gabie Renaud' law would let Quebecers see police files on intimate partners
The coalition had wanted the law named for Gabie Renaud, the 43-year-old victim of a suspected femicide who was 
found dead in her St-Jerôme apartment last September, the province's 12th suspected femicide that year. Jonathan 
Blanchet, who had at least six convictions related to conjugal violence, was arrested and charged with first-degree 
murder.
At a press conference following the tabling of the bill, Martine Biron, minister responsible for the status of women, 
said Gabie Renaud represents many women and "the law will not be personalized. There are so many victims."
But at an emotional press briefing held by women who had campaigned for the law, they called it the Gabie Renaud 
law.
Ghazal called "a Gabie Renaud law is truly a concrete and real way to assure that woman are protected" and that 
there is not another femicide.
"Behind the word femicide there is a woman, a mother, a sister, a daughter, a friend, an entire family - destroyed," 
said Gabie Renaud's sister, Rachel Renaud. "There are children who will grow up without their mother. There are 
birthdays that will never again be celebrated the same way. There are chairs which will alway be empty."
"We will remember her forever. And she's helping other women with a law with her name on," she said.
She said the law represents a possibility "of preventing, a possibility of protecting, a possibility of saving lives. ... 
The Gabie Renaud law will allow women to better know a partner's violent background and to make informed 
decisions for their safety."
She said she hoped the Coalition Avenir Québéc and opposition parties set aside partisan lines and the bill is 
passed into law before the National Assembly breaks for the summer "because the safety of women should never 
be a political issue."
Under the new law, information shared would involve intelligence gathered by police: 911 calls, complaints or police 
reports about violence, Lafrenière said at the press conference. A theft reported 20 years ago would not be 
included, but information about fraud involving intimate partners could be shared, he said. He said priority would be 
given to files referred by police or emergency shelters.
Once the information is provided to the person who requested it, that person will also be offered personalized 
support and directed to appropriate resources as needed, Lafrenière said: The goal is to provide all the necessary 
tools for people to make an informed decision about their relationship, not to be judgmental or to impose a decision 
on them, he said.
Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette acknowledged that giving someone information police have of an intimate 
partner's criminal antecedents violates that individual's right to privacy but, in this case, he said, it is justified.
The work of the S&;#151;reté du Québec will be to gather the relevant factual information, which will be sent in turn 
to women's organizations, Biron said.
"We will designate some organizations, which will do the analysis of the factual information and then meet with a 
potential victim and then do follow-up. The police work is centralized and it is factual work, but the analysis and 
meeting with the partner will be left to women's organizations."
The bill is intended as an additional mechanism to complement measures already in place to combat femicide and 
intimate partner violence in Quebec - "a supplementary tool," she said.
She said programs implemented to help victims of intimate partner violence have "saved many lives."
These measures include personnel specializing in conjugal and sexual violence being added to police forces and 
anti-proximity bracelets, and electronic geolocation devices used to prevent a person accused or convicted of an 
Page 3 of 4
'Gabie Renaud' law would let Quebecers see police files on intimate partners
offence related to conjugal violence or sexual abuse from approaching the victim; since 2021, 1,500 of these 
bracelets have been used.
Jolin-Barrette said there have been more than 100,000 free consultations with the Rebâtir line, a specialized legal 
advice service in Quebec for victims of sexual or domestic violence that provides up to four hours of free 
consultation with a lawyer for victims to discuss legal issues related to the violence they have experienced.
Rapid intervention units and crisis units to assist victims of conjugal violence have been introduced all over 
Quebec; funding has been increased to emergency shelters, 21 second-stage shelters have been opened, and 
emergency financial assistance has been provided to quickly relocate victims of sexual or conjugal violence who 
wish to leave a dangerous environment, said Biron.
But for all services available to victims, distressingly, she said none of the victims of the 10 suspected femicides in 
Quebec this year had reached out to organizations available to help victims of intimate partner violence.
Intimate partner violence is complicated, said Biron: It is known that, on average, a victim leaves a toxic relationship 
seven times before staying away for good, she said.
It is encouraging to note, however, that younger women are coming to emergency shelters and that the subject is 
being discussed among friends who pressure victims to leave, Biron said.
Said Jolin-Barrette: "If this new law prevents even one tragedy, it will be a victory."

title: 'Ghost agents' add to visa challenges Unauthorized actors profit from immigration processing delays, contribute
body:
After a two-week vacation back home in China, Amber was ready to return to work as a management consultant in 
Canada. But she didn't realize her work visa had expired until she was refused boarding for her flight.
What the Toronto resident did next would land her in a Canadian government dragnet. 
Officials were pursuing people using the services of unauthorized agents, who profit from immigration processing 
delays and play a part in the Federal Court's growing backlog. 
Amber, a former international student on a postgraduation work permit, submitted a new work visa application from 
China in 2024. After five weeks of waiting, still without the document to come back to Canada, she looked to the 
popular Chinese e-commerce platform, Xiaohongshu or Little Red Book, for advice.
There she found someone purporting to be a lawyer, advertising that he could help "force" Immigration to speed up 
visa processing for applicants. 
Anxious that she'd lose her job over prolonged unpaid leave, she e-transferred $600 for the service to prepare what 
she later learned is known as a mandamus application in court. (Court can order government officials to process 
immigration files that are unreasonably delayed.)
Amber said the scramble in 2024 was far from her mind until recently, when she found herself caught in a legal 
quagmire with 430 immigration applicants.
 It involves Chinese applicants who have applied for study, work or visitor permits; they all had asked the court to 
review the processing delays of their files and to order Ottawa to fast-track the application.
The Department of Justice accused them of misrepresentation by using unauthorized representatives to prepare 
their court applications. 
These applications were flagged because they all had "similar format, style and phrasing," and shared the same 
home addresses, phone numbers and email accounts, despite the applicants claiming to have self-represented. It 
has also asked the court to order these applicants to pay $720 to the government in costs.
Page 2 of 3
'Ghost agents' add to visa challenges Unauthorized actors profit from immigration processing delays, contribute 
to growing backlog
The use of unscrupulous "ghost agents" has posed an ongoing challenge for immigration officials and legal 
profession regulators because they operate behind the scenes and cannot be held accountable. Their 
incompetence can also lead to dire consequences for applicants and abuse of the immigration and legal systems.
Amber, who asked that her full name not be published for fear of repercussions, said newcomers are unfamiliar with 
the Canadian judicial system and she had no idea it's unlawful to hire an unauthorized representative to submit 
court applications.
"I personally didn't think what this guy did was a problem," recalled a confused Amber. "My visa was approved 
within 48 hours after he submitted the mandamus. I actually wrote him and thanked him because I was grateful. He 
provided a valuable service. I'm sure none of the 430 people knew what a mandamus was."
Amber said she sought help for her visa application out of desperation because the processing time had already 
surpassed what was listed on the Immigration Department website.
She had called the immigration hotline from abroad multiple times, but the line was cut off after she followed 
through the lengthy menu. 
Her local MP could only provide her updates on the status of the visa and was unable to push for her case.
"The root of the problem is really about immigration processing times, right?" said Amber. "It's not just processing 
times but also the lack of transparency and communication from immigration officials. It's like a black box. No one 
can tell you what has happened to your application and what's holding it up." 
In its motion to dismiss the 430 mandamus applications - many with visas still pending - the government argued it's 
the "most expeditious and economical resolution" as the court struggles with a growing backlog and wait time for 
hearings.
Immigration-related cases make up the majority of the workload of the Federal Court, which has seen a surge in 
new immigration proceedings in recent years, from 7,782 in 2019 to 24,667 in 2024. It already reached 21,581 in 
the first nine months of 2025. And the wait time for a hearing just keeps growing.
John, another visa applicant flagged in the case, said he didn't get a response for his visitor visa application for over 
a year and was referred to the same agent through word of mouth.
 He provided his immigration client number, official name and visa application details - without a contract or ever 
meeting or speaking with the agent. He received his visas two months after the agent submitted the mandamus in 
2024.
John, a Chinese national studying in the U.S., said the agent's account on Little Red Book has recently removed 
the language that promoted "quicker Canadian visa processing." Instead of submitting court files on clients' behalf, 
the agent now provides applicants step-by-step instructions and a template to file mandamus themselves, he said. 
By law, a person can only self-represent or be represented before the Federal Court by a licensed lawyer or 
authorized individual. Others cannot represent them or even provide legal advice in the judicial process. 
Like Amber, John said people go to these agents because the system is inaccessible. He said officials should 
promote the importance of using authorized representatives if they want to crack down on these unlawful practices. 
Both the Immigration Department and the Federal Court have webpages about the rules on legal representation. 
But applicants would need to recognize it as an issue to search the information, and neither Amber nor John did.
"I'm equally upset with the Immigration Department of Canada and with this agent," said John, who asked that his 
full name not be published. "Canada had my visa application for so long and I paid someone to help me. It doesn't 
make sense Immigration is going after us and not the agent."
Page 3 of 3
'Ghost agents' add to visa challenges Unauthorized actors profit from immigration processing delays, contribute 
to growing backlog
The Immigration Department urges applicants to use its official website for program information to avoid becoming 
victims of fraud or scams, adding that its "Protect yourself from immigration fraud" webpage is meant to raise 
public awareness.
"The best way to protect the public from fraud is to inform the public, and this information is regularly promoted on 
our social media platforms," the department said.
The Star has contacted the agent by email and phone, but did not receive a response.

title: 'Gross mismanagement' and other cases of wrongdoing found at Immigration department, report says
body:
An executive engaging in "gross mismanagement" by giving preferential treatment to a romantic partner, another 
executive attempting to hire a niece and an employee holding down another full-time job in the public service.
Those are among the cases of misconduct and wrongdoing found at Immigration, Citizenship and Refugee 
Canada( https://ottawacitizen.com/tag/citizenship-and-immigration-canada/ ) (IRCC), which is the latest 
department( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/ircc-will-collect-data-to-enforce-return-to-office-rules ) to 
publish their report on misconduct and wrongdoing for the 2024-2025 fiscal year.
The cases ranged from the innocuous such as calling in sick to attend a conference, to blogging as a self-identified 
Canadian diplomat where they expressed political views and "discussed aspects of their work at the embassy, 
including private conversations with embassy staff and views on the country's people and government."
Some other founded cases include cases of racism, sexual harassment, claiming overtime not worked and an 
employees providing false references in a staffing process that led to an acting opportunity elsewhere in 
governments
In total, IRCC said it had 105 cases of misconduct and wrongdoing within the department leading to a handful of 
terminations.
There one founded case of fraud and financial misconduct at IRCC; 22 cases of harassment, violence and 
disrespectful behaviours; and eight breaches of values and ethics codes.
There were also 56 cases of administrative misconduct, 13 violations of the department's directive on the use of 
networks and devices, two personnel security violations and three staffing complaints.
Three employees at IRCC lost their jobs, another was taken off of a staffing pool, while an executive voluntarily left 
the public service before disciplinary action could occur.
Dozens of other disciplinary measures at IRCC ranged from written reprimands to suspensions to forcing the 
recovery of funds to the federal government over time theft.
Ted Gallivan, deputy minister at IRCC, wrote at the beginning of the report that "some level" of wrongdoing will 
occur in an organization of more than 10,000 employees.
Page 2 of 3
'Gross mismanagement' and other cases of wrongdoing found at Immigration department, report says
"Reporting such matters is essential, as we are committed to reviewing all allegations of perceived misconduct or 
wrongdoing through thorough review and investigation, and to taking administrative action when warranted," 
Gallivan wrote.
In the report, Gallivan also says that IRCC established an ombuds office where employees can raise workplace 
concerns without fear of reprisal.
"The Ombuds Office supports employees in exploring options and navigating available resources to help resolve 
workplace issues," Gallivan added.
IRCC could not be immediately reached for comment.
In recent years, several departments have released misconduct and wrongdoing reports, aiming to increase 
transparency and accountability within federal departments.
Over the past year, Environment and Climate Change Canada, the Department of Justice, Transport Canada and 
other federal departments have published their inaugural reports on misconduct and wrongdoing.
Other departments publish misconduct and wrongdoing reports for 2024-2025
Earlier this year, Global Affiars Canada( https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/global-affairs-canada-pearson ) 
published their report on misconduct and wrongdoing for the 2024-2025 fiscal year that saw 120 cases resulting in 
disciplinary or administrative measures.
Wrongdoing accounts at the department included an employee's family member misuse a Crown-issued credit 
card, an employee using an employer credit card to buy personal plane tickets and sexual misconduct from an 
executive in one of Canada's missions abroad.
Several employees at GAC were terminated due to wrongdoing.
At the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), there were 259 founded cases of misconduct resulting in four 
terminations and 14 employees leaving the agency.
Instances of wrongdoing at the agency include associating with a known drug traffickers, driving a CBSA vehicle 
while intoxicated and hiring family members or friends.
The report says that incident of misconduct and wrongdoing at CBSA occurred in around 1.52 per cent of 
employees at the CBSA.
At Transport Canada, there were 58 founded cases of misconduct and wrongdoing. The bulk of cases were 
breaches to the code of professional conduct, making up 53 of the founded cases.
Some founded cases led to a resignation, including an employee who conducted personal business during work 
hours and used Transport Canada to travel to the location where the business activity occurred.
The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC) and Crown-Indigenous 
Relations and Northern Affairs Canada (CIRNAC) are among other departments and agencies who published 
2024-2025 misconduct and wrongdoing reports over the past several months.
The CRA had a total of 370 cases of founded misconduct including mishandling sensitive data.
Meanwhile, the IAAC had no cases of founded misconduct, and CIRNAC had only seven cases of founded 
misconduct, including submission of falsified medical documents to justify telework and misuse of a departmental 
travel card.

title: 'Henry's Law:' Saskatchewan strengthens carbon monoxide monitoring after boy's death
body:
REGINA - Saskatchewan is bolstering rules on carbon monoxide monitoring after an 11-year-old Regina boy was 
killed by the colourless, odourless gas.
Eric Schmalz, the government relations minister, says Henry Losco's December death in his family's apartment 
after a leak spurred the province to move quickly. 
"When someone passes away, you always have the thought of, 'What could we have done more?'" Schmalz told 
reporters Tuesday.
"I don't have a time machine. I don't have a way to go back and change this, but we can change it now."
He said starting Nov. 1, carbon monoxide alarms are to be required in all suites in multi-unit residential buildings. 
Previously, alarms only needed to be installed in areas around an appliance, such as a furnace. 
Schmalz said in honour of Losco and at the wishes of his family, the regulatory changes are to be called "Henry's 
Law."
Marina Hills, the boy's mother, was at the announcement. She said while nothing can ease the pain of his death, 
the changes will help protect other families.
"We want change. We want laws that help save people and families and children," she said. "This is exactly what 
my son would have wanted."
The parents were wearing green T-shirts with the wording #JusticeForHenryLosco. The minister embraced them 
after the conference.
Last month, Regina's fire department announced that a boiler malfunction caused the leak on Dec. 19.
Fire Chief Layne Jackson had told reporters there was a delayed ignition, causing the boiler to explode and blow 
apart venting equipment.

Page 2 of 3
'Henry's Law:' Saskatchewan strengthens carbon monoxide monitoring after boy's death
The manufacturer of the natural gas-fired boiler, Ariston Canada Inc., has since issued a safety notice for the 
model.
Hills has said she found the boy and her husband, Sergio Losco, unconscious in the downtown apartment in the 
evening. Henry was declared dead at the scene, and his father was treated in hospital.
The parents continue to have questions about why police weren't called earlier, Hills has said. She said alarms 
were ringing on the second floor in the afternoon but her husband didn't hear them on the fourth floor. 
Jackson has said some alarms in the building went off. He has declined to say when the boiler exploded or if 
anyone heard it, as those details remain under investigation.
The Technical Safety Authority of Saskatchewan, which is responsible for safety inspections, has said inspectors 
checked the boiler the day before the leak.
Police are also investigating.

killed by the colourless, odourless gas.
Eric Schmalz, the government relations minister, says Henry Losco's December death in his family's apartment 
after a leak spurred the province to move quickly. 
"When someone passes away, you always have the thought of, 'What could we have done more?'" Schmalz told 
reporters Tuesday.
"I don't have a time machine. I don't have a way to go back and change this, but we can change it now."
He said starting Nov. 1, carbon monoxide alarms are to be required in all suites in multi-unit residential buildings. 
Previously, alarms only needed to be installed in areas around an appliance, such as a furnace. 
Schmalz said in honour of Losco and at the wishes of his family, the regulatory changes are to be called "Henry's 
Law."
Marina Hills, the boy's mother, was at the announcement. She said while nothing can ease the pain of his death, 
the changes will help protect other families.
"We want change. We want laws that help save people and families and children," she said. "This is exactly what 
my son would have wanted."
The parents were wearing green T-shirts with the wording #JusticeForHenryLosco. The minister embraced them 
after the conference.
Last month, Regina's fire department announced that a boiler malfunction caused the leak on Dec. 19.
Fire Chief Layne Jackson had told reporters there was a delayed ignition, causing the boiler to explode and blow 
apart venting equipment.

title: 'I looked at the evidence very, very carefully' Engineer stands by testimony in cop's death, 'disturbed' with OPP
body:
A Toronto engineer is standing by his collision reconstruction report and trial testimony in the Umar Zameer murder 
case, despite a controversial Ontario Provincial Police report that claims to contradict his findings. 
"I looked at the evidence very, very carefully, before making my way into a courtroom two years ago," Barry Raftery 
said a day after the release of the OPP report that - in the words of Toronto police Chief Myron Demkiw - 
"exonerated" three officers of obstructing justice and perjury during the trial. 
Raftery's was one of two reconstruction reports presented at the trial that found Toronto Const. Jeffrey Northrup 
was on the ground and not visible to Zameer when the accountant ran over him in the parking garage below Nathan 
Phillips Square on July 2, 2021. 
The OPP's report contradicts the conclusions reached not only by Raftery - a defence witness at Zameer's trial - but 
also that of Toronto police Staff Sgt. Jeff Bassingthwaite, who was a prosecution witness, even though his 
reconstruction aligned with the defence.
Both Raftery and Bassingthwaite's reports were key evidence supporting the defence theory that Zameer did not 
knowingly drive into the officer.
 A jury found him not guilty of murder; soon after, Superior Court Justice Anne Mollow apologized to Zameer and 
made allegations that Det. Consts. Lisa Forbes, Scharnil Pais and Tony Correa had been dishonest.
On Wednesday, Raftery said he was "disappointed" and "disturbed" that the OPP - and Toronto Police Service - are 
saying he and Bassingthwaite got things wrong based on what he called unsupported assumptions about the 
evidence, including injury patterns, contact points on Zameer's BMW and Northrup's final resting position.
Bassingthwaite was "an honest cop, and he did something I think was probably difficult for him to do, in light of the 
fact it was a police officer who was killed," Raftery said. 
"To come clean and just call balls and strikes and say exactly how it was. I have a lot of respect for 
Bassingthwaite."
Page 2 of 3
'I looked at the evidence very, very carefully' Engineer stands by testimony in cop's death, 'disturbed' with OPP 
findings
Bassingthwaite, who now works with the Toronto police analytics and innovation division, could not immediately be 
reached for comment.
Also Wednesday, Premier Doug Ford suggested Molloy should apologize to three Toronto police officers for 
"accusing them of everything under the sun."
The OPP's reconstructionist, Det. Const. Mike Cooper, concluded that Northrup was standing in front of the BMW, 
which backed up the officers' testimony and, in part, led to the provincial service's conclusion that there was "no 
evidence" the trio committed a crime.
At a news conference at police headquarters on Tuesday, Demkiw urged the public to "read the report" to 
understand the OPP reconstructionist's opinions.
The OPP's report claims Raftery and Bassingthwaite both missed evidence, such as the BMW's collision sensors, 
which may have sounded an alert. (What difference would that make amid the shouting and panic, and with 
Zameer's son crying in the back seat, Raftery asked.)
Raftery, who has conducted hundreds of pedestrian/vehicle collision reconstructions over his 38-year career, noted 
the OPP report did not include Cooper's reasons for reaching his conclusions.
"They are a mystery to me," he said.
Raftery's comments come amid growing calls for an independent review.
"I just can't square the (OPP) report with what happened at that trial," said former Special Investigations Unit 
director Ian Scott, adding that the review effectively recasts Zameer's acquittal as a "wrongful" one.
The core dispute lies in the competing collision/reconstruction analyses - two tested in open court, the other 
produced behind closed doors.
"What I find completely stunning is the frontal attack on the Toronto Police Service's accident reconstructionist," he 
said.
He noted that during the Zameer trial, both the defence and Toronto police experts testified under oath and were 
cross-examined, while the OPP report includes only conclusions, with no full reconstruction report or opportunity to 
question its author. (The Star has requested the document from the OPP.)
"In my view, this cries out for a public inquiry," Scott said.
On Wednesday, Raftery reiterated what he says is the most persuasive physical evidence that the tall Northrup was 
not upright when he was hit: The absence of any evidence on the hood of Zameer's BMW - neither dents nor 
disturbances in the dust.
The OPP analysis "appears to be ignoring the fact there's no evidence of a 300-pound man striking the engine hood 
of that car," he said.
Veteran criminal defence lawyer Monte MacGregor dismissed the OPP report entirely, saying it re-evaluated the 
"factual underpinnings" of the case without any opportunity to question the authors on their findings.
"There's no forum now to test this report," he said, adding the issue of perjury should have been reviewed by 
independent assessors with experience in the criminal justice system, such as a retired judge.
He also noted it comes at a time when members of the Toronto police are under scrutiny for alleged corruption as 
part of the Project South investigation.
"It leaves a very sour taste as far as the administration of justice," he said.

title: 'I will give my all to Quebec': Fréchette says she knows she has work to do to regain confidence of voters
body:
Christine Fréchette speaks with fellow Coalition Avenir Québec leadership candidate Bernard Drainville after her 
victory in Drummondville on Sunday April 12, 2026. Montreal Gazette (Credit: John Mahoney)
QUEBEC - Premier-designate Christine Fréchette said Monday that she plans to act soon on her leadership 
campaign promise to lower or remove taxes from consumer items to ease the financial burden of Quebecers.
But Fréchette also said the government will resume work on its controversial plan to adopt a Quebec constitution( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/quebec-constitution-recognize-anglophone-rights/ ), insisting 
that she wants the bill to be adopted in the normal way and not with the rules of closure to shorten debate.
The question is whether it will be Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette who will continue to pilot the file. She 
refused to say whether he will remain in the post in her soon-to-be-formed cabinet.
In a wide-ranging news conference one day after being elected leader of the CAQ( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/quebecs-new-premier-will-be-chosen-today-at-caq-convention/ ) 
and Quebec's next premier, Fréchette said she is starting her term "with lots of humility and a profound sense of 
responsibility."
"I am well aware of the magnitude of the challenge," said Fréchette, standing alone in the lobby of the Honoré-
Mercier Building that houses the premier's offices.
"I know we have to regain confidence (from Quebecers). Confidence can't be decreed, it has to be earned, and it is 
earned with concrete actions."
But saying she wants to address Quebecers directly, Fréchette said she knows the cost of living and inflation are a 
heavy burden for many citizens.
"I want to find ways to help," Fréchette said. "We won't settle this with the wave of a magic wand. We will need a 
series of actions, different initiatives, and together they will help improve the situation of Quebecers."
Fréchette was no more specific on what measures she has in mind, urging reporters to be patient.
Page 2 of 4
'I will give my all to Quebec': Fréchette says she knows she has work to do to regain confidence of voters
She floated the plan during the 80-day leadership race, during which she also said she wanted to encourage new-
home purchases by dropping the welcome tax for first-time buyers.
"It is coming soon," Fréchette said with reference to the promises.
But Fréchette's first day was jammed with other activities, from a phone call with Prime Minister Mark Carney to a 
meeting with Quebec's top bureaucrat, secretary-general and clerk of the executive council, David Bahan.
She announced Bahan will be staying on in the same role.
There were a few other nuggets of information forthcoming. After a personal meeting Tuesday with outgoing 
Premier François Legault( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/provincial-politics/premier-legault-
steps-down-with-no-obvious-successor-in-the-wings/ ), Fréchette will be sworn in as Quebec's 33rd premier on 
Wednesday.
She will then hold a first meeting with her caucus and start the long, complicated process of forming her first 
cabinet. The cabinet is not expected to be revealed until next week.
At her news conference, she took a deep breath when it came to answering questions about the cabinet, describing 
the process, which most premiers hate, as the equivalent of "high wire acrobatics."
"We won't be able to have everyone in there," Fréchette warned, saying it will be smaller than the current 26 but still 
include parity between men and women as well as regional representation.
She said what matters more to her is competency than what was said during the recent acrimonious leadership 
campaign.
That comment comes as an olive branch to her opponent Bernard Drainville and his supporters. Moving forward, 
Fréchette has to soothe those MNAs to preserve caucus and party unity.
She got a piece of good news on that front when Drainville, who walked out of the convention in Drummondville on 
Sunday immediately after Fréchette's victory speech, rallied behind her on social media.
"The dust has started to settle after the race," Drainville said. "I want to highlight the victory of Christine Fréchette 
and assure her of my support. She will be a rigorous and determined premier who will move Quebec forward.
"Christine and I have spoken in the last few hours and have agreed to speak again today."
The two did have a meeting later Monday evening in Quebec City.
During the leadership race, Fréchette promised Drainville, the former environment minister, an important role in her 
government should she win.
But on several other questions, such as how she will act to reconnect with an estranged English-speaking 
community( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/provincial-politics/christine-frechette-launches-caq-
leadership-bid-reaches-out-to-anglos/ ), Fréchette said she has not yet decided how to proceed.
Of her call with Carney, Fréchette said the prime minister expressed renewed interest in helping Quebec and 
Newfoundland and Labrador move forward on the Churchill Falls( https://montrealgazette.com/news/legault-wants-
ottawa-to-pay-for-power-line-from-churchill-falls/ ) agreement brokered by Legault in 2024.
"I know that the federal government would prefer that this agreement be signed between Quebec and 
Newfoundland and Labrador," Fréchette said. "I felt an interest from Mr. Carney. I think it's important for the energy 
security of Canada."
Fréchette will also need to make decisions on the kind of legislative agenda she wants to set. Last week, the 
Quebec cabinet prorogued the legislature until May 5, leaving about a dozen bills in limbo.
Page 3 of 4
'I will give my all to Quebec': Fréchette says she knows she has work to do to regain confidence of voters
On Monday, she said Bill 1, creating a Quebec constitution, would proceed normally through the legislative 
process. The bill is currently bogged down at the committee stage for clause-by-clause examination.
"I invite the parliamentarians to pursue their work in the hope the work will be finished by the end of the session 
(June 12)," Fréchette said.
Asked if she would use the rules of closure to suspend the regular adoption rules and adopt the bill despite the 
objections of the opposition, Fréchette said no.
"For me, it's a text that should have a certain level of support," she said. "For me, closure is not a means to use on 
the constitution."
The news conference capped a long day for Fréchette, which started in a pastry shop in her hometown of Trois-
Rivières, where she launched her campaign for the CAQ leadership in January.
"I will give my all to Quebec, and it will start by uniting this beautiful party," Fréchette told reporters waiting for her.
In the meantime, the Parti Québécois on Monday moved to try to woo any Quebec nationalists who were in the 
CAQ and are unhappy with Fréchette's victory.
The party published full-page ads in some media outlets encouraging disgruntled CAQ nationalists to move to the 
PQ.
The headline on the ads read: "Nationalists, welcome to your party."
"While the third way (of the CAQ) has shown its limits and the Liberals seek to bring us back in time on issues of 
laicity, the protection of French, immigration and the fight against corruption, our door is wide open," said the 
message signed by PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

title: 'I will not be running' After months of mulling, John Tory opts out of mayor's race
body:
John Tory shook up the Toronto mayoral race on Tuesday, but not in the way many had expected.
After months of speculation that the politician who resigned abruptly from the city's highest office three years ago 
was planning a comeback bid this fall - and an acknowledgement from the man himself he was mulling a run - Tory 
announced he has decided not to enter the race.
In a surprise statement, Tory said he was proud of his record as mayor and thanked "all of those who have been 
urging me to run again." He acknowledged he gave another campaign "serious consideration" but ultimately 
decided: "I will not be running."
His decision, first reported by the Star shortly before he made it official, reshapes what had been expected to be a 
heavyweight electoral bout this year between the current mayor and her predecessor, and potentially leaves the 
door open for another high-profile centre-right challenger to take on progressive Mayor Olivia Chow.
Chow, who won the June 2023 byelection to replace Tory, has yet to announce her political intentions, but she's 
expected to contest the Oct. 26, 2026 vote.
Coun. Brad Bradford (Beaches-East York) has already declared he intends to run.
The 71-year-old Tory said he arrived at his choice not because he lacked "the energy or the desire" to seek office, 
but because of the toll a potentially punishing campaign would take on those close to him.
"I feel I cannot put my family and the people I care about through the inevitable attacks on me and my personal life 
that we've started to see before I've even announced my intentions," Tory said in his statement.
The popular former chief magistrate quit just months into his third term in February 2023 after the Star revealed he 
had a relationship with a woman who had worked in his office. The city integrity commissioner later found that Tory 
broke ethics rules in his handling of his affair with the staffer, who was 31 when Tory quit. Speaking on Newstalk 
1010 on Tuesday, Tory said he still has "a relationship" with the woman.
Although his statement didn't specify which attacks he was referring to, amid rumours of his potential resurgence

title: 'Revolving door' of insiders, lobbyists behind government scandal a click away with new AI tool
body:
OTTAWA - The new frontier of government accountability could be a colourful AI-generated image connecting the 
dots between all the different players in one of Canada's messiest procurement controversies.
The Phoenix pay system, which was designed to centralize payroll for the federal government but quickly racked up 
a long list of issues including overpayments, underpayments and missed payments, is estimated to have cost 
nearly $5 billion. The replacement software is now estimated to cost more than $4 billion, putting the total price tag 
of the calamity at nearly $10 billion, according to Auditor General Karen Hogan last week( 
https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/phoenix-pay-system-errors-dayforce ).
Now, using the government's lobbying registry, auditor general reports, media stories and government press 
releases, a new interactive website is drawing a vivid picture( https://idiom-bytes.github.io/canada-central-
plots/dayforce-phoenix.html ) of the complicated and frenzied lobbying activity beneath the surface of big-money 
government contracts. And the code can be used to generate a similar map of any government contract or program.
For example, click on the "revolving door" button on the "Dayforce × Phoenix Pay System - Lobbying &; 
Relationship Map" and you'll find people who have moved from government work to related private sector 
employment. The website highlights Gianluca Cairo, the former chief of staff to the federal innovation minister, who 
was in government while the Phoenix fiasco played out. He then joined Ceridian HCM Holding Inc. which was then 
one of the leading bidders to replace the pay system. In the end, Ceridian's Dayforce software won the contract and 
the federal ethics commissioner cleared Cairo's move, as long as as he obeyed ethics rules around lobbying the 
government in his new role.
When Cairo was hired by Ceridian, the Globe and Mail wrote that it was part of the company's( 
https://www.theglobeandmail.com/business/article-innovation-ministers-chief-of-staff-leaving-post-to-join-ceridian-
as/ ) "charm offensive in the past two years to make inroads in Ottawa."
Also in the "revolving door" tab of the website is Regan Watts, a former Conservative government staffer who 
logged a series of entries in the lobbying registry for Dayforce. None of the players identified on the website are 
alleged to have broken any ethics rules.
In a written response to National Post, Watts said the website is "demonstrably inaccurate and lacks even basic 
context." The tool "creates the illusion of insight while getting the fundamentals wrong. The reality is the 
Page 2 of 4
'Revolving door' of insiders, lobbyists behind government scandal a click away with new AI tool
organizations I work with see results and governments are better informed, making wiser choices as a 
consequence," he wrote.
Cairo did not respond to a request for comment.
But the AI mapping earned rave reviews from government ethics specialist Ian Stedman, a York University 
professor who previously worked for the Integrity Commissioner of Ontario.
Tools like that can help ethics commissioners across the country explain complex reports in an easy-to-visualize 
format and helps Canadians better understand the connections between people, organizations and public 
contracts, he said.
"This mapping of the characters based on official documents and official reports is absolutely brilliant. It's the kind of 
thing that commissioners ought to be doing with every one of these files for sure," said Stedman.
"This visualization of the connections, and the justification and the sources... this should be released with every 
report about conflicts of interest... to make it interactive and digestible and visual," he added.
In the case of the Phoenix pay system debacle, the web of players and their connections revealed by the AI-
generated tool shows just how complex these networks are.
"Like this revolving door, the relationships, the fact that it's one (jumping from one) company to the next, this shows 
you that it isn't easy to just have a surface level understanding and pick up on how many close relationships there 
are," he explained.
To promote transparency, government watchdogs need to ensure the data they publish are searchable, sortable 
and downloadable, so that the public and journalists can easily compile and parse the data, Stedman said.
The ethics specialist also said government watchdogs can and should adopt AI tools to help facilitate their 
compliance efforts, such as to verify a public office holder's compliance with a conflict of ethics screen.
Already in 2018, well before large-language models such as ChatGPT and Claude revolutionized coding, then 
federal ethics commissioner Mario Dion also saw the potential for AI-driven tools to facilitate his office's work.
Speaking at York University, Dion argued that artificial intelligence could help develop an "electronic oversight tool" 
that would catch compliance red flags faster and automatically.
That would allow his office to catch potential conflicts of interest before they happen, or address them immediately 
so they don't become chronic.
"One day a system could be developed that contains data not only on public office holders and members, such as 
their assets and liabilities, but also on the official decisions they are making or have made. The system would be 
able to automatically generate red flags that would alert the public office holder or member as well as the 
commissioner," he said at the time.
In a statement, Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner spokesperson Melanie Rushworth said the office is 
always looking at new technological tools to boost its work.
But she also said that the office deals in sensitive and private information that would need to be protected from third 
parties, such as AI platforms.
"This obligation necessarily limits the tools and technologies that could be considered by the Office with 
consideration of our legal obligations, mandate, and risk considerations," Rushworth wrote.
In his 2018 speech, former commissioner Dion noted that although the privacy of MPs and public office holders was 
important, there would be ways to have them consent to their information being used by an in-house AI tool.
Page 3 of 4
'Revolving door' of insiders, lobbyists behind government scandal a click away with new AI tool
A key feature of the website is a button that highlights all the lobbying contacts associated with both of the 
government's controversial pay-system contracts. Government officials are highlighted in green and lobbyists are 
red, illustrating the well-travelled path between the world of government relations and the ministers they're trying to 
persuade.
And while the lobbying and relationship map displays the Phoenix pay scandal in technicolour, it's only the first 
example of the engine powering it. The new tool, built on the AI platform Claude Code, can now find the same 
information for any government contract, lobbying relationship or interaction between a corporation and government 
department.
With some very basic coding knowledge, and using an AI model to do the heavy lifting, a user can launch an 
investigation with a simple command. The program will launch AI agents that dig through the lobbying registry, scan 
media reports, and investigate basic facts.
It means virtually any Canadian can find "revolving door" connections to virtually anything that government money 
is being used for. And it will build a website to display it for posterity - and potentially to get the attention of 
opposition MPs and journalists.

title: 'This is very much Carney's deputy minister cadre': PM shuffles top ranks of public service
body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced a significant shakeup in the senior ranks of the public service, his 
second deputy minister shuffle in less than three months.
The reorganization sees fresh faces at or near the top of the public service in 16 government organizations, 
including the foreign affairs and immigration departments, and brings another high-level banker onboard from the 
private sector.
"These leadership changes support the strong, effective delivery of priorities and results for Canadians, while 
positioning the federal government to advance Canada's interests and respond to the rapidly shifting dynamics of 
the global landscape," the Prime Minister's Office said in the announcement.( 
https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/news-releases/2026/03/04/prime-minister-carney-announces-changes-senior-
ranks-public-service )
Among the most noteworthy changes, Glenn Purves is leaving BlackRock Investment Institute to become Canada's 
deputy minister of international trade.
Following the appointment of investment banker Mark Wiseman as Canada's ambassador to the United States, 
Purves becomes yet another example of a high-profile candidate from the banking world joining the upper echelons 
of Carney's public service.
"It's a continuation of the prime minister's emphasis on people who work in finance," said Lori Turnbull, a political 
science professor at Dalhousie University.
"The focus on finance, investment - that skillset and that piece of expertise is very prominent."
Purves most recently served for about a year as global head of macroeconomics at BlackRock, an American 
multinational investment company, but previously worked for more than a decade in the Canadian public service, 
including as assistant deputy minister of economic development at the Department of Finance.
Turnbull said it's unusual for Purves to return to the public service after such a short stint in the private sector.
"Typically if someone leaves for that kind of position, they are now on a different career track, and they pursue that," 
she said.
"I think it speaks to the kind of team that Carney is trying to build."
Page 2 of 4
'This is very much Carney's deputy minister cadre': PM shuffles top ranks of public service
'Very important moment'
Turnbull said the March 4 announcement amounted to the "second half" of a deputy minister shuffle in December.( 
https://ottawacitizen.com/public-service/carney-shakeup-senior-ranks-public-service )
The latest round represents "both change and continuity," she said, with some new talent joining and other 
mainstays transitioning into new roles.
Across both recent shuffles, Turnbull said the overall number of departures, role changes and new appointments 
represents a significant break from the regime under former prime minister Justin Trudeau.
"This is very much Carney's deputy minister cadre," she said, adding Carney in some ways inherited Trudeau's 
institutions: his cabinet, caucus and even public service.
The recent deputy minister shuffles represent a break from that legacy, Turnbull said.
"This is institutionally a very important moment for him, in terms of shaping support around him," she said.
Michael Wernick, a former clerk of the Privy Council, said several shakeups since Carney took over as prime 
minister have left most current deputy ministers in jobs that Carney and Privy Council Clerk Michael Sabia put 
them in.
"It's very much Mark Carney's team now, and Michael Sabia's team," he said.
"He's kind of moulded the senior ranks to his priorities and management style as well."
Wernick said the staffing decisions paint a picture of Carney's top priorities: international relations and attracting 
investment from overseas.
Other notable changes
Another notable change sees Rob Stewart, former deputy minister of international trade, moving into a role where 
he will oversee the creation of the Financial Crimes Agency.
