title: 'Toxic' behaviour fuelled city hall union drive Political staffers describe burnout, bullying, insults and harassment
body:
Tears. Anxiety attacks. Burnout. Depression.
These are among the reasons why political staff at Toronto City Hall say they organized in secret before kick-
starting a process last year to join a union.
For some of the staff on the small teams that make city hall's elected offices run behind the scenes - from fixing 
local issues to providing the research and logistical muscle needed to pass policies at council - the union drive is 
about breaking free from what they describe as ill treatment, at-times low pay and, in severe cases, sexual 
harassment and intimidation at jobs they otherwise enjoy.
It's an effort that, if successful, would make Toronto the first municipality in Canada to have unionized staff who 
work for elected officials.
The city, which is contesting the proposal at labour board hearings that will last through the fall, has argued that 
forming one unit under a sole employer would make bargaining "unwieldy, cumbersome, if not an impossibility" - 
and that the city is not the employer, but rather it's the 26 elected officials for whom the staffers work.
City councillors, most of whom have applied as interveners in the hearings, say they want to continue operating 
autonomously, like 26 individual administrations, and as the employers of their own staff. Each office, they argue, 
has its own political mandate and structure.
"This really is a monumental test case in many ways," said Carlo Fanelli, a York University professor in labour 
studies and employment law.
"It would be wise for policymakers and governments to take such requests seriously," Fanelli said. "I imagine a lot 
of different groups are watching this case very closely and it will have implications whether it's successful or not."
The Star has spoken to 17 current and former political staff over the past year about the working conditions on city 
hall's second floor, where council offices are located.
Because staff who spoke asked not to be identified for fear of professional reprisals, the Star has been unable to 
put their allegations to councillors and give them the chance to respond directly. As a result, the Star is not 
identifying particular councillors in this story.
Page 2 of 5
'Toxic' behaviour fuelled city hall union drive Political staffers describe burnout, bullying, insults and harassment
Some councillors' offices 
are 'toxic,' staff say
Multiple political staff told the Star that yelling so often crosses the line into belittling and personal insults that crying 
is a common occurrence.
One staffer described a councillor's "temper tantrums" as so persistent and reliable - whenever the councillor had 
a bad day - that she would cry while hiding at work. She said the "toxic" environment sometimes prevented her and 
her colleagues from getting back to constituents on time, if at all.
"You cannot make mistakes," she said, adding that she's been kicked off files she was passionate about over a 
small hiccup. "It sucks that you're sold a dream but it's actually a nightmare."
In other offices, there are serious allegations of sexual misconduct.
A second staffer said they have been sexually harassed and inappropriately touched by a councillor - despite 
repeated objections.
A third staffer described being sexually harassed by a colleague, including extremely intimate and unwelcome 
questions about their body parts - with no reprimand from the councillor once it was raised. This staffer said, 
meanwhile, they would often get "disparaging" personal feedback rather than constructive criticism about the work 
itself. They eventually took a leave of absence.
Several staff said the second floor is rife with name-calling from some councillors or senior staff, and often toward 
women. Insults range from being called "stupid" or "a f---ing bitch" when talking about council work, to more 
provocative labels such as "sluts" or "pussies" to bullying antics such as fat-shaming and mocking disabilities.
"I feel like I'm in an abusive relationship and I don't know how to leave," a fourth staffer said. 
A fifth staffer, who also experienced persistent and unwanted sexual comments from a councillor, said on top of 
her "crippling" workload, her stress levels resulted in chronic physical pain, according to her doctor who she said 
recommended leaving her job.
"I was the councillor in every way except by name," she said, noting the lack of sleep and stress eventually 
affected how well she performed. "Then a small typo in a draft newsletter would get me reprimanded harshly. It was 
a vicious cycle."
Meanwhile, religious holidays, illnesses or permanent health conditions are ignored or downplayed, doctor's 
appointments have been used to dock pay and taking a sick leave has put some at risk of getting fired, the Star was 
told.
During the last election in 2022, a few staff said they were forced to door-knock with masks, despite being ill with 
COVID-19 and showing symptoms. "Can you imagine how many residents we gave the virus to?" a sixth staffer 
said.
"We don't even get time in lieu. If we do, (the councillor) tells us when we can have it," the fourth staffer said, 
recalling the last election when they worked 12-hour days, seven days a week for several months - then were 
granted one day in lieu.
Salaries for the same job title, with varying responsibilities, also differ significantly from each other, since each office 
runs autonomously and elected officials make their own judgment calls.
Coun. Lily Cheng - who was not mentioned in the complaints shared by staff - said in a statement that any ill 
treatment against staff should be met with "meaningful" and "robust" accountability.
Page 3 of 5
'Toxic' behaviour fuelled city hall union drive Political staffers describe burnout, bullying, insults and harassment
"I am deeply disturbed to hear these allegations," she said. "Abuse, harassment, discrimination, sexual 
misconduct and retaliation against staff are unacceptable under any circumstances."
'It's death by a thousand cuts'
A few councillors' offices have become central to the union bid, either because of the councillors themselves or their 
most senior staff - or both. Both act as managers and at times like human resources officers.
"I wouldn't say it's widespread," the second staffer said, a sentiment echoed by several others. However, in those 
few offices, "it's death by a thousand cuts. When there's a new employee, some joke they'll be gone in a couple of 
months."
The staffer underscored, as did others, that they love being part of the public service - whether it's helping a 
resident with a noise complaint, getting answers about unplowed streets or fixing issues with local parks.
"But the problem is it's day in and day out, and the city is only getting harder," they said. "You will deal with horrid 
cases of near-homelessness or death or suicide, and it will happen out of the blue. We are not trained for that. We 
get no support."
While city workers such as bureaucrats or paramedics have unions such as CUPE and a formal HR process, the 
closest thing political staff have is the city clerk's office.
Councillors and their chiefs of staff do not get robust HR or employer training. Staff are expected to abide by an 
ethics framework but councillors are expected to know and manage their offices according to various rules including 
that framework, the council code of conduct, and the city's and province's statutory obligations.
According to several council staff, few email the clerk's office to complain about workplace issues because it's not 
seen as effective or trustworthy.
Some who have complained "were fired within days," the fourth staffer told the Star. "We feel trapped."
When the Star put these claims to the clerk's office and the city's lawyers on the union drive, Russell Baker, the 
city's director of communications, said in a statement that elected officials are responsible for hiring, pay rates and 
managing workplace conditions, but the clerk's office "supports" with "certain HR services" like payroll.
If staff complain to the clerk's office, "the clerk's team makes recommendations based on the situation, which can 
include referring them to the integrity commissioner's office, responsible for overseeing the member code of 
conduct."
However, the only penalties the integrity commissioner's office can recommend - which need to be voted on by 
council - include a pay suspension, a reprimand or an apology.
Meanwhile, quitting isn't as simple as it sounds. Staff who want to pursue a career in politics say their references 
and reputation matter. "Whether you're a good or bad staffer in the councillors' eyes, word gets around in the small, 
tangled world of politics," the second staffer said. After all, "each office revolves around one person's personality 
and preferences."
What the councillors think 
of the union bid
Fanelli, the York professor, said that in the Canadian municipal system there's a long-standing norm that political 
staff are supposed to be loyal to their elected official, rather than to an institution like the city. So, "historically, it's 
been this cultural disposition that has discouraged unionization."
Page 4 of 5
'Toxic' behaviour fuelled city hall union drive Political staffers describe burnout, bullying, insults and harassment
Coun. Jamaal Myers - who was not mentioned in the complaints shared by staff - said the main reason he applied 
for intervener status at the hearings was to "be at the table in order to actually effect change," because "there are 
things that can be done (to rectify issues) without saying that my staff are no longer my staff."
Myers continued: "I can acknowledge there are problems ... I think where a lot of us, myself at least, draw the line is 
the distinction between not whether they're unionized ... it's whether or not they're my staff. Because that actually 
affects how you run your office, how you hire, how you fire, what you're able to do."
But the union the political staff are trying to join says that wouldn't change, even if their union drive is successful.
"There is nothing about being unionized that dictates that they could not choose their own staff," said Rob Smalley, 
chief operating officer at the Association of Management, Administrative and Professional Crown Employees of 
Ontario.
Smalley said the point of unionization is to offer staff, who are at a "severe power imbalance" with councillors, a 
stronger voice in their workplace than simply training their bosses to be better managers.
During the first day of the labour board hearings into the union bid last week, lawyer Jack Siegel said in his opening 
statement that the 15 intervening councillors he representsaren't suggesting "in any way that collective bargaining is 
at all inappropriate." However, they don't think the city has any role to play in any collective bargaining framework 
that might be put in place: "This is between (councillors) and their staff."
Siegel said if the city were classified as the true employer, it would result in an "absurdity" where members of the 
same bargaining unit would routinely be working against one another. "In the example of the almost-certain 
mayoralty campaign we're about to see, members in one office are going to be actively seeking the defeat of 
opposing members," Siegel said.
That is the nature of political employment, Siegel added. "No collective agreement can alter that fundamental fact - 
but it can disrupt it."
Myers said there are many nuances that have to be thought through so councillors can still run their offices 
according to their political priorities, the stakes, the high pressure, the standards that come with it - and while 
ensuring staff work in better conditions.
"At the end of the day ... you still need people to be able to react" and perform at a high standard, Myers said. "This 
is political jobs everywhere."

at all inappropriate." However, they don't think the city has any role to play in any collective bargaining framework 
that might be put in place: "This is between (councillors) and their staff."

mayoralty campaign we're about to see, members in one office are going to be actively seeking the defeat of 
opposing members," Siegel said.

title: 'We need to help Quebecers' cope with cost of living, Premier Fréchette says
body:
Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette Fréchette has not ruled out spending more than the $250 million budgeted for 
the winner of the CAQ leadership race to spend on campaign promises. Montreal Gazette (Credit: Evan Buhler)
LÉVIS - Premier Christine Fréchette says if Montreal's hockey teams have been able prove their naysayers wrong 
this season, so can her Coalition Avenir Québec party and win the fall general election.
Noting analysts and columnists have been predicting the demise of the CAQ for months, Fréchette told troops at a 
general council meeting Saturday the party still has some fight left in it. Two fresh polls have shown the party under 
her leadership is gaining momentum.
Evan Buhler / Montreal GazetteQuebec Premier Christine Fréchette Fréchette has not ruled out spending more 
than the $250 million budgeted for the winner of the CAQ leadership race to spend on campaign promises.
"To prove the predictions wrong, I will need you, each of you," Fréchette told delegates in the hall. "I need you to 
convince Quebecers, to convince your families, your friends, your neighbours, your work colleagues.
"We must meet each Quebecer. We must shake every hand and knock on every door. We will have to say, loudly 
and strongly, why Quebec needs our coalition to defend our autonomy and propel our economy.
"If we do this, we'll resemble our hockey teams, our Victoire of Montreal, and the Canadiens of Montreal. We will 
prove all the predictions wrong, and we'll win the next elections. Let's get to work and Go Habs Go."
The crowd of 650 CAQ members - many of them dressed in hockey jerseys - loved it, breaking into a chorus of Bell 
Centre style Olé Olé Olé chanting. Fréchette herself arrived for the meeting, the last one before the next election, 
wearing a Victoire jersey.
When she visited Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada in April, Fréchette sported a Canadiens jersey.
It's unclear the CAQ as a political organization can get a bounce out of the current good mood of Quebecers, but 
Fréchette seems ready to tap in.
She is also continuing to put more and more distance between her "new" government and the unpopular one 
headed by former premier François Legault.
Page 2 of 5
'We need to help Quebecers' cope with cost of living, Premier Fréchette says
In a 15-minute speech, she ran down a long list of what she has accomplished in the 40 days she has been 
premier; from money for hospitals, tax cuts for small- and medium-size businesses and farmers, to economic 
missions to Ottawa, Washington and Paris.
She added to the list new legislation to renew the notwithstanding clause shielding Bill 96 from court challenges.
"We did all this in 40 days, imagine what can do in four years," Fréchette told the crowd, which stood banging 
thunder sticks and waving signs.
After saying the new No. 1 priority now is helping Quebecers deal with the soaring cost of living, Fréchette 
announced a new measure: the government is cutting the provincial sales tax on certain products at the grocery 
store and pharmacies.
The list of products that will not be subject to the tax includes prepared fruits and vegetables, granola bars, muffins, 
nuts and bathroom tissue. The initiative will be announced Monday at a news conference in Sherbrooke.
The sales tax cut will mean savings of about $50 a year per household, but cost the treasury about $100 million. 
Other measures are also in the works.
Fréchette said she wants to give Quebecers "a bit of air and the hand" they need.
"Despite all we have done we have to do still more," Fréchette said. "We have to go still further."
Her speech was also an effort to stimulate the troops for the battle ahead.
It was all positive spin for the CAQ and all negative for the two main opposition parties, which she said want to bring 
Quebec back 30 years in time with their talk of federalism vs. independence.
She said Quebecers on Oct. 5 will have three options: voting for resignation, illusion or ambition.
Resignation is represented by the Quebec Liberals, which she said are weak on language, laicity and even the fight 
against corruption.
The Parti Québécois represents the illusion of another referendum, which two-thirds of Quebecers don't want.
"Hello, planet Earth," Fréchette quipped.
She said only the CAQ, representing ambition, remains the best option for Quebecers.
"Only a month ago, people did put much stock in our prospects," Fréchette said. "Even today, there is a lot of doubt 
that we have a chance to win the next election.
"I'm convinced we can do it and I am convinced we will do it."
Her speech came on the same days as Frechette said she has not excluded spending more than the $250 million 
her finance minister, Eric Girard, left in the March budget to cover her leadership campaign promises, including the 
sales tax cut.
"We need to help Quebecers because the cost of living is very difficult for Quebecers," Fréchette told reporters in 
the morning. "We need to take actions to answer the needs.
"We need also to manage public finances in a responsible way. Both are my objectives. We need a good balance 
between the two.
"We'll see how it evolves. So far, we have been respecting the envelope that was set out. We will announce new 
actions in the coming days."
Page 3 of 5
'We need to help Quebecers' cope with cost of living, Premier Fréchette says
Fréchette specifically did not rule out spending more than the $250 million and she has already used some of it. 
She has announced the government would refund the welcome tax for first-time home buyers at a cost of $140 
million.
She announced a tax cut for small- and medium-size businesses( https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-
news/quebec-tax-cuts-small-medium-businesses-frechette-tariffs/ ) at a cost of $50 million for 2026. Refunding the 
carbon tax for agricultural producers, another promise, will cost the treasury $40 million.
The $100 million cost of cutting the sales tax will bring the total of Fréchette's recent spending to $330 million.
But in an email sent by Girard to Fréchette and obtained by Radio-Canada( https://ici.radio-
canada.ca/nouvelle/2256049/frechette-girard-courriel-ministre-finances ), Girard appears to warn the premier he is 
worried about her spending.
"I have to underline that I am worried about the number of announcements made by the government since your 
election," Girard wrote.
He added Quebecers are "intelligent" and "know how to count" and prefer a premier who acts responsibly and not 
spend wildly, a perception Quebecers had of the government when François Legault was premier( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/quebec-premier-francois-legault-resigns/ ).
The email is dated May 2, which was two weeks after Fréchette was sworn in( 
https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/provincial-politics/christine-frechette-sworn-in-as-quebec-
premier-promises-to-govern-with-ambition-and-determination/ ) as premier.
Fréchette, however, downplayed the email.
"Mr. Girard is doing his job, I am doing mine," Fréchette said. "We have to find the balance between managing the 
public finances as well responding to the needs of Quebecers in a difficult situation.
"Right now we are within the allocated amount that was foreseen. We will see how it evolves in time."
But she added there is a lot of pressure on the finances of Quebecers, caused by multiple factors that are lasting 
longer than anticipated.
Fréchette mentioned the continuing blockage of the Strait of Hormuz, which is pushing gas prices ever higher.
"The situation is not easy for Quebecers whether we consider the cost of living, the cost of groceries, the price of 
housing and rents. All this puts pressure on them, including the price of gas."
Meeting reporters earlier, Girard downplayed the importance of the email, adding in his career he has written many 
similar emails as part of his job.
"I assume my responsibilities, it's my job. I am the guardian of public finances," he said.
Girard added, however, people need to be aware of the context. In his March budget, Quebec projected that the 
Strait of Hormuz would be reopened in six weeks.
It is now Week 13 and the conflict is not resolved and the price of gas keeps rising.
"To date, what has been announced is within the $250 million," Girard said. "Other acts are being considered. The 
impact (of the world context) on Quebecers is real. The price of gas is visible at the pump.
"So we need to take the right actions at the right time to help Quebecers."
Behind closed doors, the party held workshops to prepare for the election.
Page 4 of 5
'We need to help Quebecers' cope with cost of living, Premier Fréchette says
Responding to critics who have said the party appears to be slow in announcing the names of its election 
candidates, CAQ party director general Brigitte Legault said the roll out is proceeding normally.
She noted of the 79 remaining CAQ MNAs, between 55 and 60 have decided to seek re-election. Some have 
decided to not run again, but Legault said all will be settled by the end of May.
She dismissed speculation the party is having trouble finding candidates given its low standing in the polls.
"It's not because they are not announced that we don't have them ready," Legault told reporters. "We are a banner 
which is still attracting candidates."
Asked if new faces are approaching the party, Legault said: "Big time, big time."
"People are coming forward, people are enthusiastic, we have women, we have youth. We have people from all 
over Quebec."

title: 'We're taking back control': Carney defends his record on immigration after damning auditor report
body:
OTTAWA - Prime Minister Mark Carney defended his government's record on immigration on Wednesday, 
following a report from the auditor general this week that showed the international student program lacked proper 
controls.
"We're taking back control on immigration," said Carney, on his way into a caucus meeting.
"You've seen temporary worker numbers down by 50 per cent, asylum claims down by a third," he said. "New 
foreign student numbers down by 60 per cent since this government came in, and 100 per cent investigations since 
2025, which is as long as I've been prime minister."
Carney's comments come two days after a new report by the auditor general's office showed Canada's immigration 
department in a two-year period only investigated a fraction of the 153,000 international students flagged for non-
compliance and potential fraud.
Between 2023 and 2024, the department only had the capacity to investigate just over 4,000 cases. When the 
cases were investigated, the department took "limited action" in confirming non-compliance beyond contacting the 
student for more information.
The audit also highlighted that the department failed to follow up on 800 cases where fraudulent documents were 
used. The report also found that the department failed to monitor which students were expected to leave each year 
and which students had left the country.
In response to the report, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab said her department would be centralizing 
investigations and sharing more information with the Canada Border Services Agency. Diab also said since 2025, 
100 per cent of the discrepancies reported were "followed up."
Diab was not immigration minister during the period that was audited, instead, it was Marc Miller, who is now the 
heritage minister, and Sean Fraser, now the justice minister.
On Tuesday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Carney should fire Diab, Miller and Fraser over their 
handling of the immigration file.
Page 2 of 3
'We're taking back control': Carney defends his record on immigration after damning auditor report
In 2022, the Canadian population grew by more than one million people, thanks to record immigration designed to 
ease labour shortages. In 2023 and 2024, Canadian attitudes towards immigration hit a 30-year low, according to 
the immigration department's own tracking surveys.
The Liberal government reversed course on some of its immigration policies starting in 2024, bringing in stricter 
rules for work and study visas, while also introducing an international students cap.
The government's 2025-2027 Immigration Levels Plan projected a decrease in overall permanent resident 
admissions to 395,000 in 2025. Canada let in a total of 393,530 people in 2025, compared to 483,655 in 2024.
The 2026-2028 levels plan stabilizes permanent resident admission targets at 380,000 per year for three years, 
while setting a target for new temporary resident arrivals at 385,000 in 2026 and 370,000 in 2027 and 2028.
Canada's population shrank by 0.2 per cent in the third quarter of 2025, marking the country's first decrease since 
the COVID pandemic in 2020.
The department's 2024 online tracking survey showed that when informed the target was 395,000 for 2025, 63 per 
cent of Canadians still thought that figure was too many, while 28 per cent thought it was either about right or too 
few.

title: 'Whatever it takes:' Trump says U.S. prepared for Iran operation to last a month or 'far longer'
body:
On the third day after the U.S. and Israel's joint strike on Iran, conflict in the Middle East threatens to escalate 
further. Iran has carried out retaliatory strikes on nine countries, targeting U.S. bases and energy sites in Saudi 
Arabia, Bahrain, U.A.E, Qatar and elsewhere.
U.S. has said it expects to incur casualties as Iran presses on with its attacks. Flights through the region's hub 
airports have been cancelled, disrupting international travel for many thousands of people, Agence France-Presse 
reports.
Here's the latest:
Countries largely urge diplomacy, remain on sidelines
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte praised the U.S. and Israeli military campaign but added that there are no 
plans for the alliance to enter the conflict.
"It's really important what the U.S. is doing there, together with Israel, because it is taking out, degrading the 
capacity of Iran to get its hands on nuclear capability, the ballistic missile capability," he told German broadcaster 
ARD, according to Reuters.
"There are absolutely no plans whatever for NATO to get dragged into this or being part of it, other than individual 
allies doing what they can to enable what the Americans are doing together with Israel," he added.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz gives a statement to the media following the U.S.-Israeli killing of Iranian 
Ayatollah Khamenei on March 01, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz left for Washington on Monday to meet with U.S. President Donald Trump 
ahead of a previously scheduled meeting on Ukraine. Merz, who has been a vocal critic of Iran's regime expressed 
"relief" that the "mullah regime is coming to an end," AFP reported.
Germany, U.K. and France have said they are prepared to offer "defensive" support against Iran to protect their 
interests in the Gulf region if necessary. Canada, while expressing approval for the U.S. attack, has said it would 
not become involved.
Page 2 of 6
'Whatever it takes:' Trump says U.S. prepared for Iran operation to last a month or 'far longer'
The British government has said it would allow the U.S. to use British bases during its war with Iran and after a 
Royal Air Force base in Cyprus was struck by an Iranian-made drone.
France to increase stockpile of nuclear warheads for first time since 1992
French President Emmanuel Macron announced Monday that France will increase its nuclear arsenal and for the 
first time allow the temporary deployment of its nuclear-armed aircraft to allied countries, in a new strategy aimed at 
strengthening Europe's independence.
To be free, one needs to be feared," Macron said.
Macron said the new posture could "provide for the temporary deployment of elements of our strategic air forces to 
allied countries," but said there would be no sharing of decision-making with any other nation regarding the use of 
the nuclear weapons.
Talks about such arrangements have started with Britain, Germany, Poland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, 
Sweden and Denmark, Macron said.
Additionally, in response to Iranian threats to ships in the Strait of Hormus, France was sending two more warships 
to beef up Operation Aspides, the bloc's naval mission in the region. But they would only deploy to the distant Red 
Sea and Gulf of Aden - gateways to the Suez Canal, which links the Red Sea to the Mediterranean - to join three 
other ships already in place.
This satellite image taken by 2026 Planet Labs PBC on March 1, 2026 shows a smoke plume billowing from 
Tehran's District 7 area.
China, Russia condemn attacks
China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said one of its citizen was killed by Saturday's strikes and more than 3,000 have 
been evacuated. Experts tell AFP a prolonged war in the region would prove costly for China, which receives much 
of its energy through the Strait of Hormuz.
The country's leadership repeatedly called for an end to the conflict since it began on Saturday. "The attack and 
killing of Iran's supreme leader is a grave violation of Iran's sovereignty and security. It tramples on the purposes 
and principles of the UN Charter and basic norms in international relations. China firmly opposes and strongly 
condemns it," the foreign ministry wrote yesterday on X( https://x.com/MFA_China/status/2028061647269773386 ).
Russian leader Vladimir Putin called Ali Khamenei's "a murder committed in cynical violation of all norms of human 
morality and international law."
"In our country, Ayatollah Khamenei will be remembered as an outstanding statesman who made a huge personal 
contribution to the development of friendly Russian-Iranian relations, bringing them to the level of a comprehensive 
strategic partnership," the Russian president said, according to Euro News.( https://www.euronews.com/my-
europe/2026/03/01/putin-calls-the-death-of-irans-ali-khamenei-a-cynical-murder )

title: 'You can hide everything in a story' Filmmaker Alexandre Trudeau on his new thriller and his brother's
body:
Alexandre Trudeau says he discovered his limits as a documentary filmmaker around the time his elder brother 
stepped into the country's highest office.
It was late 2015 when Justin Trudeau led the Liberals to a majority government. Not long after, Alexandre, the 
second-oldest son of the late prime minister Pierre Trudeau, realized some things in his life had to change.
One of them was his role as a visual storyteller. Much of his career had focused on stories of geopolitical strife, 
often through documentaries produced for Canadian television.
In his 2003 documentary "Embedded in Baghdad," which aired on CTV's now-defunct "W5" news magazine series, 
Trudeau gave a first-person account of how the 2003 invasion of Iraq impacted one middle-class family, while 
"Refuge: A Film About Darfur," examined Sudan's humanitarian crisis. He worried that making other documentaries 
in that vein might be a lightning rod for controversy for both him and his brother.
"I didn't want to be in a position where I'm criticizing his government, nor could I imagine making films without 
speaking my mind," the 52-year-old director told the Star.
"So, it made sense to go into fiction."
His first narrative feature, "Hair of the Bear," now in theatres, grew out of Trudeau's decision to pull away from 
political issues that had defined his previous work.
The tense wilderness thriller stars Malia Baker (Netflix's "The Baby-Sitters Club") as a troubled teenager whose 
self-harm prompts her mother to send her to a remote cabin for two weeks in hopes she'll reconnect with her 
grandfather, an experienced survivalist (Roy Dupuis of TV's "Nikita").
As the two begin to bond, their relationship is thrown into turmoil when two young men unexpectedly arrive at the 
cabin seeking help. The pair's intentions seem nefarious from the get-go, and it doesn't take long before both sides 
are caught in a battle against the elements and each other.
"Hair of the Bear," shot in Manitoba, was co-written and co-directed by James McLellan, whom Trudeau has known 
since they both served as young officers in the Canadian Armed Forces.
Page 2 of 4
'You can hide everything in a story' Filmmaker Alexandre Trudeau on his new thriller and his brother's 
relationship with Katy Perry
Neither of them had co-directed together before, and nearly a dozen screenplays Trudeau wrote over the years 
inspired by his own documentaries never panned out as feature films. His ideas, he said, were often too grand for 
Canadian budgets.
With McLellan, he saw the opportunity to shape a feature together. McLellan is a film teacher at a Winnipeg high 
school, and his direct experience with teenage depression and suicide provided insight to build the central 
character.
Around 2018, they set out together to write the story and storyboard all of the action.
"James is like a brother that I don't fight with," Trudeau said.
"To have two of us carrying this really made sense."
"Hair of the Bear" also offered Trudeau a chance to continue working in film without getting tangled in his familial 
ties.
Shortly after his brother took office, the filmmaker found himself at the centre of a controversy over his decision to 
sign an open letter that called on Canada's public safety minister to halt the deportation of terror suspect 
Mohamed Harkat, an Algerian man accused of being an al-Qaida sleeper agent.
Trudeau had long opposed security certificates, a provision of Canada's immigration law used to remove non-
citizens suspected of extremism or espionage from the country, including Harkat. He had produced a 2007 
documentary on the subject. 
"I wasn't even making a project, I was just signing a letter saying give these people due process," he said.
An Ottawa watchdog saw the filmmaker's involvement as a conflict of interest and called for the prime minister 
to publicly recuse himself from deciding Harkat's fate. That experience, the director said, made him reconsider 
where he dedicated his energy.
"Hair of the Bear" keeps its distance from anything overtly political, though Trudeau insists buried within its snowy 
conflict is some subtext. In particular, there's the symbolic presence of unwanted guests treading on foreign 
territory, which for some may evoke the ongoing threats to Canada's sovereignty by U.S. President Donald Trump.
"That's the joy of stories: you can hide everything in a story," he said.
"This film is metaphorically about fighting for your life. I believe that's a clear message for everyone. We have to 
fight for our lives."
With his debut fictional narrative complete, Trudeau said he's turned his attention elsewhere.
Instead of making another film, he's writing a book of political philosophy that explores topics he's felt unable to 
discuss in recent years. He said it frames the rapid deterioration of democratic norms against nearly a century of 
history, starting around the Second World War and leading to the "post-truth era" born from a freer exchange of 
information, which he believes helped erode trust in political systems.
"I don't have the restraints now that my brother is out of politics," he said.
"I can get back to telling (these stories). This world needs more understanding; it's gone sour on us in a big way. 
And I think the first step is saying what happened, why it happened and what can be done about it."
While Trudeau forges ahead with his own career, he said he's pleased to see his brother find stability in his 
personal life after separating from wife Sophie Grégoire Trudeau in 2023.
Page 3 of 4
'You can hide everything in a story' Filmmaker Alexandre Trudeau on his new thriller and his brother's 
relationship with Katy Perry
The former prime minister captured international headlines last year when he started appearing in public with pop 
star Katy Perry. The pair seemed to make their relationship more official when she was seen with him this year at 
the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.
"I don't ask my brother about his personal life," Trudeau said. "If it gets serious, he'll tell me - and he did - so I was 
super happy for him. You like to see your family members in stable, healthy relationships."
While the unconventional couple raised eyebrows in some circles, Trudeau insists it always made sense to him.
"They're world-stage performers," he said. "She's a hard-working woman, as well. (They're) people who gave 
everything to the show.
"To share that with someone, I'm sure it makes their life easier. They can value privacy, in their own way, and know 
the strength of performance at the same time. So, they're a good match."

As the two begin to bond, their relationship is thrown into turmoil when two young men unexpectedly arrive at the 
cabin seeking help. The pair's intentions seem nefarious from the get-go, and it doesn't take long before both sides 
are caught in a battle against the elements and each other.
"Hair of the Bear," shot in Manitoba, was co-written and co-directed by James McLellan, whom Trudeau has known 
since they both served as young officers in the Canadian Armed Forces.
Page 2 of 4
'You can hide everything in a story' Filmmaker Alexandre Trudeau on his new thriller and his brother's 
relationship with Katy Perry
Neither of them had co-directed together before, and nearly a dozen screenplays Trudeau wrote over the years 
inspired by his own documentaries never panned out as feature films. His ideas, he said, were often too grand for 
Canadian budgets.
With McLellan, he saw the opportunity to shape a feature together. McLellan is a film teacher at a Winnipeg high 
school, and his direct experience with teenage depression and suicide provided insight to build the central 
character.
Around 2018, they set out together to write the story and storyboard all of the action.
"James is like a brother that I don't fight with," Trudeau said.
"To have two of us carrying this really made sense."
"Hair of the Bear" also offered Trudeau a chance to continue working in film without getting tangled in his familial 
ties.
Shortly after his brother took office, the filmmaker found himself at the centre of a controversy over his decision to 
sign an open letter that called on Canada's public safety minister to halt the deportation of terror suspect 
Mohamed Harkat, an Algerian man accused of being an al-Qaida sleeper agent.
Trudeau had long opposed security certificates, a provision of Canada's immigration law used to remove non-
citizens suspected of extremism or espionage from the country, including Harkat. He had produced a 2007 
documentary on the subject. 
"I wasn't even making a project, I was just signing a letter saying give these people due process," he said.
An Ottawa watchdog saw the filmmaker's involvement as a conflict of interest and called for the prime minister 
to publicly recuse himself from deciding Harkat's fate. That experience, the director said, made him reconsider 
where he dedicated his energy.
"Hair of the Bear" keeps its distance from anything overtly political, though Trudeau insists buried within its snowy 
conflict is some subtext. In particular, there's the symbolic presence of unwanted guests treading on foreign 
territory, which for some may evoke the ongoing threats to Canada's sovereignty by U.S. President Donald Trump.
"That's the joy of stories: you can hide everything in a story," he said.
"This film is metaphorically about fighting for your life. I believe that's a clear message for everyone. We have to 
fight for our lives."
With his debut fictional narrative complete, Trudeau said he's turned his attention elsewhere.
Instead of making another film, he's writing a book of political philosophy that explores topics he's felt unable to 
discuss in recent years. He said it frames the rapid deterioration of democratic norms against nearly a century of 
history, starting around the Second World War and leading to the "post-truth era" born from a freer exchange of 
information, which he believes helped erode trust in political systems.
"I don't have the restraints now that my brother is out of politics," he said.
"I can get back to telling (these stories). This world needs more understanding; it's gone sour on us in a big way. 
And I think the first step is saying what happened, why it happened and what can be done about it."
While Trudeau forges ahead with his own career, he said he's pleased to see his brother find stability in his 
personal life after separating from wife Sophie Grégoire Trudeau in 2023.

relationship with Katy Perry
The former prime minister captured international headlines last year when he started appearing in public with pop 
star Katy Perry. The pair seemed to make their relationship more official when she was seen with him this year at 
the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland.
"I don't ask my brother about his personal life," Trudeau said. "If it gets serious, he'll tell me - and he did - so I was 
super happy for him. You like to see your family members in stable, healthy relationships."
While the unconventional couple raised eyebrows in some circles, Trudeau insists it always made sense to him.
"They're world-stage performers," he said. "She's a hard-working woman, as well. (They're) people who gave 
everything to the show.
"To share that with someone, I'm sure it makes their life easier. They can value privacy, in their own way, and know 
the strength of performance at the same time. So, they're a good match."

title: 10 at the top From war and moral collapse to family fracture and memory loss, our critic on the Cannes
body:
One of the daily fixtures of The Hollywood Reporter during the Cannes Film Festival is a short column of 
international news briefs headlined "Meanwhile, in the Real World ... "
The title is a joking nod to a very real feeling on the sun-splashed French Riviera: for 12 days, nothing seems to 
matter more than the world premieres of new films by many of the planet's leading directors.
This year at Cannes, though, the real world refused to stay offstage. The cinematic bounty kept pulling us back to 
the planet's troubles, past and present. War, child abuse, moral collapse, dementia, corruption and murder were 
among the many grim subjects canvassed in the 79th edition of the world's most celebrated film festival.
What follows are my 10 favourite films from this year's fest, starting with the two I'd give the best shot at the Palme 
d'Or when Park Chan-wook's competition jury hands out prizes at Saturday's closing ceremony. 
Minotaur
In a strong but uneven Cannes '26 Palme competition, this slow-burning thriller by Russian exile Andrey 
Zvyagintsev stands out as an indisputable triumph. Adapted from Claude Chabrol's 1969 film "The Unfaithful Wife," 
Zvyagintsev's first feature in nearly a decade, following a near-fatal illness, shows he's lost none of his mastery of 
form and storytelling. Nor has he softened his focus on moral collapse, here embodied in a man whose personal 
downslide mirrors the corruption and expediency of Vladimir Putin's war with Ukraine. Protagonists in Zvyagintsev 
films resemble spiritual zombies. This describes Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), an affluent CEO in Russia in 2022, who 
finds his once-profitable transport company under siege from corporate pressures, staff defections, layoffs and 
compulsory military call-ups. Worst of all, Gleb also learns that his wife (Iris Lebedeva) is having an affair. Action 
must be taken, morals be damned.
Fatherland
Germany, 1949. The war is over, but the rancour continues in a divided and shattered land while denial about its 
Nazi past accelerates. Into this maelstrom, and before the luminous B&W lens of Lukasz Zal, rides Thomas Mann 
(Hanns Zischler), the Nobel laureate and novelist, who naively believes he can instruct both the capitalist West and 
the communist East about the civilizing insights of Goethe. He's accompanied by his daughter, Erika (the great 
Sandra Hüller), who knows the dangers and folly of this road trip and who laments her father's inability to love his 
Page 2 of 4
10 at the top From war and moral collapse to family fracture and memory loss, our critic on the Cannes 
festival's best movies
own family, let alone the country of his birth. Writer/director Pawel Pawlikowski ("Cold War") observes history with 
wisdom, grace and caustic humour.
Paper Tiger
"Paper Tiger" roars out of the chute as one of James Gray's best films and a genuine Cannes Palme contender, 
channelling Agamemnon's warning about greed: "Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who 
will ask no further." Brash ex-cop Gary (Adam Driver) and mild civil engineer Irwin (Miles Teller) are brothers in 
1986 New York who think they've found a pot of gold in the polluted Gowanus Canal. Honest but not wise, they 
launch a canal-cleanup consultancy, only to land a first big client in a gang of profiteering Russian polluters 
interested purely in covering up their crimes. Scarlett Johansson plays Irwin's wife, Hester, trying to shield her 
husband and their two sons even as she grapples with her own mounting crisis. The finely tuned ensemble is 
matched by Gray's lean, sinewy filmmaking.
Fjord
Mountains rise straight out of the water in Cristian Mungiu's latest social inquiry, an apt image for how hemmed in 
the Gheorghiu family feels in their new life in Norway. Led by Romanian father Mihai (Sebastian Stan) and 
Norwegian mother Lisbet (Renate Reinsve), they struggle to fit in as locals eye their conservative Christian values 
and strict parenting with suspicion. When adolescent daughter Elia arrives at gym class with troubling bruises, a 
teacher's call to child services sets off a cascade of custody battles that fracture both family and community. 
Mungiu lets the tensions speak for themselves, but he wants the audience to judge. The mountains loom. An 
avalanche is coming.
Tangles
Canadian creativity and compassion times two at Cannes as Vancouver cartoonist Sarah Leavitt's graphic novel 
about coping with Alzheimer's disease is transformed into a crackerjack animated debut feature by fellow 
Vancouverite Leah Nelson. The difficult topic and mostly B&W lensing might suggest a darker tone than the film 
uses, but neither director/co-writer Nelson nor co-writer Leavitt want us to wallow in misery - especially with a richly 
comic voice cast that includes Bryan Cranston, Sarah Silverman, Wanda Sykes, Bowen Yang and co-producer 
Seth Rogen.
Set in the late '90s and transposed to the U.S., it follows queer cartoonist Sarah (Abbi Jacobson) as she navigates 
a new job and lover in San Francisco while her beloved mother, Midge (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), struggles with rapidly 
advancing Alzheimer's back home in small-town Maine. Anyone familiar with how a loved one's cognitive decline 
ravages families will doubtless recognize and appreciate the emotional turbulence that's expressed with truth and 
grace.
The Beloved
Lights, camera ... aggression! Javier Bardem's Esteban, a volcanic director whose Oscars and Palme have gone 
straight to his head, tears into a tableful of actors for failing to convincingly chew their food. One of them is Emilia 
(Victoria Luengo), his long-estranged daughter, gritting her teeth as she pretends she signed on to this godforsaken 
desert shoot for art rather than to please an emotionally abusive, neglectful father. Rodrigo Sorogoyen serves up 
one of the most combustible pairings at Cannes '26: Bardem and Luengo, both giving awards-worthy performances, 
look as if they might start a war just by sharing a scene.
Moulin
A trip to hell in the company of a man of principle and honour. László Nemes may never surpass his debut "Son of 
Saul" for unflinching Nazi horror, but he comes close with this biopic of real-life Resistance hero Jean Moulin, 
played with astonishing grace by Gilles Lellouche. Parachuted into occupied France in 1943 to unite feuding 
Resistance factions, Moulin is captured by the Gestapo and singled out for sadistic interrogation by Klaus Barbie 
Page 3 of 4
10 at the top From war and moral collapse to family fracture and memory loss, our critic on the Cannes 
festival's best movies
(Lars Eidinger), the Butcher of Lyon. Will Moulin crack under torture and betray his friends and their noble cause? 
The film is a gruelling yet gripping watch, made all the more artful by cinematographer Mátyás Erdély's Rembrandt-
like shadings of black and gold.
Gentle Monster
Marie Kreutzer's devastating drama of suspected evil has "Anatomy of a Fall" vibes from three Cannes fests ago: 
accusations arrive faster than the truth. Léa Seydoux is Lucy, the pop pianist wife of failing filmmaker Philip 
(Laurence Rupp), whose burnout has prompted the city couple to move with their young son to new digs in rural 
Bavaria. Their new life barely begins before a knock on the door upends it: German cops are investigating Philip 
and seizing his computers on suspicion of him possessing child pornography. As Marie struggles to believe her 
husband's claim of "contextual" innocence, police investigator Elsa (Jella Haase) has family problems of her own: 
her father's advancing dementia is causing seriously inappropriate behaviour.
John Lennon: The Last Interview
Steven Soderbergh reshapes tragedy into something like spoken-word cinema with a documentary premiering at 
Cannes. On Dec. 8, 1980, a disturbed fan shot and killed John Lennon. Earlier that same day, Lennon and wife 
Yoko Ono had sat down with a radio team for a wide-ranging interview that would become his final recorded words. 
Soderbergh builds the film entirely from that audio, setting it adrift in a collage of images and music. Lennon speaks 
with relish about "Double Fantasy," his first album in five years, and riffs on subjects as varied as feminism, 
parenting, disco and even breakfast habits. He also talks about returning to the road for the first time since the 
Beatles' last tour in 1966. What survives here is something unexpectedly uplifting: a vivid record of a man who, on 
his last day, seemed not only at peace but genuinely excited about what lay ahead.
Teenage Sex and Death 
at Camp Miasma
Never let it be said Jane Schoenbrun doesn't make good on descriptive horror film titles. Following "I've Seen the 
TV Glow" and "We're All Going to the World's Fair," Schoenbrun's latest strikes a balance between campy and 
creepshow with a story that indeed delivers on the sex and death but does so from a serious queer awakening 
perspective. Hannah Einbinder (TV's "Hacks") plays a horror director uneasily assigned to reboot a problematic 
slasher franchise (think "Friday the 13th"); Gillian Anderson plays the reclusive "final girl" of the original film who is 
now deep into Norma Desmond-style seclusion and delusions. This one's designed to make us shriek, smirk and 
think in equal measure.

title: 10/3 podcast: Could Alberta actually separate? Breaking down the movement and the politics
body:
Talk of Alberta separatism is reaching a simmer as supporters of independence brought forward what they say is a 
successful petition drive to get a question put to voters.
But the story has been hit with scandal as another pro-independence group has come under fire for allegedly 
leaking the province's list of electors.
This is all coming together as Alberta's premier is trying to put a lid on such talk as she negotiates a new deal with 
Ottawa that may put some grievances to bed.
Calgary Herald columnist Don Braid joins the show to discuss who some of the key figures are, why they're arguing 
for separation, and how the debate has affected politics in Alberta.

title: A Ford by name, not temperament Premier's nephew has been consulting public for months about potential run
body:
Former city councillor and MPP Michael Ford, nephew of Premier Doug Ford, says he has been consulting 
Torontonians for "months" about a potential mayoral run on issues such as low property taxes, public safety and 
fighting traffic gridlock.
In a statement to the Star on Friday, Ford also seemed to take a veiled swipe at Coun. Brad Bradford - a potential 
mayoral rival on the political centre-right, with similar stated priorities - noting that as a city councillor, Ford was 
always "firmly opposed to calls to defund the police when some believed it was politically popular."
Bradford voted with some colleagues in 2020 for a failed motion to redirect some police funding to social programs. 
He later said he was reacting to a "particular moment in time," following the Minneapolis police murder of George 
Floyd, and as Toronto's next mayor would boost public safety and policing, including putting officers at every TTC 
station.
Ford's public musings about returning to politics, after low-profile stints at city hall and Queen's Park, and now as a 
lobbyist, toss a curveball into a campaign that doesn't officially start until May 1 but which has unofficially raged for 
months.
The spectre of another Ford at city hall comes shortly after former mayor John Tory abandoned thoughts of trying a 
comeback via a right-flank challenge to progressive Mayor Olivia Chow, who is expected to seek re-election.
It could also split the centre-right vote and present a serious challenge to Bradford, recently photographed meeting 
with Ford after the latter confirmed a potential candidacy.
Ford, noting he is giving "serious consideration" to a run, told the Star that "over the past several months, I've been 
meeting with people from across the city, including community leaders, representatives from Toronto's diverse 
cultural communities, business leaders, and current and former elected officials."
Calling such discussions "incredibly valuable," he said they will also continue with "family and close advisers." 
If Ford does run, he'll capitalize on name recognition but position himself as more collaborative and less 
confrontational than his famous uncles - Doug, a former councillor, and Rob, who died in 2016 after a long council 
Page 2 of 3
A Ford by name, not temperament Premier's nephew has been consulting public for months about potential run 
for mayor
stint and one scandal-plagued term as mayor - say people familiar with his deliberations but not authorized to 
discuss them.
Ford, they said, would "create some space between himself and the province," rather than run as a city hall proxy 
for his outspoken and hard-charging Uncle Doug, who as a Progressive Conservative premier, frequently 
intervenes in local Toronto issues such as keeping bike lanes off major arterial roads - a position Michael Ford says 
he shares.
The premier, for his part, has not appeared to be keen on the notion of his sister Kathy's son taking a run at Chow, 
with whom Doug Ford has forged an unlikely political partnership. "That's going to be strictly up to Michael," Doug 
Ford recently told reporters when asked about the potential candidacy that would continue a family tradition.
Although the mayoral musings caught former colleagues off guard, a little more than a year after he decided to not 
seek re-election to Queen's Park following a health leave, the fact he would present as a kinder, gentler Ford is no 
surprise.
"Michael Ford is a really nice guy - amicable with everyone and earnest, and he tries to be very helpful, cordial, 
collegial," said Liberal MPP Mary-Margaret McMahon, a former city council colleague who later, at Queen's Park, 
sat in opposition across from Ford when he was citizenship and multiculturalism minister.
"He had a good track record as school trustee and he really seemed to like being a city councillor."
Centre-right Coun. Jon Burnside said Ford's name immediately makes him a contender.
"He's every bit as passionate about public service, about the community, but he presents a little quieter," than his 
uncles, Burnside said, adding that Ford "would definitely be starting from behind" Bradford and Chow.
Coun. Gord Perks, a Chow ally, called Ford "profoundly arrogant" for thinking he could lead Canada's most 
populous city based on his track record at city hall as a one-term councillor.
"I can't think of a single thing that he actually accomplished when he was here," the longtime Parkdale 
representative said. "On the occasions when he did get up to say something at council, mostly it was just to talk 
about how great his uncles were."
NDP MPP Kristyn Wong-Tam, who also sat on council with Ford, called him "friendly ... extremely cordial and quite 
approachable," but said she doubts he can handle the demands of being Toronto mayor - a job that sometimes 
requires standing up to the premier.
"Michael's mayoral candidacy cannot be a surrogacy for Doug to hold a mayorship and to do the bidding of the 
premier," Wong-Tam said. "I think he would actually have to explain ... his bill of health to (Torontonians) to take on 
a job that requires a lot of energy, time and emotional, physical and intellectual commitment."
Ford rejected the notion of meagre accomplishments or fragile health. He said during his 2016-'22 council tenure he 
fought for "practical transit solutions," including light-rail lines, helped advance approvals for a major redevelopment 
of land around Woodbine race track and voted to keep property tax hikes as low as possible.
Noting he returned to Queen's Park after a two-month health leave, Ford said: "I made the personal decision not to 
seek re-election at that time, which also allowed me to consider future opportunities, including a potential mayoral 
run.
"Following my time at Queen's Park, I spent approximately three weeks in Thailand, where I travelled and 
participated in a fitness retreat." 
Ford's friends told the Star he does indeed appear healthier and happier, with a fitness regime.
Page 3 of 3
A Ford by name, not temperament Premier's nephew has been consulting public for months about potential run 
for mayor
Political observers say his future success in politics, however, comes down to platform and performance after being 
out of the public eye since leaving Queen's Park. 
Randy Besco, a University of Toronto political scientist, said that with no political parties at city hall "name 
recognition matters a lot," and that's why Michael Ford is already polling at 16 per cent support - a number that took 
Bradford a couple of years of unofficial campaigning to reach, before hitting 26 per cent following Tory's decision 
not to run.
This is despite "people having no idea what Ford has done or what he stands for," Besco said. "Even though 
Bradford has been around for a long time, still lots of people have never heard of him."

Body: Former city councillor and MPP Michael Ford, nephew of Premier Doug Ford, says he has been consulting 
Torontonians for "months" about a potential mayoral run on issues such as low property taxes, public safety and 
fighting traffic gridlock.
In a statement to the Star on Friday, Ford also seemed to take a veiled swipe at Coun. Brad Bradford - a potential 
mayoral rival on the political centre-right, with similar stated priorities - noting that as a city councillor, Ford was 
always "firmly opposed to calls to defund the police when some believed it was politically popular."
Bradford voted with some colleagues in 2020 for a failed motion to redirect some police funding to social programs. 
He later said he was reacting to a "particular moment in time," following the Minneapolis police murder of George 
Floyd, and as Toronto's next mayor would boost public safety and policing, including putting officers at every TTC 
station.
Ford's public musings about returning to politics, after low-profile stints at city hall and Queen's Park, and now as a 
lobbyist, toss a curveball into a campaign that doesn't officially start until May 1 but which has unofficially raged for 
months.
The spectre of another Ford at city hall comes shortly after former mayor John Tory abandoned thoughts of trying a 
comeback via a right-flank challenge to progressive Mayor Olivia Chow, who is expected to seek re-election.
It could also split the centre-right vote and present a serious challenge to Bradford, recently photographed meeting 
with Ford after the latter confirmed a potential candidacy.
Ford, noting he is giving "serious consideration" to a run, told the Star that "over the past several months, I've been 
meeting with people from across the city, including community leaders, representatives from Toronto's diverse 
cultural communities, business leaders, and current and former elected officials."
Calling such discussions "incredibly valuable," he said they will also continue with "family and close advisers." 
If Ford does run, he'll capitalize on name recognition but position himself as more collaborative and less 
confrontational than his famous uncles - Doug, a former councillor, and Rob, who died in 2016 after a long council

for mayor
stint and one scandal-plagued term as mayor - say people familiar with his deliberations but not authorized to 
discuss them.
Ford, they said, would "create some space between himself and the province," rather than run as a city hall proxy 
for his outspoken and hard-charging Uncle Doug, who as a Progressive Conservative premier, frequently 
intervenes in local Toronto issues such as keeping bike lanes off major arterial roads - a position Michael Ford says 
he shares.
The premier, for his part, has not appeared to be keen on the notion of his sister Kathy's son taking a run at Chow, 
with whom Doug Ford has forged an unlikely political partnership. "That's going to be strictly up to Michael," Doug 
Ford recently told reporters when asked about the potential candidacy that would continue a family tradition.
Although the mayoral musings caught former colleagues off guard, a little more than a year after he decided to not 
seek re-election to Queen's Park following a health leave, the fact he would present as a kinder, gentler Ford is no 
surprise.
"Michael Ford is a really nice guy - amicable with everyone and earnest, and he tries to be very helpful, cordial, 
collegial," said Liberal MPP Mary-Margaret McMahon, a former city council colleague who later, at Queen's Park, 
sat in opposition across from Ford when he was citizenship and multiculturalism minister.
"He had a good track record as school trustee and he really seemed to like being a city councillor."
Centre-right Coun. Jon Burnside said Ford's name immediately makes him a contender.
"He's every bit as passionate about public service, about the community, but he presents a little quieter," than his 
uncles, Burnside said, adding that Ford "would definitely be starting from behind" Bradford and Chow.
Coun. Gord Perks, a Chow ally, called Ford "profoundly arrogant" for thinking he could lead Canada's most 
populous city based on his track record at city hall as a one-term councillor.
"I can't think of a single thing that he actually accomplished when he was here," the longtime Parkdale 
representative said. "On the occasions when he did get up to say something at council, mostly it was just to talk 
about how great his uncles were."
NDP MPP Kristyn Wong-Tam, who also sat on council with Ford, called him "friendly ... extremely cordial and quite 
approachable," but said she doubts he can handle the demands of being Toronto mayor - a job that sometimes 
requires standing up to the premier.
"Michael's mayoral candidacy cannot be a surrogacy for Doug to hold a mayorship and to do the bidding of the 
premier," Wong-Tam said. "I think he would actually have to explain ... his bill of health to (Torontonians) to take on 
a job that requires a lot of energy, time and emotional, physical and intellectual commitment."
Ford rejected the notion of meagre accomplishments or fragile health. He said during his 2016-'22 council tenure he 
fought for "practical transit solutions," including light-rail lines, helped advance approvals for a major redevelopment 
of land around Woodbine race track and voted to keep property tax hikes as low as possible.
Noting he returned to Queen's Park after a two-month health leave, Ford said: "I made the personal decision not to 
seek re-election at that time, which also allowed me to consider future opportunities, including a potential mayoral 
run.
"Following my time at Queen's Park, I spent approximately three weeks in Thailand, where I travelled and 
participated in a fitness retreat." 
Ford's friends told the Star he does indeed appear healthier and happier, with a fitness regime.

for mayor
Political observers say his future success in politics, however, comes down to platform and performance after being 
out of the public eye since leaving Queen's Park. 
Randy Besco, a University of Toronto political scientist, said that with no political parties at city hall "name 
recognition matters a lot," and that's why Michael Ford is already polling at 16 per cent support - a number that took 
Bradford a couple of years of unofficial campaigning to reach, before hitting 26 per cent following Tory's decision 
not to run.
This is despite "people having no idea what Ford has done or what he stands for," Besco said. "Even though 
Bradford has been around for a long time, still lots of people have never heard of him."

title: A new reckoning for monarch who protected former prince New biographies offer insights on crises that rocked
body:
April 21 marks the 100th anniversary of the birth of Queen Elizabeth II. She spent 70 years on the throne crafting a 
reputation as a pragmatic monarch who knew her lane and stuck to it. Elizabeth knew that being in charge of a 
family business such as the House of Windsor meant her primary imperative was not to establish her own legacy 
but to hand over the throne in good shape to the next generation.
Now, less than four years after her death, a reappraisal has begun of a woman who, in private, was far more 
complex than she appeared in public. Two masterful new biographies by Hugo Vickers and Robert Hardman 
showcase a bounty of revelations from insiders, often talking on the record more frankly than they would have in the 
past for fear of upsetting the monarch or her family. 
In particular, they offer new insights on the crises of the last decade of Elizabeth's life, especially the departure of 
her grandson and his wife - Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex - and the long-running toxic scandal 
engulfing her son, the former prince Andrew, over his relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. 
While Harry and Meghan's actions distressed the monarch - she couldn't understand why her grandson abandoned 
his royal role to be "a carer for Archie," Vickers writes in "Queen Elizabeth II: A Personal History" - the Epstein 
scandal festered into a putrid sore on the monarchy, in part because Elizabeth had to be pushed to protect the 
monarchy from the actions of her boorish, self-centred son.
"The Queen did not believe he had behaved improperly," Vickers writes, adding, "It is fortunate that she did not live 
to witness the denouement." 
The ultimate human frailty
Throughout her reign, Elizabeth and her staff took drastic action to cauterize wounds that threatened her throne, 
including those from her own family. Elizabeth told her sister, Margaret, that she could marry her divorced love, but 
she'd have to give up her succession rights. She forced Charles and Diana to separate when their very public 
marital collapse endlessly dominated the front pages. After the Windsor Castle fire in 1992, the palace announced 
the Queen would pay taxes on her personal wealth and opened Buckingham Palace to visitors to pay for the 
restoration. More recently, the Queen nixed Harry and Meghan's desired half-in, half-out role, believing such 
intermingling of duty and commercial gain was a recipe for disaster.

Queen, Royal Family
Yet, she couldn't apply the same impersonal thinking with Andrew. "She loved her son; she trusted him," explained 
Hardman in an interview with the Star in London. At the same time, "She hated confrontation. She didn't want to be 
put in a formal situation where she might have to discipline Andrew but she knew what was happening." 
What is remarkable about Elizabeth's slow-mo decisions regarding Andrew is that pragmatism was her default 
setting throughout her reign, Hardman writes in his biography, "Elizabeth II: In Private. In Public. The Inside Story." 
She was able to modernize the institution of the monarchy but could not hold her son accountable. Her motherly 
protection of Andrew was the ultimate human frailty that hurt her reputation and that of the monarchy as the 
Andrew-Epstein scandal hung over the last years of her reign. Whenever she was forced to act, she did the bare 
minimum needed at the time.
In 2011, former prime minister David Cameron informed the Queen that Andrew would have to step down from his 
role as trade envoy, in part because of his friendship with Epstein - the British press had recently published an 
image of Andrew walking through Central Park with Jeffrey Epstein well after his conviction - and in part because 
the opinionated prince was offering too many inappropriate opinions to foreign leaders and diplomats. In Hardman's 
book, Cameron offers one bit of backhanded praise for Andrew: "He was very good with all the tyrants." 
Support amid scandals
In 2019, the Queen forced Andrew to cease being a working royal following his disastrous interview on the BBC 
regarding his relationship with Epstein, in which he cast doubt on Virginia Giuffre's claims that she was forced to 
have sex with Andrew by Epstein when she was an underage teen. But Andrew kept all other trappings of royal life, 
including his title, Duke of York. Three years later, just before he settled a civil case brought by Giuffre for a 
reported $20 million without admitting liability, the negative publicity over the case forced another royal retreat: 
Andrew gave up being called "His Royal Highness."
Yet, through those same years, Elizabeth repeatedly signalled her support for her embattled son. In 2017, two 
years after Giuffre's accusations became public, she appointed him colonel of the Grenadier Guards. A few months 
after settling the Giuffre civil case, he escorted his mother to the memorial service of Prince Philip at Westminster 
Abbey. 
The lingering Andrew mess was a rare exception to Elizabeth's pragmatic streak. Another was her decision not to 
fly the Union Jack over Buckingham Palace in the days following the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. Elizabeth 
refused to break the tradition of never flying a flag when the monarch was absent from her London home despite 
mounting public anger over the uncaring symbolism of an empty palace. "The times she put [pragmatism] on hold, it 
did not serve her well," Hardman told the Star.
The short-term damage to the monarchy can be seen in opinion polls. While Elizabeth's popularity is undented, 
YouGov reports that 58 per cent of Britons believe that the Royal Family reacted too slowly to the Epstein 
revelations while half say senior royals should have done more to condemn Andrew. 
A complicated legacy
As revelations continue to surface, the final reckoning may take time to appear. This month, Buckingham Palace 
will announce the name of Queen Elizabeth II's official biographer - believed to be Anna Keay - who will be given 
free rein to scour private diaries, archives and state documents. The massive research and writing process of 
documenting the life of one of the longest-reigning monarchs in history is daunting - Elizabeth's first Canadian 
prime minister, Louis St-Laurent was born in 1882; her last, Justin Trudeau, was born in 1971.
Now, it is King Charles III who is tackling the difficult issues left behind by his mother, especially the Andrew-
Epstein scandal, which turned white hot after the U.S. Department of Justice released millions of damaging 
documents that showed the extent of Andrew's relationship with Epstein. In October, the monarch summarily 
stripped his brother of all royal trappings, reducing him to Mr. Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. On Feb. 19, Andrew 
Page 3 of 4

Queen, Royal Family
was arrested by police in the United Kingdom on suspicion of misconduct in public office, believed to be related to 
his decade-long role as trade envoy. He has not been charged with any crime and has strenuously denied any 
wrongdoing. While Charles' short reign has been dogged by the Epstein scandal, it has been far more successful 
than critics expected.
"A lot of people predicted that when she died, the wheels would fall off; the monarchy would enter some existential 
crisis," writes Hardman. "It just hasn't happened." There was also a fear that most of the 15 realms of which King 
Charles III is head of state would quickly jettison the monarchy to become republics. That hasn't happened - yet. In 
Canada, the endless "whither the monarchy" debate largely stopped after the King issued an emotional defence of 
the country during his opening of Parliament in 2025. 
On Tuesday, the centenary of her birth, the royal family and public will see the final plans for a large memorial 
devoted to Elizabeth that will be constructed in parkland near Buckingham Palace. The King's brother is not 
expected to attend.

title: Accounting watchdog to investigate Deloitte over fake citations in $1.6-million healthcare report
body:
A professional accounting watchdog has launched an investigation into Deloitte’s production of a $1.6-million 
healthcare report to the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador which contained AI-generated errors.
After reviewing a complaint from a resident of the province, Chartered Professional Accountants Newfoundland 
and Labrador (CPANL) has decided to investigate Deloitte’s use of artificial intelligence in the Health Human 
Resources Plan the global accounting and consulting firm created for the province as part of the government’s 
efforts to address the crisis in healthcare staffing.
Provincial legislation gives CPANL the authority to investigate allegations against individuals or corporations which 
sell accounting services, determine whether the accused party is culpable of professional misconduct or 
professional incompetence, among other things. Part of the organization’s stated mission is to ensure its more 
 than 2,000 members “uphold the highest professional and ethics standards.”
Confirmation of the investigation was sent to Codroy Valley resident Chris Bruce, who filed the complaint last 
November after The Independent reported the Deloitte report contained errors likely generated by AI. CPANL 
Complaints Authorization Committee Chair Trevor McCormick says in his letter to Bruce that his committee “met to 
discuss and review” the complaint, and that it has “decided to conduct an investigation.”
Chris Bruce filed his complaint with CPANL Nov. 28, 2025. Photo submitted.
If the committee decides there are “reasonable grounds” to believe Deloitte “has engaged in conduct deserving of 
sanction,” according to the province’s Chartered Professional Accountants and Public Accountants Act, it can 
“suspend or restrict either or both” of Deloitte’s licence or certificate, refer the complaint to its disciplinary panel, or 
simply “counsel or caution” the firm.
In his complaint, Bruce said he has “substantial concerns” with Deloitte’s use of fabricated sources in the 
healthcare report, noting the firm had recently been caught in a similar scandal in Australia, in which Deloitte 
refunded a portion of public money it was paid to produce a report for the federal government.
Days after The Independent first reported the fake citations in Deloitte’s Health Human Resources Plan, an 
anonymous spokesperson for the firm admitted in an emailed statement that Deloitte used AI “to support a small 

Page 2 of 3
Accounting watchdog to investigate Deloitte over fake citations in $1.6-million healthcare report
number of research citations” in the report and said the firm was “revising the report to make a small number of 
citation corrections, which do not impact the report findings.” Deloitte “firmly stands behind the recommendations 
put forward,” the statement said.
Responding to the scandal, Premier Tony Wakeham instructed Government Services Minister Mike Goosney to 
develop guidelines “to stop this from happening in the future.” The government did not respond to The 
 Independent’s request for an update on the matter by the time of publication.
Bruce’s concerns go beyond Deloitte’s alleged minimal use of AI for the research citations. The fact AI was used 
for citations, in and of itself, is “ a very backwards way to do research,” he says. “That’s not how you’re supposed 
to research. You’re supposed to begin with a robust review of literature and then draw conclusions based on that.”
Bruce says Deloitte appears to have used AI “in bad faith,” saying the firm was “not trying to find the best path 
forward” for the province’s healthcare staffing crisis. “They were trying to sell a particular path.”
He wants Deloitte and CPANL to “be clear that fabricated sources are not acceptable,” Bruce writes in his 
complaint, and he wants this done “soon and loudly to restore public confidence.” Bruce also notes the province 
“shouldn’t be expected to pay anywhere near the full price,” which came in at $1.6 million for the 526-page report. 
“Further, every hour of additional government staff effort could and perhaps should be seen as damages,” he says 
in the complaint. “This is work the government shouldn’t need to do, and is a waste of valuable and scarce public 
 resources.
“The most important and immediate concern,” he says, “is the need for an admission that selling false sources is 
fraudulent business activity, and not acceptable from anyone, let alone Deloitte.” 
Deloitte Canada did not respond to The Independent’s request for comment.
