title: Close nomination loopholes exploited by Longest Ballot Committee, MPs say
body:
OTTAWA - A committee studying the impact of protest group the Longest Ballot Committee (LBC) in recent 
Canadian elections is calling on Parliament to close nomination loopholes the group has used to flood ballots with 
paper candidates.
In a report released Tuesday( 
https://www.ourcommons.ca/Content/Committee/451/PROC/Reports/RP13978481/procrp20/procrp20-e.pdf ), MPs 
representing a multipartisan House of Commons committee on democratic procedures recommended multiple 
revisions to the Elections Act to make it harder for frivolous candidates to appear on the ballot. Such revisions 
include a prohibition on signing more than one candidate's nomination papers per cycle and, pivotally, an 
amendment to prohibit individuals from serving as the official agent for more than one candidate per electoral 
district.
LBC member Tomas Szuchewycz has been the official agent for hundreds of protest candidates in eight federal 
election races since 2021, including more than 200 candidates( https://www.oyenecho.com/articles/214-candidates-
on-battle-river-crowfoot-ballot ) in last summer's byelection in Battle River-Crowfoot, Alta.
The report said that allowing an individual to be the official agent for more than one candidate in a given riding 
"seems to run contrary to the very nature of elections, which are competitive contests, with only one candidate 
declared the winner in every riding."
"If anything, having the same official agent for two or more candidates who are competing against each other in the 
same riding places the official agent in an apparent, if not real, conflict of interest," continues the report.
The report also delved into allegations of questionable practices by the LBC in nominating candidates, including 
accusations that the group collected signatures on a nomination form where the candidate's name was left blank in 
contravention of the law.
Tomas Szuchewycz denied this accusation in a statement, saying that the MP's on the committee got 
"bamboozled" by the deceptive editing of right-leaning YouTube channel( 
https://www.youtube.com/@northernperspective00 ) Northern Perspective.
Page 2 of 3
Close nomination loopholes exploited by Longest Ballot Committee, MPs say
"This is just another clear example which demonstrates exactly why MPs should not be in charge of their own 
election rules, wrote Szuchewycz. "(They) were so eager to believe anything that would put the (LBC) in a bad light, 
they left their critical faculties at the door."
The report noted that there were "approximately 18,000 complaints" submitted to elections officials about the LBC's 
activities during the April 2025 general election.
Bonnie Critchley, who ran as an independent in the Battle River-Crowfoot byelection, estimates the LBC cost her 
"at least 20 per cent of the vote."
Critchley, who finished runner-up to Pierre Poilievre with just under 10 per cent of the vote( 
https://enr.elections.ca/ElectoralDistricts.aspx?ed=2530&;lang=e ), says the LBC hampered her ability to run a non-
partisan, local issues focused campaign.
She noted that her name was lost in a sea of hundreds of gag candidates, who also bore the "independent" label, in 
printed candidate lists distributed to voters.
"Deputy returning officers at multiple polling stations were witnessed handing out a book of candidate names with 
those attached to parties listed at the front and independents listed at the back," said Critchley.
Critchley says her team lodged multiple complaints about the LBC.
Szuchewycz, for his part, was unrepentant about the LBC's activities and said the group will move forward with a 
plan to flood the ballot in the upcoming Apr. 13 byelection in Terrebonne, Qc.
"The only recommended change that would impact us would be a new ban on voters nominating more than one 
candidate, but we are looking forward to meeting this new challenge," wrote Szuchewycz.
Government House Leader Steven MacKinnon, the minister responsible for the Elections Act, didn't immediately 
reply to a media inquiry about the report.

title: Coleman hears public input on future of Bass Lake campground
body:
Sue Nielsen
Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
COLEMAN TOWNSHIP — The ongoing issue of how to handle upgrades to the Bass Lake campground were 
addressed at a public meeting April 20 at the Coleman Township hall on Marsh Bay Road.
There were 50 people in attendance, 32 were in person and 18 were watching online.
The purpose of the meeting was to hear from campers, taxpayers and others about the future of Bass Lake Park.
“It really was meant as an opportunity for the public to provide feedback to council,” said CAO Chris Oslund.
Coleman has identified significant upgrades needed for the upper and lower campgrounds that include septic 
system improvements, electrical upgrades and new water lines. The upgrades have been pegged at roughly $1 
million in total costs.
The campground infrastructure dates back to 1977 after the Cobalt fire when the upper campground was created.
The township has presented four options for the future of the site:
• continue the full campground operations for both the upper and lower campgrounds, which would require major 
upgrades
• close the lower campground with the exception of the Lodge and three cabins to continue a revenue stream
• close the upper campground and continue using the lower area and the lodge and cabins
• shift the focus away from camping and allow day-use only with the public accessing the beach area and the 
cabins and lodge.
NOHFC FUNDING

Page 2 of 3
Coleman hears public input on future of Bass Lake campground
The township has applied for Northern Ontario Heritage Fund Corporation (NOHFC) funding of $500,000 to help 
with the upgrade costs.
Chamber of Commerce member Darcy Griffith was the master of ceremonies for the public portion of the meeting 
where people in attendance and online could voice their thoughts on the four options.
Each speaker had five minutes to sum up their thoughts on the park’s future.
”I grew up at Bass Lake, it was the place to go. I feel option four is the best way to go,” said Gino Chitaroni, 
Coleman resident and owner of Portage Bay Lodge.
“There are lots of opportunities for back-lot sales in the upper campground, sell it off. I am in favour of keeping the 
lower campground. Option four would also be the cheapest. I want to commend council on this work, these are 
difficult decisions and it all costs money. This is a very emotional issue for people.”
He said he felt it was unfair to his business that the township is operating Bass Lake as a tourist camp destination.
“I have not seen a decent business plan on the options and I would like to see better numbers.”
Suzanne Paquette, an upper campground user, said she has camped there for 13 years and she wondered why 
couldn’t the entire upgrades for the park be put into one project for funding.
She referred to a letter she received from the township on April 9 stating the upper campground is closed until 
further notice saying this was concerning and wonders “when can we access our spaces at the upper 
campground?”
Oslund said the township is having an Environmental Compliance Approval (ECA) assessment done of the septic 
system in the upper campground, which has been contracted to Phippen Waste Management.
“We want to see what is going on there and the inspection is weather-dependent. I don’t anticipate it will take that 
long.”
Councillor Lois Perry said the Bass Lake campground normally opens the May long weekend and she said there is 
plenty of time for the inspection to take place.
In the meantime a letter was sent to the campers stating the upper park is closed until the ECA process has been 
completed on the septic system in the upper campground. Oslund estimated this will likely be done by mid-May.
BEAUTIFUL PARK
Laura Seguin owns a trailer in the upper campground and has been enjoying Bass Lake for the last six years.
She spoke about the beauty of the park and how much her two children love to spend time at the lake.
“The park means a great deal to my family,” she said. “It’s been difficult to explain to my kids what is going on at the 
park. We have a real community at the park in the summer. This needs to be really thought out before it is taken 
away. You need a business plan for the park instead of flying by the seat of your pants.”
Richard Simpkin owns a trailer in the upper campground and he is concerned about the upper park being closed. 
He asked if he would be able to get into the park and see his property as he may wish to sell his trailer.
Oslund assured him that they could make arrangements for him to visit his trailer whenever he deems it necessary.
Wayne Knight, a Coleman resident and manager of the Bass Lake Park last year, said he feels there are many 
ways the township can improve the park without huge costs. He believes if the upper campground was opened up 
and more trailer spaces created that would increase revenues.
Page 3 of 3
Coleman hears public input on future of Bass Lake campground
Francine Brazeau, who has a home on Bass Lake, asked council to provide more detailed documentation about the 
park including a business plan and how many employees are needed to maintain the facility.
Joe Duval, who also has a home on Bass Lake, said he was concerned that there are still many unresolved issues 
with no documentation at the park.
“Do not open the campground without standards being met. I agree with Gino, this is a conflict of interest with 
other campgrounds in the township.”
There were three letters sent to the township from taxpayers about the future of Bass Lake.
One of those letters referred to having a Bass Lake committee to oversee the operations of the park.
Councillor Perry explained at this time that it might not be the best time for committee input and she said all of the

Title: Coleman hears public input on future of Bass Lake campground

Body: Sue Nielsen
Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
COLEMAN TOWNSHIP — The ongoing issue of how to handle upgrades to the Bass Lake campground were 
addressed at a public meeting April 20 at the Coleman Township hall on Marsh Bay Road.
There were 50 people in attendance, 32 were in person and 18 were watching online.
The purpose of the meeting was to hear from campers, taxpayers and others about the future of Bass Lake Park.
“It really was meant as an opportunity for the public to provide feedback to council,” said CAO Chris Oslund.
Coleman has identified significant upgrades needed for the upper and lower campgrounds that include septic 
system improvements, electrical upgrades and new water lines. The upgrades have been pegged at roughly $1 
million in total costs.
The campground infrastructure dates back to 1977 after the Cobalt fire when the upper campground was created.
The township has presented four options for the future of the site:
• continue the full campground operations for both the upper and lower campgrounds, which would require major 
upgrades
• close the lower campground with the exception of the Lodge and three cabins to continue a revenue stream
• close the upper campground and continue using the lower area and the lodge and cabins
• shift the focus away from camping and allow day-use only with the public accessing the beach area and the 
cabins and lodge.
NOHFC FUNDING

Page 2 of 3
Coleman hears public input on future of Bass Lake campground
The township has applied for Northern Ontario Heritage Fund Corporation (NOHFC) funding of $500,000 to help 
with the upgrade costs.
Chamber of Commerce member Darcy Griffith was the master of ceremonies for the public portion of the meeting 
where people in attendance and online could voice their thoughts on the four options.
Each speaker had five minutes to sum up their thoughts on the park’s future.
”I grew up at Bass Lake, it was the place to go. I feel option four is the best way to go,” said Gino Chitaroni, 
Coleman resident and owner of Portage Bay Lodge.
“There are lots of opportunities for back-lot sales in the upper campground, sell it off. I am in favour of keeping the 
lower campground. Option four would also be the cheapest. I want to commend council on this work, these are 
difficult decisions and it all costs money. This is a very emotional issue for people.”
He said he felt it was unfair to his business that the township is operating Bass Lake as a tourist camp destination.
“I have not seen a decent business plan on the options and I would like to see better numbers.”
Suzanne Paquette, an upper campground user, said she has camped there for 13 years and she wondered why 
couldn’t the entire upgrades for the park be put into one project for funding.
She referred to a letter she received from the township on April 9 stating the upper campground is closed until 
further notice saying this was concerning and wonders “when can we access our spaces at the upper 
campground?”
Oslund said the township is having an Environmental Compliance Approval (ECA) assessment done of the septic 
system in the upper campground, which has been contracted to Phippen Waste Management.
“We want to see what is going on there and the inspection is weather-dependent. I don’t anticipate it will take that 
long.”

plenty of time for the inspection to take place.

completed on the septic system in the upper campground. Oslund estimated this will likely be done by mid-May.

title: Complaint last summer spurred probe into councillor OPP investigating politician accused of soliciting money
body:
The complaint that appears to have prompted a police investigation into a Scarborough city councillor was 
referred to law enforcement last summer, according to Toronto's ethics watchdog.
The office of integrity commissioner Paul Muldoon confirmed Tuesday that it received a complaint about Coun. 
Parthi Kandavel on July 8, 2025. The watchdog said it passed the file to the Toronto Police Service two weeks later, 
on July 22.
Toronto police haven't confirmed when they were made aware of allegations against Kandavel, but have said they 
referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police in order to avoid any perceived conflict of interest. The OPP's 
investigation is ongoing, according to the provincial force. 
The authorities and Kandavel haven't divulged the nature of the allegations against him. But as the Star reported 
Monday, the investigation appears to be focused on the councillor's dealings with developers. 
One source, who spoke to the Star on condition of anonymity due to fears of political retribution and professional 
fallout, said they were left with the impression Kandavel wanted a substantial payment to allow a development in his 
ward to proceed. 
Kandavel, who was elected to represent Scarborough Southwest in November 2023, has denied any wrongdoing, 
and has said he has "strived to maintain the highest standards of ethics and integrity." 
"I am still learning about these allegations, and it is not lost on me that they've come during the election period.
 Regardless, my intention is to respect the process and let the OPP complete their work," he said in a statement 
Monday.
The councillor has said he learned of the investigation last Friday. 
The integrity commissioner is responsible for investigating potential breaches of council's code of conduct. 
Page 2 of 3
Complaint last summer spurred probe into councillor OPP investigating politician accused of soliciting money 
from developers
A spokesperson for Muldoon wouldn't provide details of the July 2025 complaint, but said that under the City of 
Toronto Act, the commissioner is obligated to "immediately refer the matter to appropriate authorities" if they 
determine there are "reasonable grounds" to believe the Criminal Code or other legislation has been violated. 
Under the act, the commissioner must also suspend its investigation pending the outcome of the police probe and 
any resulting charges. 
The commissioner wouldn't say who filed the complaint, or confirm news, reported Tuesday by the Star, that it was 
lodged by a representative of the owners of a development in Kandavel's ward.
 The company's lawyer said that someone acting on behalf of the corporation, called Kennedy Road Holdings Ltd., 
complained to the commissioner. The lawyer wouldn't say what the complaint related to, other than to stress his 
clients weren't under investigation. 
The OPP has sought information about the Kennedy development as part of its probe, according to a source.
The company's representative filed the complaint less than two weeks after its development at 708-712 Kennedy 
Rd. went to city council. Staff had previously expressed concerns about the size of the project just south of Eglin- 
ton Avenue, which proposed 682 units in two towers of 21 and 42 storeys. 
On June 9, 2025, the owners offered the city a settlement that would resolve their appeal of the project at the 
Ontario Land Tribunal. They proposed reducing the height of the highest tower by four storeys and providing 1,500 
square feet of non-residential space in the building.
A source, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to share the information, said 
that at council's June 25-26, 2025 meeting, the city solicitor recommended in a confidential report that the city 
accept the offer.
Kandavel moved a motion on the second day of the session amending her advice, however, directing council to 
approve the settlement but attaching a requirement that the developers provide 4,000 square feet of non-residential 
space. 
Last October, the land tribunal sided with the company and said that amount wasn't justified. 
Toronto's municipal election is Oct. 26. Before news of the investigation broke, Kandavel said he planned run for re-
election. He has not yet registered. Nominations opened May 1.

title: Complaints against feds inundate watchdog Fiscal update failed to fix funding crisis, integrity chief says
body:
The regime to investigate wrongdoing and protect whistleblowers within the federal government is on the verge of 
collapse under a relentless surge of allegations and complaints, Canada's integrity commissioner says - and the 
fiscal update did nothing to address the growing problem. 
Public sector integrity commissioner Harriet Solloway described Wednesday how her team of nine investigators and 
seven lawyers is drowning under a deepening caseload it doesn't have the resources to get under control.
Her request to have $14 million added to her office's annual budget - pegged at almost $8.2 million in the 2025-26 
fiscal year - went unanswered in Tuesday's spring economic statement that detailed tens of billions of dollars in new 
spending by the federal government. 
Now, with a backlog of more than 300 submissions waiting for initial assessments, and 73 investigations currently 
underway, Solloway says she can no longer guarantee her office will be able to examine all the complaints and 
allegations that need to be investigated, while those already underway will take years to finish. 
In the fiscal year that ended in March, her office received 680 submissions for investigation, up 56 per cent from the 
previous year, and more than double the number from two years earlier. 
"At what point in time - and this is more a question than a statement - does the investigation become almost futile? 
If it takes three years, four years, five years, six years, is that helpful?" she asked. "We're on the precipice, if not 
over it."
Solloway said it's not clear what is driving the surge of complaints.
"What I believe is happening is that knowledge of (the office) has been increasing," she said, referring to the more 
330,000 workers in the federal public service. 
Since it was established in 2007, in the aftermath of what became known as the "sponsorship scandal," the 
mandate of the public sector integrity commissioner has been to investigate allegations of significant wrongdoing 
within government, as well as complaints of reprisals from whistleblowers. Both categories have "skyrocketed" in 
recent years, Solloway said.
Page 2 of 2
Complaints against feds inundate watchdog Fiscal update failed to fix funding crisis, integrity chief says
Her office also accepts submissions from the public, which has led to an increase in general inquiries as well as 
"misguided" complaints from people who report things like how they dislike the prime minister or their local MP. 
As more people become aware of her office, Solloway fears an "exponential effect" that will mean further increases 
in complaints, allegations and inquiries for the "foreseeable" future. 
"There's no end in sight," she said. "It's rising every week."
Solloway and her team have tried to address the situation before. After she was appointed in September 2023, 
Solloway asked the government for an additional $1.6 million to deal with the problem, but got $900,000, she said. 
In 2025, her office requested $7.9 million and received $1 million. 
Solloway said continuing delays could eventually discourage people with legitimate allegations from submitting 
them, since they won't have faith the office can get to them in a timely manner.
Investigations can also be hampered, she said, as evidence disappears or the memories of potential witnesses 
fade, and any "deterrence effect" could be lost if wrongdoing isn't consistently investigated.
She said her office is working to make investigations more efficient and has managed to complete a growing 
number of analyses in recent years - up from 157 in 2020-21 to 558 in 2025-26.

title: Conestoga audit raised red flags over 'significant non-compliance'
body:
Conestoga College handed out pay raises with no justification, awarded contracts to higher bidders without 
explanation, allowed an executive to take part in recruiting their daughter into a management position, and had 
such poor oversight of procurements and purchase orders that one for $11,000 was recorded at $126 billion - and 
no one noticed.
These are among the damning details contained in a recent, confidential two-part audit of the Kitchener-area 
college that rates the school as "high" risk, according to executive summaries obtained by the Star.
The provincial auditors also recommend the college "recalculate" a controversial retirement package for former 
longtime president John Tibbits - estimated at around $4 million - and "obtain legal advice to assess whether an 
overpayment occurred and determine appropriate remediation."
The auditors' findings, submitted to the government in January and April, prompted Colleges and Universities 
Minister Nolan Quinn last week to fire the board of governors and appoint a supervisor to run the school. 
While the college has rules around expenses and procurements, "as well as a board of governors with defined roles 
... our audit identified pervasive non-compliance with (public sector) requirements and Conestoga policies," one of 
the summaries states. 
" ... Our audit identified numerous control failures that collectively diminish transparency to stakeholders, weaken 
the college's ability to demonstrate prudent stewardship and value for money, and increase the risk for fraud."
Phase two "found that Conestoga has significant control weaknesses in executive compensation governance, hiring 
practices, and related oversight processes," and "significant non-compliance" with public sector salary laws, with 
auditors blaming the "most significant issues" on negligent oversight by senior leaders and the board of governors.
Last Thursday, in a first for Ontario, the government sacked the college's board and appointed Linda Franklin, the 
former longtime president and CEO of Colleges Ontario, to be its administrator. 
Quinn has told reporters that Tibbits' 55 per cent salary increase over two years, hitting a high of $636,000 - making 
him the highest paid in the sector - was "egregious" and prompted the audit, which then uncovered numerous areas 
of concern. 
Page 2 of 3
Conestoga audit raised red flags over 'significant non-compliance'
Conestoga had come under heavy criticism for its massive growth in international students in recent years, and was 
blamed in part for the federal government cutting back on its numbers; at one point, the college had the most 
foreign students of any post-secondary institution in the country. 
The audit notes that in 2023-24, the college had a surplus of $251 million, and a $121-million surplus in 2024-25 - 
but amid a 62 per cent drop in international students, it was projecting a deficit this school year, and it warns that 
colleges in general are grappling with reductions in revenue that could "(create) potential fiscal exposure for the 
province."
Conestoga has also implemented the deepest job cuts out of all the Ontario colleges, with about 550 layoffs in the 
last year alone, and the local union estimates a total of 2,700 losses in the past couple of years. 
The auditors' findings touch on several areas, and they note lax controls over purchase orders, including one 
valued at $11,000 recorded as $126 billion and another valued at $15,000 recorded as $261 million.
"Both errors remained uncorrected and open at the time of our audit, indicating significant weaknesses in purchase 
order review and approval processes," one audit summary states. "This deficiency increases the risk of 
overpayments to vendors, spending beyond approved limits," plus "heightened exposure to fraud or 
misappropriations due to the lack of effective oversight." (The orders were corrected after the provincial auditors 
pointed them out.)
In procurements, the college provided "no documented rationale for higher-priced vendor selection, as high was 
$57,240 compared to the lowest bid of $45,000," the auditors said, and in one case, work began before a contract 
was in place.
As for travel and food expenses by senior staffers, pre-approvals were missing, "inconsistent, retroactive and 
undocumented," along with "selection of premium accommodations without required approvals and supporting 
documentation," including a $23,000 trip to Italy. They also found prohibited claims for alcohol, including a $1,300 
dinner for Conestoga executives, where drinks comprised about half the bill.
On the job front, they found candidates were sourced "through informal referrals," an executive who didn't declare a 
conflict in their daughter's recruitment and eventual hiring, and urged the college to "implement a formal recruitment 
process that includes public postings, structured evaluation criteria, and documented rationale for all selection 
decisions." In some cases, lower-scoring applicants were hired without explanation. 
In its response, the college agreed to the auditors' recommendations in all areas, including tightening procurement 
and purchasing, and improving transparency and documentation around hirings, promotions and pay raises. 
"Management acknowledges (government auditor) recommendations and has committed to the following action 
plans: Conestoga should enforce mandatory written pre-approvals, prohibit retroactive approvals, and strengthen 
documentation standards for travel and hospitality expenses ... and agrees that strengthening controls around travel 
and hospitality expenditures will enhance compliance, transparency, and financial stewardship," states the college's 
response.
The auditors also found salary and termination payments went beyond what's allowed, and that executives were 
given pay hikes without proper proof that the extra pay was necessary, and estimated the college spent about $1 
million over six years in raises for executives alone, despite a provincial freeze on wage hikes.
As for Tibbits, auditors "identified two postfreeze increases to the president's non-salary compensation terms, a 
retirement allowance from 12 to 24 months, and a vacation carry-forward from a 10-day maximum to 196 banked 
days."
Tibbits retired suddenly in January, and his package was voted on by the board despite members saying they were 
not provided any particulars; last week, the province said the former president's payout was equal to 83 times his 
monthly salary.
Page 3 of 3
Conestoga audit raised red flags over 'significant non-compliance'
While recommending seeking legal advice, the auditors said "payments made under the president's retirement 
agreement at the end of employment exceeded the limits established in the executive compensation framework, 
and the college's calculation may have also overstated the retirement allowance. These conditions created 
significant compliance and financial exposure, including the potential for overpayments equal to at a minimum 
approximately five years of salary."

title: Conservatives call on Carney not to 'stack the deck' by using majority to shut opposition out of committees
body:
OTTAWA - The Opposition Conservatives are calling on the Liberals not to overhaul the makeup of parliamentary 
committees, which Prime Minister Mark Carney signalled would be coming in the wake of securing a majority.
Conservative House Leader Andrew Scheer appeared before reporters on Thursday to underscore how the 
membership of committees - bodies where MPs can launch studies into issues and where legislation is sent to be 
dissected and amended - has up until now been decided through negotiations between the parties based on the 
most recent election results.
"We are in unprecedented territory," Scheer said, referring to how the Carney government elevated its status to 
majority from minority on Monday, thanks to three byelection wins but in large part because of five MPs crossing the 
floor, four of which came from the Conservatives and one from the New Democrats.
He called on the majority Liberals to "uphold the tradition" that the makeup of committees be decided by the 
outcome of the last election.
In last April's general election, Carney won a minority with 169 seats in the House of Commons. The Conservatives 
had 144 seats, with the Bloc Quebecois at 22 and the New Democrats at 7.
The Liberals went into Monday's three byelections one seat shy of crossing that 172-seat majority threshold, which 
it did by winning those races, increasing its seat count to 174. With four MPs defecting to the Liberals, Conservative 
Leader Pierre Poilievre saw his seat count in the House of Commons drop to 140, while the NDP now have six 
MPs.
Poilievre has slammed Carney's majority as being achieved through "backroom deals," which Scheer repeated on 
Thursday.
"Never before has the prime minister fundamentally tried to change the nature of the government that he was 
elected on from the people through these kinds of backroom deals, so we are in unprecedented territory."
"We are calling on Liberals not to stack the deck."
Page 2 of 3
Conservatives call on Carney not to 'stack the deck' by using majority to shut opposition out of committees
Earlier this week, Carney signalled that he has his sights set on changing the makeup of committees to reflect the 
majority the Liberals now have in Parliament and to reduce what the prime minister characterized as 
"showboating" he has seen from opposition MPs at some meetings.
Opposition MPs can use committee tactics to force delays or amendments to government legislation.
Since Carney assumed office last year, the Liberals have repeatedly accused the Conservatives of blocking 
progress on numerous pieces of government legislation.
Poilievre's Conservatives have pointed the finger back at the Liberals for how the party has handled its own 
agenda. However, since the start of 2026 the Conservatives have adopted a more collaborative tone, in part to 
avoid giving the Liberals reason to seek a snap election, saying it was willing to support government bills where it 
found agreement.
When it comes to forthcoming committee changes, Government House Leader Steven MacKinnon told reporters on 
Wednesday that he believed it to be "pretty generally accepted" that the makeup of committees reflect the number 
of seats parties have in the House of Commons.
On Thursday, Scheer said MacKinnon has not reached out to discuss changes to committees.
In a statement, MacKinnon reiterated his position that the makeup of these bodies ought to reflect the number of 
seats in the House of Commons, calling that a "long-established principle."
"There will be proposals made in this regard in due course. We'll have news soon on that."
Scheer defended the role Conservative MPs have played on committees over the years, saying their members 
have driven investigations into how the government has handled issues from Indigenous procurement to contracts 
related to the ArriveCAN app.
"At the very least, they should preserve the power of the opposition to investigate Liberal corruption scandals and 
to litigate bad Liberal policy," he said.

title: Conservatives say Champagne is avoiding committee study into Alto rail connection
body:
OTTAWA - The Conservatives are accusing the Liberals of blocking a House of Commons committee from 
questioning Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne about his personal connection to the Alto high-speed 
rail project.
Champagne's partner, Anne-Marie Gaudet, is a vice-president of environment at Alto, the Crown corporation 
responsible for the $90-billion rail project that would connect Toronto and Quebec City. She was hired in August 
2025.
Conservative ethics critic Michael Barrett tried to launch a study at the ethics committee to question Champagne, 
the CEO of Alto Martin Imbleau and Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner Konrad von Finckenstein about 
the minister's relationship with Gaudet and the decisions he's made in government since she was hired.
"We are facing a filibuster that's gone on for more than 12 hours, a Liberal filibuster designed to block basic 
accountability," Barrett said Thursday.
John Fragos, a spokesperson for the Office of the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, said in an email that 
it’s up to parliamentary committees themselves to agree on which individuals they’d like to see testify.
"What’s already agreed upon, however, is the understanding that the minister acted proactively and above and 
beyond the guidance outlined in the act to safeguard against the perception of a conflict," he said. "The 
commissioner himself determined as much in August, saying, 'There is no risk of a conflict and no screen is 
required.'"
"The minister opted to recuse himself anyway and had a screen imposed proactively."
After questions arose in the media about Champagne's connection to Alto, the finance minister's office shared a 
letter he sent last September to Prime Minister Mark Carney and to von Finckenstein.
The letter states that Champagne was proactively implementing a conflict-of-interest screen "due to a personal 
connection to someone close to me in the organization, to safeguard against any real or perceived conflict of 
interest."

Page 2 of 3
Conservatives say Champagne is avoiding committee study into Alto rail connection
Champagne's office said the minister has not participated in any discussions or decisions tied to Alto since then. 
His office also said the initial funding for the project was announced in February 2025 and allocated in the main 
estimates in 2025, all before Gaudet was hired.
A compliance officer in the ethics commissioner's office wrote to Champagne earlier this month to say there was no 
risk of a conflict because "Alto is a Crown corporation accountable to Parliament through the minister of transport 
and as minister of finance you have no decision-making authority over matters of human resources at Alto, you do 
not have an opportunity to further the interest of any specific Alto employee."
Barrett has formally asked the conflict of interest and ethics commissioner to investigate.
He pointed out that the government included legislation to enable the Alto project in its omnibus budget bill, which 
Champagne introduced and championed in Parliament.
"Why wasn't the bill with respect to the high-speed rail network act brought forward by the transport minister and 
not by the finance minister?" he asked.
During the ethics committee's last meeting, MPs debated for hours but did not vote on whether the minister should 
appear to answer questions.
The Liberals have four members on the committee, while the Conservatives have four and the Bloc Québécois has 
one. That means opposition members could outvote the government members and request that Champagne 
appear.
"This is the opposite of what the prime minister said that Canadians should expect from parliamentarians at 
committee, and it is counter to the basic accountability that Canadians should demand of all parliamentarians," 
Barrett said Thursday.
Earlier this week, Carney told reporters that his new majority Liberal government would engage in serious debate 
and accused the opposition of "showboating" and filibustering in committee.
Now that the Liberals have a majority, they could vote in the House of Commons to change the makeup of 
committees. Majority governments historically have held a majority of seats on committees — a key step in the 
legislative process where bills are scrutinized and amended.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published April 16, 2026.

title: Converting to Christianity 'the easiest way' to get asylum for Iranians in Canada
body:
VANCOUVER - At a downtown Vancouver church, a Christian baptism takes place during a recent Sunday service. 
Amid?the incense and infants dressed in white getting ready to receive the holy water is a group of four Iranian 
nationals also waiting to receive adult baptisms.
As with past baptisms, some of them will likely not return to the church after receiving their baptismal certificate. It is 
simply a means to an end - claiming asylum.
When a parishioner congratulates one of the newly baptized Farsi speakers, mentioning Iran's significant Christian 
and Jewish populations, as well as Muslim, they reply in heavily accented English.
"I hate Muslims."
While not quite the Christian message one might have expected, the conversion of Iranians to Christianity has been 
an increasingly popular trend over the past decade (one study( https://spectator.com/article/iranians-are-risking-
everything-to-convert-to-christianity/ ) suggests as many as 1.2 million Christian converts in Iran alone).
It seems partly motivated by contempt for Iran's authoritarian regime, which is conflated with the faith of over a 
billion people - the same sentiment shared by crowds of anti-regime protesters flooding the downtown cores of 
Canadian cities most weekends since late December.
But it's also a pragmatic way to gain asylum at a time when war and sanctions make Iran a difficult place to live, say 
community leaders, experts and other insiders.
In 2025, there were just over 7,100 asylum claims in Canada from Iranian nationals, the third largest number of 
claims by country of alleged persecution after India and Haiti. Approximately half - 3,456 - were accepted, according 
to figures( https://irb-cisr.gc.ca/en/statistics/protection/Pages/RPDStat2025.aspx ) from the Immigration and 
Refugee Board of Canada, while 11,448 Iranian asylum claims are still pending. It is unknown how many of those 
were claims related to religious conversion.
While there is technically religious freedom for "native" Iranian Christians, mainly Armenians and Assyrians, 
conversion from Islam to another faith can be grounds for persecution - including execution - based on Iran's 
apostasy laws.
Page 2 of 4
Converting to Christianity 'the easiest way' to get asylum for Iranians in Canada
The conversion route to asylum and immigration fraud has been well publicized in the United Kingdom, where a 
2024 public inquiry( https://www.infomigrants.net/fr/post/55113/uk-government-launches-probe-into-migrant-
conversions-to-christianity ) by the Home Secretary held Church of England officials to account for alleged 
complicity in fraud and collusion with people smugglers. Justin Welby, Archbishop of Canterbury at the time, 
refuted claims that the church was a "conveyor belt for asylum seeker fake conversions( 
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2024/feb/10/c-of-e-refutes-claims-of-conveyor-belt-of-asylum-seeker-fake-
conversions )."
Former Canadian Border Services officers and community leaders say it is happening here too. While there are 
undoubtedly many sincere seekers amid the converted, the coveted baptismal certificate has become a commodity 
for many seeking refuge from Iran, be they dissidents, economic migrants or, as some contend, vehicles for IRGC 
members to enter the country.
"It's the easiest way to get asylum," said Kelly Sundberg, a former CBSA agent turned criminology professor at 
Mount Royal University in Calgary, "and not only for Iranians."
He told the National Post that during his time as an officer he saw dozens of bogus asylum claims from Iranians 
based on fake conversions to Christianity, but he "turned a blind eye" to "people who were just trying to have a 
better life" and who, in his estimation, posed no security threat. In fact, he said that he and his understaffed 
colleagues were "more concerned about Christian Canadians embracing Islam."
In the past few years, he said, that has changed dramatically.
After the protests in Iran in 2022,( https://nationalpost.com/opinion/terry-glavin-mahsa-aminis-death-epitomizes-the-
depravity-of-irans-theocratic-regime ) he contends, members of the regime "saw the writing on the wall" and were 
coming to Canada for both their own survival and often to spy upon immigrant communities.
According to some published reports( https://thehub.ca/2026/03/06/u-s-intelligence-sees-canada-as-serious-place-
of-concern-for-iranian-activity-national-security-analyst/ ) there are "hundreds" of Iranians connected to the regime 
in Canada, and 20 "senior Iranian officials" living in Vancouver, which has one of the largest Iranian diasporas in 
North America after Los Angeles and Toronto.
Canada officially listed( https://www.canada.ca/en/public-safety-canada/news/2024/06/government-of-canada-
lists-the-irgc-as-a-terrorist-entity.html ) the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist entity in June 
2024. There have been reports of IRGC people pretending to be dissidents to hide their identity.
On March 10 in Parliament, Green Party leader Elizabeth May expressed concerns( 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O--FiQgPfzw ) about IRGC agents converting to Christianity as a means to 
claim asylum in Canada.
"The way you can tell who is an IRGC member," said Farid Rohani, a prominent Vancouver businessman and 
Iranian community member "is if they convert to Judaism." He was only half-joking. Rohani, a past Vancouver chair 
of the Institute for Canadian Citizenship, said there have been cases of Iranians converting to Judaism as a means 
of both seeking asylum and establishing a deep cover.
Rohani, who is a Bahai, said that his own religious community has thwarted such immigration fraud by making a 
rule that no Iranian national can convert before they have received permanent resident status.
He is concerned about the fraudulent conversions because they are "unfair to legitimate asylum seekers who get 
pushed to the back of the line." Rohani, who participates in many interfaith activities, said he has spoken to 
Christian priests locally about the issue, including an Anglican minister, who seemed unconcerned and told him, 
"the word of God can change things."
"I think the church is trying to raise an army," he said. "Whoever has more soldiers in the end is the winner." What is 
certain is that traditional mainstream Canadian churches are seeing an alarming drop in numbers( 
Page 3 of 4
Converting to Christianity 'the easiest way' to get asylum for Iranians in Canada
https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/article/new-report-suggests-opening-churches-to-the-masses-as-attendance-
dwindles/ ) and welcome new parishioners.
Rohani doubts that Iranian Muslims who convert to Christianity are at risk if they return to Iran.
"I had two Iranian employees who, after their work visas ran out, applied for asylum based on conversion to 
Christianity." They returned to Iran several times without incident, he said. The danger, it seems, is greater for 
Christian converts who practice their new faith openly in Iran.
At Saint Christopher's Anglican Church in West Vancouver, about 20 per cent of the 80-year-old parish is Farsi 
speaking. Rector Jonathan Pinkney, who had baptismal and book of common prayer liturgy translated into Farsi via 
a grant from the diocese, told the National Post that those who convert to Christianity are sincere, and that only a 
handful of the approximately 20 new parishioners who have joined in the past four years were seeking asylum.
Rector Jonathan Pinkney of St. Christopher's Anglican Church in West Vancouver at a special Norouz - Iranian 
New Year - lunch at the parish hall.. He preaches the gospel of integration and works to connect Iranian 
parishioners with others at the church.
"Bishop John Stephens" he told the Post "is aware of the situation (around bogus conversions) but has asked us to 
exercise caution while remaining open hearted."
Pinkney employs an approach centred around "community building." He preaches the gospel of integration. To that 
end, he ensures connection by having new Iranian parishioners assigned positions in the choir, kitchen and various 
other committees alongside established parishioners.
He also contends that fear of persecution is legitimate, and that his Iranian parishioners have expressed "genuine 
concern" about returning to their homeland.
At a special Norouz - Iranian New Year - lunch held in the parish hall this past Sunday, 94-year-old parishioner 
George Richards told the Post that the new Iranian converts have injected much needed life and energy into the 
congregation. 'They've been a real boon to this parish," he said.
A young man who can't be identified or photographed to protect his extended family in Iran said that, religion aside, 
above all the church is a place of "social integration for newcomers."
With a huge influx of immigrants and refugees but little in the way of support for integration into communities, he 
notes, there are few opportunities for Iranians and others to connect with locals. "My first experience of being 
invited to a Canadian home for dinner came through the church," he said.
While against the U.S.-Israeli war on his homeland, he said he can't share his views publicly for fear of reprisal in 
the Iranian diaspora community. But rather than demonizing Islam like some of his fellow converts, he sees a 
connection between all the great faiths.
As for the "fake converts" he said, "Even 'scammers' can come here and find community. Why not? All are 
welcome."

auditor-report )

title: Council seeks removal of GM catwalk by December, refuses to address broader safety concerns at
body:
The City of St. Catharines and Government of Ontario have made clear in recent years that neither wants to take 
responsibility for enforcing a clean-up at the contaminated and crumbling former General Motors property in 
downtown St. Catharines.
The City fought for two years to keep disturbing environmental assessment reports from the public. The reports 
exposed contamination levels for certain dangerous toxins as much as 1,100 times higher than allowable limits. The 
City claimed releasing them would damage GM’s corporate reputation. 
Meanwhile, City officials and council have consistently refused to explain why action is not being taken to address 
serious safety issues on the site, despite the legislated powers to do so. The municipality’s apathy toward an issue 
that residents in the area have been demanding action on for almost a decade was exemplified in the admission 
late last yearby St. Catharines senior officials that they had no idea if a filtration system meant to clean stormwater 
on the site of dangerous PCBs was operational. It wasn’t. 
The Government of Ontario has been equally guarded on its involvement in monitoring the contamination, 
providing few details to residents about what is being done to ensure a laundry list of cancer-causing chemicals 
found in the soil and groundwater are not migrating off the site or into nearby Twelve Mile Creek. Provincial staff 
have ignored requests from The Pointer to get answers and have misled the public on the site’s danger, despite the 
concerns of local health officials. Provincial officials maintain the site is secure, and contamination is contained, but 
have not provided studies to support their claims. 
Obtaining even small pieces of information has been a struggle for residents and the media. An investigation 
apparently ongoing by the provincial environment ministry has included few details to the residents who live next to 
the contaminated blight.
Last Monday, following repeated requests from the community, council finally agreed to take action on the property, 
after months of advocacy, media scrutiny and despite repeated attempts by Mayor Mat Siscoe to prevent residents 
from speaking about the former GM site at council. 

Page 2 of 5
Council seeks removal of GM catwalk by December, refuses to address broader safety concerns at 
contaminated St. Catharines site
On February 23, councillors passed a motion requesting staff “work with the property owners to have the overhead 
structure removed, with a target date of December 1, 2026.”
The catwalk was recently examined through a visual inspection by engineers hired by the property owner. It was 
deemed structurally sound and safe. It’s a conclusion that did not completely satisfy residents and some councillors 
who saw the lack of inspection of the catwalk’s foundations to be a glaring omission. 
The motion does not compel the landowner—an Ontario numbered company—to remove the structure. It directs 
staff to work with the owner toward that outcome, but stops short of issuing an order or outlining consequences 
should the December 1, 2026 target date pass without action. While it formally signals council’s intent to see the 
catwalk removed, how the property owner responds, and whether the City is prepared to escalate its efforts if 
removal does not occur, remains to be seen.
Gwen Kennedy spoke to councillors last Monday on behalf of the Coalition for a Better St. Catharines, a community 
group that has advocated for cleanup of the former General Motors site for eight years. 
(Editor’s Note: Reporter Ed Smith is a member of the Coalition for a Better St. Catharines.) 
Kennedy came prepared to outline the community concerns about the site.
She was barely into her remarks before Mayor Siscoe interrupted her. It was the first of many interjections by the 
mayor, who repeatedly admonished Kennedy and warned her to confine comments strictly to the subject of the 
catwalk. Kennedy’s delegation related to a motion—carried over from a previous council meeting—from Councillors 
Bruce Williamson and Marty Mako related to the catwalk. Council’s procedural bylaw limits delegations to speak 
only on matters on the meeting’s agenda. 
It is common practice, including in St. Catharines, for delegates to be given some leeway to introduce both 
themselves, and the topic they want to discuss. That leeway was not given Monday. 
When Kennedy attempted to establish her credibility, referencing her work engaging residents and collecting 
approximately 1,200 signatures calling for cleanup of the site, Mayor Siscoe cut her off, labelling any mention of her 
broader community interactions “off topic”. It was unusual conduct for a council member chairing a meeting that is 
meant to be for the public, to address the business of taxpayers. It is rare for a member of the public to be 
prevented from outlining their experience and involvement with a matter being dealt with in the public chamber. 
In all, Siscoe cut into her remarks at least four times.
“It made it virtually impossible to complete my remarks,” Kennedy told The Pointer. “His tone was intimidating. I also 
saw similar behaviour directed at others during the meeting when they expressed views that differed from his. From 
what I observed, there appeared to be very little room for perspectives that didn’t align with the mayor’s position.”
After the delegations on the matter concluded, the mayor provided his own thoughts, which went well beyond the 
scope of the motion that was being discussed, referencing the broader condition of the site, the secondary planning 
process, and development opportunities that had nothing to do with the motion, or the topic of the discussion.
Council carried out a lengthy debate before arriving at the final motion. 
In discussing the recent engineering report, Councillor Bruce Williamson made it clear he was not satisfied with the 
conclusion that the catwalk was safe, because of the “glaring omission” of not addressing the structure’s 
foundations. 
“It wasn’t what I expected, I expected a report that would cover the legs of the table as well as the tabletop,” he told 
his fellow council members.
Mayor Siscoe pushed back against these concerns. 
Page 3 of 5

contaminated St. Catharines site
“If you’re going to declare that a bridge is structurally sound and in good condition and that it’s safe for vehicle and 
pedestrian access below the bridge in its condition, they’ve looked at the whole bridge,” he asserted. A similar 
statement was made by Councillor Bill Phillips, who suggested the engineer would have looked at how the 
structure was connected and ensured it was safe. 
The report is explicit.
“The existing bridge foundations were not visible at the time of inspection.” 
It further clarifies: “Our review focused exclusively on the framing of the bridge, with the focus on the structural 
integrity of the existing structure. No analysis was performed and no other portions of the structure were examined 
unless explicitly noted.”
Kennedy expressed the same concern to council members during her delegation. 
“If I was purchasing a home,” she said, “I would want the inspector to tell me what was happening with the 
foundation of the home.”
For reasons never explained, the City’s Director of Engineering, Anthony Martuccio, was not called upon to weigh in 
on the structural discussion. It is common practice to have staff at the centre of a report present at a council 
meeting so members and the public can get clarification on key issues. 
When directing a question on the analysis to staff, Mayor Siscoe at first appeared uncertain on who should answer. 
He acknowledged that Martuccio “has engineering in his title”, but ultimately requested Tami Kitay, the Director of 
Planning, to answer the question, and for Martuccio to add further comments after, if he chose. 
Martuccio is a licensed professional engineer and would presumably be well positioned to address technical 
questions about the catwalk’s structural integrity. Kitay’s background is in public administration, urban planning, and 
environmental studies. Martuccio did not provide any comments on the report. 
Kitay attempted to defend the report’s conclusion. 
“It would have been the responsibility of that qualified person to review the structural integrity of the entire gantry 
system, including what it's fastened to… ensuring that how the gantry was connected to the building was also safe 
and that there was no movement present, that there was no substantial structural cracks and if they had seen 
anything that was of concern they would have had a duty to report that.”
The report contains no reference to movement analysis. No documentation of inspecting concealed anchor points. 
No description of examining what the gantry is fastened to.
It explicitly notes the foundations were not visible and that the review focused exclusively on framing.
The Pointer submitted detailed questions to the City regarding Kitay’s statements. No response was provided.
Eventually, following an amendment from Councillor Kevin Townsend to direct staff to work with the owner to have 
the catwalk removed, council was finally able to agree on a path forward. 
“It’s important to hear what residents have to say about this,” Townsend said, admitting he is also concerned about 
the catwalk. “When I drive underneath this structure I do feel unsafe and I actually do speed up.”
The motion eventually passed unanimously. 
Council’s handling of this most recent report on the catwalk closely mirrors its response to a previous report 
submitted after concerns about the filtration system connected to the stormwater collection pond. In both cases, the 
documents were prepared by consultants retained by the owner, and then presented to the City, where they were 
accepted with little challenge, questioning or independent verification.
Page 4 of 5
Council seeks removal of GM catwalk by December, refuses to address broader safety concerns at 
contaminated St. Catharines site
As reported, the stormwater collection report concluded the water collecting on the site was safe based on two 
samples that were tested. Both samples were collected at a depth of one metre below the surface of the stormwater 
pond. No samples were taken from any other depths. 
The Pointer consulted three experts in environmental sampling, including specialists in PCB analysis in water 
systems. While none reviewed the site directly, their comments were consistent: hydrophobic contaminants such as 
PCBs do not easily remain suspended in water. They bind to sediment particles and those particles then settle to 
the bottom of a pond.
In practical terms, experts indicated that in a pond environment, the majority of hydrophobic compounds like PCBs 
are likely to accumulate in bottom sediments rather than remain in surface or mid-depth water. Sampling exclusively 
at one metre below the surface, without any sediment testing or multi-depth sampling is not an adequate way to test 
for PCB’s in a pond. 
City officials, despite the shortcomings, were quick to embrace the report, and ward Councillor Caleb Ratzlaff 
declared the site safe and “stable” based on the report. 
MPP Jennie Stevens has been critical of what is happening with the site and has pressed the environment ministry 
for answers that lie outside of the landowners reports.
On January 9, Stevens sent a second letter to the Environment Minister, Todd McCarthy, expressing her “deep 
concern” over the unanswered questions about the status of the site and the risk to her constituents. She received a 
response from the Minister on Feb 23 in which Minister McCarthy stated in part that, “The sewage works’ 
operation is currently under investigation, so further comment would be inappropriate at this time.” 
According to Stevens, it is not clear if this refers to the same investigation into concerns with stormwater on the 
site—first acknowledged in the Minister’s November 3 letter—or something else. 
“Unfortunately, it is unclear to me if the initial storm water collection investigation mentioned on November 3rd is the 
same investigation being referred to in the February 23rd letter,” Stevens said, indicating she will continue to follow-
up with the minister. “From what I can gather, this letter does not reveal any new information about the filtration 
system,” she said. “It does provide updated information about collection pond sampling that took place November 
13, 2025 by a private consulting firm. According to this letter, the firm was hired by the property owner, not MECP 
directly.”
For residents, the situation feels all too familiar. 
“We have been waiting for action on this site for years. Tonight, the Mayor and council did not demonstrate the level 
of leadership that would convince residents they are prepared to take the strong action required to ensure the entire 
site is cleaned up,” Kennedy said last week. “Once again, their approach appeared measured in a way that favours 
the landowner, it feels like deja vu.”

title: Councillor accused of asking developer for money Kandavel denies wrongdoing as OPP probe interactions with
body:
A Toronto city councillor's dealings with developers appear to be the focus of the police investigation into 
allegations against him. 
The Ontario Provincial Police probe into Coun. Parthi Kandavel was prompted by a watchdog complaint from the 
owners of a development in his Scarborough Southwest ward, according to the company's lawyer, while sources 
allege he sought money in exchange for allowing a different project in the area to go ahead. 
In an email to the Star on Monday, John J. Pirie, a partner at Baker McKenzie LLP, said a representative of his 
clients, Kennedy Road Holdings Ltd., made a complaintagainst the councillor to Toronto's integrity commissioner. 
According to Pirie, the commissioner then referred the matter to the Toronto police, without the input of his clients.
The company owns a property at 708-712 Kennedy Road, and has been seeking permission to replace two midrise 
rental buildings at the site with a pair of highrises. Pirie declined to provide details of the complaint, but stressed 
that the company "is not under investigation."
Integrity Commissioner Paul Muldoon couldn't immediately be reached for comment Monday. His office previously 
told the Star it "does not routinely confirm or deny whether he has received a complaint." 
Meanwhile, a source with knowledge of another development in Scarborough Southwest said they were left with the 
impression that Kandavel wanted a significant financial payment from the proponents to allow the project to 
proceed. 
A second source confirmed hearing the same account. The OPP has reached out regarding the development, 
according to the first source. In a statement in response to the allegations, Kandavel said: "There has been no 
wrongdoing on my part, which I'm confident the OPP investigation will conclude."
"I am still learning about these allegations, and it is not lost on me that they've come during the election period. 
Regardless, my intention is to respect the process and let the OPP complete their work."
The councillor announced in a social media post on Sunday that he was under investigation by the OPP. He 
didn't provide details of the allegations, and said news of the investigation had taken him by surprise when he 
learned about it Friday afternoon. 
Page 2 of 3
Councillor accused of asking developer for money Kandavel denies wrongdoing as OPP probe interactions with 
local builder
He wrote in the post that he had "worked hard to earn the trust of the people of Scarborough Southwest, which I 
take seriously. I've strived to maintain the highest standards of ethics and integrity and will address any allegations 
that suggest otherwise." 
The Toronto Police Service received the initial complaint about the councillor but referred it to the OPP "to avoid 
any perceived conflict of interest," TPS spokesperson Stephanie Sayer said Monday. City councillors sit on the 
Toronto Police Service Board and vote on its annual budget. Neither the TPS nor OPP has said who filed the 
complaint, or detailed the allegations against Kandavel. The forces didn't immediately return a request for 
confirmation Monday night about who made the complaint.
The Star reported on Sunday that, according to one source, as part of its probe, the OPP had sought information 
about the development at 708-712 Kennedy Road. In 2022, the owners of the property submitted a request for a 
zoning bylaw amendment to demolish the existing 98 rental units at the site and redevelop it. A revised submission 
the company made in 2024 proposed two residential towers of 21 and 42 stories, for a total of 682 units, including 
98 rental replacements. 
The owners appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal in May 2024 after council failed to make a decision within the 
required timelines.
In June 2025, the owners submitted a settlement offer to resolve the OLT appeal, which reduced the height of the 
highest tower by four stories. That month, city solicitor Wendy Walberg submitted advice to council about the 
settlement. While the advice was confidential, according to one source with knowledge of her report, she 
recommended council accept the settlement, which included a concession from the owners to provide 1,500 square 
feet of non-residential uses. Kandavel moved a motion amending her advice however, requesting that the city 
approve the settlement but require 4,000 square feet. 
According to an October 2025 OLT decision, the city and the owners resolved most aspects of the appeal, but 
continued to disagree on the amount of non-residential space. The owner successfully convinced the tribunal it 
didn't need to include as much as Kandavel's motion requested, with the tribunal writing that the city hadn't provided 
evidence for "why 4000 sq. ft. would be appropriate, how that precise number was good planning, or how exactly 
the development would have to be changed" to accommodate it.
Kandavel is a former elementary school teacher and Toronto District School Board trustee. He was elected to 
council in a November 2023 byelection, with about 27 per cent of the vote. Earlier this month his office told the Star 
he intends to run for re-election this year, but he has yet to sign up for the Oct. 26 contest. Nominations opened 
May 1. 
A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said Monday she wouldn't answer questions about an active investigation, 
but Toronto residents "expect every councillor and the mayor to act with integrity."

Title: Councillor accused of asking developer for money Kandavel denies wrongdoing as OPP probe interactions with

Body: A Toronto city councillor's dealings with developers appear to be the focus of the police investigation into 
allegations against him. 
The Ontario Provincial Police probe into Coun. Parthi Kandavel was prompted by a watchdog complaint from the 
owners of a development in his Scarborough Southwest ward, according to the company's lawyer, while sources 
allege he sought money in exchange for allowing a different project in the area to go ahead. 
In an email to the Star on Monday, John J. Pirie, a partner at Baker McKenzie LLP, said a representative of his 
clients, Kennedy Road Holdings Ltd., made a complaintagainst the councillor to Toronto's integrity commissioner. 
According to Pirie, the commissioner then referred the matter to the Toronto police, without the input of his clients.
The company owns a property at 708-712 Kennedy Road, and has been seeking permission to replace two midrise 
rental buildings at the site with a pair of highrises. Pirie declined to provide details of the complaint, but stressed 
that the company "is not under investigation."
Integrity Commissioner Paul Muldoon couldn't immediately be reached for comment Monday. His office previously 
told the Star it "does not routinely confirm or deny whether he has received a complaint." 
Meanwhile, a source with knowledge of another development in Scarborough Southwest said they were left with the 
impression that Kandavel wanted a significant financial payment from the proponents to allow the project to 
proceed. 
A second source confirmed hearing the same account. The OPP has reached out regarding the development, 
according to the first source. In a statement in response to the allegations, Kandavel said: "There has been no 
wrongdoing on my part, which I'm confident the OPP investigation will conclude."
"I am still learning about these allegations, and it is not lost on me that they've come during the election period. 
Regardless, my intention is to respect the process and let the OPP complete their work."
The councillor announced in a social media post on Sunday that he was under investigation by the OPP. He 
didn't provide details of the allegations, and said news of the investigation had taken him by surprise when he 
learned about it Friday afternoon.

local builder
He wrote in the post that he had "worked hard to earn the trust of the people of Scarborough Southwest, which I 
take seriously. I've strived to maintain the highest standards of ethics and integrity and will address any allegations 
that suggest otherwise." 
The Toronto Police Service received the initial complaint about the councillor but referred it to the OPP "to avoid 
any perceived conflict of interest," TPS spokesperson Stephanie Sayer said Monday. City councillors sit on the 
Toronto Police Service Board and vote on its annual budget. Neither the TPS nor OPP has said who filed the 
complaint, or detailed the allegations against Kandavel. The forces didn't immediately return a request for 
confirmation Monday night about who made the complaint.
The Star reported on Sunday that, according to one source, as part of its probe, the OPP had sought information 
about the development at 708-712 Kennedy Road. In 2022, the owners of the property submitted a request for a 
zoning bylaw amendment to demolish the existing 98 rental units at the site and redevelop it. A revised submission 
the company made in 2024 proposed two residential towers of 21 and 42 stories, for a total of 682 units, including 
98 rental replacements. 
The owners appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal in May 2024 after council failed to make a decision within the 
required timelines.
In June 2025, the owners submitted a settlement offer to resolve the OLT appeal, which reduced the height of the 
highest tower by four stories. That month, city solicitor Wendy Walberg submitted advice to council about the 
settlement. While the advice was confidential, according to one source with knowledge of her report, she 
recommended council accept the settlement, which included a concession from the owners to provide 1,500 square 
feet of non-residential uses. Kandavel moved a motion amending her advice however, requesting that the city 
approve the settlement but require 4,000 square feet. 
According to an October 2025 OLT decision, the city and the owners resolved most aspects of the appeal, but 
continued to disagree on the amount of non-residential space. The owner successfully convinced the tribunal it 
didn't need to include as much as Kandavel's motion requested, with the tribunal writing that the city hadn't provided 
evidence for "why 4000 sq. ft. would be appropriate, how that precise number was good planning, or how exactly 
the development would have to be changed" to accommodate it.
Kandavel is a former elementary school teacher and Toronto District School Board trustee. He was elected to 
council in a November 2023 byelection, with about 27 per cent of the vote. Earlier this month his office told the Star 
he intends to run for re-election this year, but he has yet to sign up for the Oct. 26 contest. Nominations opened 
May 1. 
A spokesperson for Mayor Olivia Chow said Monday she wouldn't answer questions about an active investigation, 
but Toronto residents "expect every councillor and the mayor to act with integrity."

title: Councillor to fight food costs with public grocery stores
body:
A city councillor has opened the door to what food experts are calling an "exciting" discussion: Toronto's first-ever 
public grocery stores to tackle rising food costs.
In a news release Thursday, Coun. Anthony Perruzza (Humber River-Black Creek) said he intends to introduce a 
motion during the March 26 council meeting, to establish a pilot for four city-run grocery stores across the city, 
prioritizing neighbourhoods with limited access to grocery stores and lower income households.
Council declared a food insecurity emergency in January.
A draft of his motion also proposes waiving property taxes and development charges for the stores to help keep 
prices as low as possible.
"Things are just simply very expensive for people, I hear it all over the place wherever I go," Perruzza said in an 
interview, pointing to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's similar pilot. "We need to take bold steps and this is 
one of them."
Perruzza argued the city has the money to do this "in the blink of an eye," and when asked why not request a 
feasibility study first, the councillor argued it's best to learn by launching it and a study "might actually dissuade us 
from doing something like this." He pointed to New York City, which jumped straight to a pilot project.
However,Mamdani built his pilot based on an existing feasibility study elsewhere. During his mayoral campaign, 
Mamdani referred to a 2023 study from Chicago which concluded that municipal grocery stores were "necessary, 
feasible, and implementable." Mamdani adjusted the figures for New York City's higher cost of living and real 
estate, and used it as the basis for his $70-million (U.S.) budget request for five public grocery stores across the 
city's boroughs. 
The pilot was funded by redirecting money from the city's FRESH program, which gives tax breaks to private 
developers to build grocery stores.
Aaron Vansintjan, a policy manager with Food Secure Canada, said he "absolutely" believes public grocery stores 
are feasible and necessary given only three companies control 75 per cent of Canada's food market and "prices are 
through the roof."
Page 2 of 3
Councillor to fight food costs with public grocery stores
Vansintjan, whose non-profit researches and advocates to transform the national food system, studied how the idea 
could work in Canada alongside two U.S. researchers who did a similar study for Mamdani's campaign.
 Vansintjan said their January study found public grocers could lead to price reductions of 25 to 30 per cent in 
urban areas, which could save a family between $2,500 and $10,000 a year.
"The key part is that you need economies of scale. So think more like a Costco. You need to have large 
warehouses to be able to have a large procurement practice," Vansintjan said. 
Perruzza said while logistics, size and scale need to be hashed out, he sees the stores charging people what it 
costs to operate them.
"The smaller your economy of scale, the more support it will need from the city or the federal government," 
Vansintjan said, noting that is the main reason other public grocer pilots, like in Kansas, had to close. "The idea that 
it would pay for itself needs to be looked into because the smaller you go, the more you're going to have to put into 
it."
It's unclear right now what the price tag for four stores in Toronto would be.
Government-run grocery stores could also promote urban agriculture and drive up demand for local products, said 
Michael Classens, an assistant professor at the University of Toronto who studied food systems. It would not only 
give Canadian farmers greater economic stability, he said, it would safeguard shoppers from cost fluctuations due 
to supply chain disruptions and shifting tariff landscapes.
These stores would also break up the grocery oligopoly in Canada, which has been embroiled in price-fixing 
scandals, Classens continued. 
"These public grocery stores are already operating in many places in the world," he said. There are, for example, 
government-owned chains in Mexico and on U.S. military bases. "The LCBO is also a publicly run entity."
An LCBO-but-for-food would yield great savings for residents, Classens said. 
He added that Perruzza's proposal is feasible in Toronto, but it would be more feasible if it were a federal 
undertaking, a network across Canada with local markets that could benefit from a large economy of scale.
With files from Ben Cohen
