title: Ka-pow! batman kicks butt at 60; Campy 1960s TV series created new generation of superhero fans
body:
Holy Zellers, Batman! What's a defunct Canadian department store doing in a story about Gotham City's most 
decorated Caped Crusaders? With apologies to the Boy Wonder, it helped cement the stretch-fabric superheroes' 
place in the pop-culture pantheon.
How exactly did a long-departed retailer carve its place in history? It's hardly an enigma worthy of the Riddler: in the 
mid-1980s Zellers released a series of TV ads featuring Batman and Robin peppered with cornball puns promoting 
its cut-price merchandise.
The commercials captured the affection the show commanded from the moment the program premièred on ABC in 
January 1966, triggering a "Batmania" tsunami never quite replicated. In 30-minute all-action episodes, Batman - 
played in deadpan brilliance by Adam West - and his sidekick Robin, the Boy Wonder, rendered with youthful zest 
by Burt Ward - engaged the enemies of law and order in an unrelenting campaign of moral worthiness.
The live-action spoof of the comic book series ran for 120 episodes over three seasons, generating huge profits and 
stellar ratings. But success was fleeting, with the U.S. network axing the Dynamic Duo on March 14, 1968, amid 
slumping viewership. NBC offered to take over the dark knight's mantle, but 20th Century Fox had already 
demolished the expensive Batcave, and so ABC's cost-conscious rival withdrew its bid.
Its run may have been brief but its influence was far-reaching - not least in elevating Robin's "Holy" asides to 
linguistic lore: from "Holy Agility!" to "Holy Zorro!", Robin uttered more than 350 of his zippy catchphrases, 
delighting adult audiences who appreciated its camp humour, while kids lapped up the Bop! Bam! Ka-pow! overlays 
and the vibrant costumes and sets - not to mention the groovy Batmobile, based on a 1955 Lincoln Futura.
The show's Dragnet-lite seriousness was played for laughs, yet it too was influential. While Sgt. Joe Friday was 
more wooden than a chopping block, West delivered his sermons with a kindly twinkle, even encouraging the Boy 
Wonder to buckle up when seatbelt use was still in its infancy. The use of guns and extreme force was also ruled 
out, lest it encourage young copycats.
That said, scenery-shredding villains were essential to the mix. The Joker, the Riddler, Penguin, the Scarecrow, 
Catwoman - all enlivened the crimesoaked Gotham backdrop. Stars clamoured for cameos, and some of the 
biggest stars of the day - Cesar Romero, Vincent Price, Burgess Meredith, Joan Collins - mugged their way through 
guest appearances as dastardly evildoers. No villain loomed larger, however, than self-styled moral guardian 
Page 2 of 3
Ka-pow! batman kicks butt at 60; Campy 1960s TV series created new generation of superhero fans
Frederic Wertham, whose 1954 book Seduction of the Innocent threatened to permanently clip Batman's wings. He 
accused comic books of corrupting impressionable young readers, charging Batman and Robin in particular with 
flaunting a gay lifestyle, which West vehemently rejected.
"They live in sumptuous quarters, with beautiful flowers in large vases, and have a butler," Wertham thundered. "It 
is like a wish dream of two homosexuals living together." Holy moral outrage, Batman! Wertham's fevered rantings 
fizzled, yet comic-book writers later introduced female love interests for both Batman and Robin in reaction to the 
backlash.
Executive producer William Dozier wasn't concerned about butlers tending gladioli in gaily painted vases - he just 
hated comic books. His solution was a full-on send-up of comics, a bold gamble that paid off even if it alienated fans 
of the dark origins of Batman in DC Comics in 1939.
West was in no doubt about the show's cultural heft, branding it one of the "three Big B's" of the 1960s alongside 
The Beatles and superspy James Bond. Of his superhero role, Westwho died in 2017 at age 88 - humbly observed: 
"Actors wanted to be loved; Batman has done that for me."
And for the rest of us, Caped Crusader. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2026 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Kicking away the chaos and constraints Canada Soccer deal buys belief to grow the game
body:
Two years and a week ago, Kevin Blue was named CEO and general secretary of Canada Soccer. Seven months 
later, he put out a statement announcing a collective agreement with national team players, which included the next 
critical stop for a sport at a crossroads: a revision of the Canada Soccer Business deal. The new agreement, Blue 
said, was contingent on that.
People with knowledge of the dynamic scoffed. CSB's position all along had been that it had a legally enforceable 
contract, and therefore all the leverage. The deal was suffocating. Starting in 2019, CSB paid a flat rate for 
sponsorship and broadcast rights to Canada's national soccer teams, and as the two teams succeeded the number 
was laughably low: a maximum guarantee of $4 million in any given year, locked in through 2037. The company did 
raise the base payment within the last two years, but not nearly enough to make Canada Soccer whole.
Then last month, while the Olympics occupied the sports world, Canada Soccer announced a new future for the 
sport in Canada. They didn't quite put it that way, but it was clear. The new deal with CSB - which rebranded in 
February to Canadian Soccer Media & Entertainment, or CSME - is a sea change.
"We think of this as a structural shift that allows us and everybody in the sport to work together to bring more 
investment into the sport, and for that to directly impact the growth of the sport, the growth of national teams, the 
growth of the grassroots game," Blue said in an interview. 
It feels like the end of Canadian soccer's civil war. Canada Soccer estimates the new contract will add well over 
$100 million of revenue to the organization by 2037. One clause includes a payment of either $19.5 million from 
CSME to Canada Soccer, or an increase in Canada Soccer's gross revenue share in 2028 and 2029. Canada 
Soccer is guaranteed at least 50 per cent of revenue in this contract. Under the previous contract, Canada Soccer 
was guaranteed a maximum of $67 million by 2037, no matter how revenue grew.
In the best case, Canada Soccer may have just about tripled its core sponsorship and broadcast revenue. And 
while the projections assume increased revenue, it gives you an idea how much money was being diverted from 
Canada Soccer in the first place. With price inflation, competitive inflation and a capped payment, Canada Soccer 
would have seen core financial support depreciate every year through 2037.
"If you have a payment that doesn't escalate as costs go up with every year that goes by, you have a 
compoundingly worse situation," said Blue. "The previous situation was not advantageous, but it was not as 
Page 2 of 4
Kicking away the chaos and constraints Canada Soccer deal buys belief to grow the game
problematic as it would be had that situation continued for multiple years down the road. And certainly in the out 
years, it was completely untenable."
'Growing pains'
As Canadian soccer bloomed, the CSB deal created problems. In 2022, then Canada Soccer president Nick Bontis 
flew out to Vancouver and said he literally got on his knees while explaining to the men's team why there was no 
more money to offer them. He cited the CSB deal and said the nascent Canadian Premier League, whose owners 
also owned CSB, needed the cash. Players were bewildered and furious.
In 2023, the women's team budget was cut almost in half, according to Star sources with internal knowledge of the 
team's finances, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The men's budget was cut 
as well. Age-group national team budgets were sliced. In 2024, Canada Soccer raised player registration fees from 
$9 to $13.
"It was growing pains that happened really quickly," said former general secretary Earl Cochrane, who was there in 
2022 and 2023.
In one lawsuit filing, it was revealed that CSB sold Canadian broadcast rights for the national teams to a company 
called Mediapro for $8.7 million per year, or more than double what CSB was paying for sponsorship and broadcast 
rights combined. Industry sources who have negotiated soccer deals, granted anonymity in order to comment 
without jeopardizing their own business, estimated the lost revenue at $7 million to $10 million a year. As one 
former Canada Soccer board member told the Star, also granted anonymity in order to speak freely: "It was worse 
than a hostile takeover. They basically sold Canada Soccer down the river." 
Meanwhile, the idea of a Canada Soccer philanthropy arm was tied up in the backroom conflict. And all this was 
happening with a men's team that reached the World Cup for the first time since 1986, and a women's team that 
won Olympic gold. Inside Canada Soccer there was a worry Canada was in danger of squandering twin golden 
generations in the world's most popular sport.
Head coach John Herdman left because of the financial picture, long before the spying scandal instigated by then-
women's coach Bev Priestman ever surfaced. Player strikes and lawsuits surfaced on both sides of the program. It 
was an almost non-stop cavalcade of crisis.
The future
So why did this happen? Two CPL teams have folded since its founding in 2019; the old deal helped fund that 
league. The old CSB approach was resolute. They didn't want to change.
Nobody at Canada Soccer will say anything, but it's clear the organization has pushed back for years now. Under 
Blue and new CSME CEO James Johnson, who had a previous professional relationship, the shift was hard but 
achievable. 
"I think that when people started to understand the impact of it for us, and understood the impact of it generally on 
the sport, and then also understand the impact of it for them, there became consensus amongst all parties that 
things had to change," says Blue.
"The real motive is to grow, and not just our own business but the broader sport," said Johnson. "There might have 
been some sensitivities, but ultimately I think everyone wants to do the right thing ... and ensuring those interests 
are aligned is absolutely critical.
"We want to be partners and we want Canada Soccer to feel loved, and we want them to know that we're good 
partners."
There is a chance these parties are now actually aligned rather than joined by the barrel of a contractual gun, and it 
happened without public animosity, without Canada Soccer mess. Blue has also untangled the philanthropy puzzle, 
Page 3 of 4
Kicking away the chaos and constraints Canada Soccer deal buys belief to grow the game
and Canada Soccer has raised $16 million of the goal of $25 million by the end of 2027, and Blue says more 
opportunities are in the pipeline.
"This is significantly different than, you know, zero in 2023," he says.
This should mean training camps, equipment and coaching can all be maintained at competitive levels. Canada 
Soccer will focus as well on reinvesting in the youth national team system. Blue says Canada trails in youth national 
structure versus similarly ranked nations.
"We were less than 10 elite youth national team camps in 2024, and I think this year we're going to be between 19 
and 22 depending on who qualifies for what," says Blue. "But look, it's not that this is a windfall situation in the short 
term. It's a structural repair that needed to happen."
The deal also pushes the national teams back into the spotlight. Instead of being locked on CSB's OneSoccer 
channel, which was a niche product, the new deal specifies that national teams need to be back on major broadcast 
television - that means TSN, Sportsnet or CBC. That's critical.
"Very, very important for our community, for the exposure of the players, for the stature of the national teams, 
extremely important," says Blue.
Blue sees this as a critical period for the game. He mentions not just games in Toronto and Vancouver as part of 
the United States/Canada/Mexico World Cup, and a women's World Cup in Brazil next year, and the Olympics in 
Los Angeles in 2028.
"We're in a critical, critical period for being able to grow resources to help our federation invest in the sport, so that's 
a responsibility that we obviously take (seriously)," says Blue. "It's massive. Our whole team, our senior team (at 
Canada Soccer), we talk about this a lot. We're working really, really hard right now as you might imagine ... We 
also have an obligation to get this right for Canadian sport at large. We're understanding of that responsibility."
It sure looks like Blue and his staff lived up to that responsibility. You can't say Canada Soccer has saved the sport, 
because it was going to survive. But soccer in Canada now has a chance to grow without unnecessary chaos or 
artificial constraints, and it will grow or stagnate, succeed or fail, based on what it can put on the field. The civil war 
looks like it's over, and soccer in Canada can finally just be whatever it can be.

"We think of this as a structural shift that allows us and everybody in the sport to work together to bring more 
investment into the sport, and for that to directly impact the growth of the sport, the growth of national teams, the 
growth of the grassroots game," Blue said in an interview. 
It feels like the end of Canadian soccer's civil war. Canada Soccer estimates the new contract will add well over 
$100 million of revenue to the organization by 2037. One clause includes a payment of either $19.5 million from 
CSME to Canada Soccer, or an increase in Canada Soccer's gross revenue share in 2028 and 2029. Canada 
Soccer is guaranteed at least 50 per cent of revenue in this contract. Under the previous contract, Canada Soccer 
was guaranteed a maximum of $67 million by 2037, no matter how revenue grew.
In the best case, Canada Soccer may have just about tripled its core sponsorship and broadcast revenue. And 
while the projections assume increased revenue, it gives you an idea how much money was being diverted from 
Canada Soccer in the first place. With price inflation, competitive inflation and a capped payment, Canada Soccer 
would have seen core financial support depreciate every year through 2037.
"If you have a payment that doesn't escalate as costs go up with every year that goes by, you have a 
compoundingly worse situation," said Blue. "The previous situation was not advantageous, but it was not as 
Page 2 of 4
Kicking away the chaos and constraints Canada Soccer deal buys belief to grow the game
problematic as it would be had that situation continued for multiple years down the road. And certainly in the out 
years, it was completely untenable."
'Growing pains'
As Canadian soccer bloomed, the CSB deal created problems. In 2022, then Canada Soccer president Nick Bontis 
flew out to Vancouver and said he literally got on his knees while explaining to the men's team why there was no 
more money to offer them. He cited the CSB deal and said the nascent Canadian Premier League, whose owners 
also owned CSB, needed the cash. Players were bewildered and furious.
In 2023, the women's team budget was cut almost in half, according to Star sources with internal knowledge of the 
team's finances, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. The men's budget was cut 
as well. Age-group national team budgets were sliced. In 2024, Canada Soccer raised player registration fees from 
$9 to $13.
"It was growing pains that happened really quickly," said former general secretary Earl Cochrane, who was there in 
2022 and 2023.
In one lawsuit filing, it was revealed that CSB sold Canadian broadcast rights for the national teams to a company 
called Mediapro for $8.7 million per year, or more than double what CSB was paying for sponsorship and broadcast 
rights combined. Industry sources who have negotiated soccer deals, granted anonymity in order to comment 
without jeopardizing their own business, estimated the lost revenue at $7 million to $10 million a year. As one 
former Canada Soccer board member told the Star, also granted anonymity in order to speak freely: "It was worse 
than a hostile takeover. They basically sold Canada Soccer down the river." 
Meanwhile, the idea of a Canada Soccer philanthropy arm was tied up in the backroom conflict. And all this was 
happening with a men's team that reached the World Cup for the first time since 1986, and a women's team that 
won Olympic gold. Inside Canada Soccer there was a worry Canada was in danger of squandering twin golden 
generations in the world's most popular sport.
Head coach John Herdman left because of the financial picture, long before the spying scandal instigated by then-
women's coach Bev Priestman ever surfaced. Player strikes and lawsuits surfaced on both sides of the program. It 
was an almost non-stop cavalcade of crisis.
The future
So why did this happen? Two CPL teams have folded since its founding in 2019; the old deal helped fund that 
league. The old CSB approach was resolute. They didn't want to change.
Nobody at Canada Soccer will say anything, but it's clear the organization has pushed back for years now. Under 
Blue and new CSME CEO James Johnson, who had a previous professional relationship, the shift was hard but 
achievable. 
"I think that when people started to understand the impact of it for us, and understood the impact of it generally on 
the sport, and then also understand the impact of it for them, there became consensus amongst all parties that 
things had to change," says Blue.
"The real motive is to grow, and not just our own business but the broader sport," said Johnson. "There might have 
been some sensitivities, but ultimately I think everyone wants to do the right thing ... and ensuring those interests 
are aligned is absolutely critical.
"We want to be partners and we want Canada Soccer to feel loved, and we want them to know that we're good 
partners."
There is a chance these parties are now actually aligned rather than joined by the barrel of a contractual gun, and it 
happened without public animosity, without Canada Soccer mess. Blue has also untangled the philanthropy puzzle, 
Page 3 of 4
Kicking away the chaos and constraints Canada Soccer deal buys belief to grow the game
and Canada Soccer has raised $16 million of the goal of $25 million by the end of 2027, and Blue says more 
opportunities are in the pipeline.
"This is significantly different than, you know, zero in 2023," he says.
This should mean training camps, equipment and coaching can all be maintained at competitive levels. Canada 
Soccer will focus as well on reinvesting in the youth national team system. Blue says Canada trails in youth national 
structure versus similarly ranked nations.
"We were less than 10 elite youth national team camps in 2024, and I think this year we're going to be between 19 
and 22 depending on who qualifies for what," says Blue. "But look, it's not that this is a windfall situation in the short 
term. It's a structural repair that needed to happen."
The deal also pushes the national teams back into the spotlight. Instead of being locked on CSB's OneSoccer 
channel, which was a niche product, the new deal specifies that national teams need to be back on major broadcast 
television - that means TSN, Sportsnet or CBC. That's critical.
"Very, very important for our community, for the exposure of the players, for the stature of the national teams, 
extremely important," says Blue.
Blue sees this as a critical period for the game. He mentions not just games in Toronto and Vancouver as part of 
the United States/Canada/Mexico World Cup, and a women's World Cup in Brazil next year, and the Olympics in 
Los Angeles in 2028.
"We're in a critical, critical period for being able to grow resources to help our federation invest in the sport, so that's 
a responsibility that we obviously take (seriously)," says Blue. "It's massive. Our whole team, our senior team (at 
Canada Soccer), we talk about this a lot. We're working really, really hard right now as you might imagine ... We 
also have an obligation to get this right for Canadian sport at large. We're understanding of that responsibility."
It sure looks like Blue and his staff lived up to that responsibility. You can't say Canada Soccer has saved the sport, 
because it was going to survive. But soccer in Canada now has a chance to grow without unnecessary chaos or 
artificial constraints, and it will grow or stagnate, succeed or fail, based on what it can put on the field. The civil war 
looks like it's over, and soccer in Canada can finally just be whatever it can be.

title: Late queen pushed for Andrew's trade post; Official Papers
body:
Late queen Elizabeth II pushed for her son Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor to be given a high-profile job as a trade 
envoy, a senior official said in a 2000 document released by the government on Thursday.
The British government agreed to release the documents related to the disgraced former prince's role as trade 
envoy from 2001 to 2011, amid the fallout from the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.
Mountbatten-Windsor, who was stripped of his remaining royal titles following the release of U.S. files related to 
Epstein last year, was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office linked to the late American 
sex offender.
He is accused of sharing sensitive information with Epstein during his time as an official trade envoy for Britain.
The former prince was released after being questioned for hours by police and has not been charged. He denies 
any wrongdoing.
The 11 documents published by the government discuss the appointment of the former prince as a special envoy 
for British Trade International (BTI), which promoted the U.K. abroad.
Following a "wide-ranging conversation" with the queen's private secretary, BTI head David Wright wrote to the 
then-foreign minister to say it was the queen's "wish" that Andrew, then the Duke of York, be appointed to the role.
"The Queen is very keen that the Duke of York should take on a prominent role in the promotion of national 
interests," said the letter d -at ed Feb. 25, 2000.
One month earlier, in a message with the subject "Duke of York's travel", head of protocol Kathryn Colvin advised 
that the Duke of York "should not be offered golfing functions abroad."
Colvin also noted that the former duke preferred "more sophisticated countries" and "liked travelling, especially 
when on royal business."
The role was unpaid, but during his time as envoy, the then-prince was dubbed "Air Miles Andy" as he jetted around 
the world with his expenses, including luxury hotels, covered by taxpayers.
Page 2 of 2
Late queen pushed for Andrew's trade post; Official Papers
In a written statement to parliament, trade minister Chris Bryant said "we have found no evidence that a formal due 
diligence or vetting process was undertaken."
However, this was "understandable" as the "new appointment was a continuation of the Royal Family's involvement 
in trade and investment promotion work."
Peter Mandelson, former U.K. ambassador to the U.S. who was sacked over his ties to Epstein, is also being 
investigated for misconduct in public office when he was a government minister in the 2000s.
The Liberal Democrat party, which moved the government to release documents related to Mountbatten-Windsor, 
has also asked for the publication of any correspondence between Mandelson and the former prince. The former 
duke has been long embroiled in scandals over his friendship with Epstein.

title: Laughs for Lake Simcoe supports water health through comedy
body:
Water quality is no laughing matter, but it doesn’t hurt in raising awareness for the Rescue Lake Simcoe Coalition.
This Thursday, May 21, the Coalition will host Laugh for Lake Simcoe, a showcase of Canadian comedy intended 
to raise funds to support projects protecting and restoring Lake Simcoe and its watershed. Showtime is 7 p.m. at 
Newmarket’s Old Town Hall.
“Laugh for Lake Simcoe is a great night out for a great cause,” said Bradford-West Gwillimbury Councillor 
Jonathan Scott, Executive Director of the Rescue Lake Simcoe Coalition. “Every ticket sold helps support practical 
action and effective advocacy to keep Lake Simcoe healthy.”
Headlining the event are comedians Mike Wilmot, with Rob Bebenek and Laurie Elliott.
“Plan a night out with your friends, your sweetie, or your co-workers in the historic downtown Newmarket. Get 
connected to the Rescue Lake Simcoe community and our programs. Bid on a silent auction item, have a drink, and 
kick back to laugh,” say organizers.
The Rescue Lake Simcoe Coalition is a charitable organization dedicated to protecting and restoring Lake Simcoe 
through research, education, and advocacy.
For more information about the Laugh for Lake Simcoe event, including tickets, visit 
rescuelakesimcoe.org/events/7961.

title: Laval won't have to pay ex-mayor's $1 million tax debt
body:
The City of Laval won't be required to pay $1 million to cover taxes former mayor Gilles Vaillancourt owes on 
money he collected through a municipal corruption scheme.
After the city contested the issue, the federal government has decided to cover the payment "in the interest of 
fairness," Canadian Finance Minister FrançoisPhilippe Champagne announced Thursday.
"Minister Champagne ... will authorize an ex gratia payment of $1.1 million to rectify this wholly unfair situation and 
bring fairness to the City of Laval and its residents," his office said in a statement.
Vaillancourt, who served as mayor from 1989 to 2012, pleaded guilty in 2016 to participating in a corruption 
scheme that plagued the city for years.
Vaillancourt admitted he took part in a conspiracy to use his position as mayor to fill Swiss bank accounts with 
millions of dollars. He later returned roughly $8 million to the city, which was directed into a fund aimed at helping 
disadvantaged youths.
In March, Laval Mayor Stéphane Boyer spoke out against the fact that the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) was 
seeking to have the city pay $1 million to Vaillancourt so he could pay taxes on the stolen money.
The agency was looking to collect a 14 per cent tax on a sum of roughly $7 million. It had reportedly first attempted 
to collect the money from Vaillancourt, but his lawyers argued it should come from the city since he had returned 
the stolen funds.
Boyer had denounced the situation as unjust and called on the federal government to intervene. He pointed to how, 
in 2016, the Quebec government reimbursed Laval for money Vaillancourt owed to Revenu Québec.
Champagne's office referred to the provincial government's approach Thursday, stating it was making the payment 
"in keeping with the Quebec government's own handling of the tax matter at the time."
"This payment will be made in recognition of a payment the City of Laval is required to make to the Canada 
Revenue Agency," it said.
Boyer welcomed the outcome as an "important victory" for Laval residents.
Page 2 of 2
Laval won't have to pay ex-mayor's $1 million tax debt
"The people of Laval have already paid a heavy price for the criminal acts committed by Mr. Vaillancourt," he said in 
a statement.
"We can now finally put this unjust chapter behind us."
Vaillancourt received a six-year prison sentence for his crimes in late 2016.
He was granted full parole in 2018 but continued to minimize his role in the scheme.

title: Less than 1% of OSAP cases flagged as ineligible Data casts doubt on Ford's claims of abuse as rationale for
body:
Ontario data reveals that $13.1 million in financial aid over two years - a small fraction of total disbursements - was 
wrongly granted to students later found to be ineligible, with no cases referred to police, raising questions about the 
scale of alleged abuse Premier Doug Ford cited, in part, to justify overhauling OSAP.
Last year, $8,332,363 in student assistance was wrongly issued due to "false or invalid information, incorrect 
statuses, participation in non-bona fide studies or other discrepancies," according to records obtained by the 
Toronto Star through a freedom-of-information request. In 2024, the amount was $4,719,310.
In the fiscal year 2024-25, the government spent $1.7 billion in OSAP grants and $301 million on loans, assisting 
473,000 students. Based on these figures and the new data, the payments found to be ineligible represent less 
than one per cent of total disbursements and number of students affected. (The proportions of ineligible aid may in 
fact be overstated as the wrongly granted aid covers two whole years as opposed to one fiscal year.)
"Any inappropriate use of OSAP funding is unacceptable," Bianca Giacoboni, press secretary to Colleges and 
Universities Minister Nolan Quinn, told the Star on Monday. "We have a robust framework in place to protect 
OSAP from fraudulent use, and we are implementing new technology and exploring other avenues to strengthen 
the program's integrity."
The records requested by the Star did not disclose how much of the funding has been recouped, noting that a 
"standard OSAP repayment process" applies. They note that while some cases may result in defaulted loans that 
proceed to collections, "we do not have aggregate numbers based on investigations and do not track this data."
In February, the government, as part of its announcement of a $6.4-billion investment in post-secondary and the 
lifting of the tuition freeze, said it was revamping the Ontario Student Assistance Program, moving from a largely 
grant-based model to one where three-quarters of aid would be in the form of repayable loans. 
The ministry, which estimated the cost of OSAP could hit $4.1 billion by 2028-29, explained that the changes would 
strengthen the long-term sustainability of the program and bring it in line with other provinces.
Days later, Premier Ford focused on allegations of misuse, saying he had received thousands of calls along with 
accounts of students using OSAP funds to purchase luxury items. "I've heard some nightmare stories ... about kids 
Page 2 of 3
Less than 1% of OSAP cases flagged as ineligible Data casts doubt on Ford's claims of abuse as rationale for 
changes to student aid
going out there buying fancy watches and cologne and not needing it," he said. "That doesn't fly with the 
taxpayers."
Quinn later told the Globe and Mail that over the past two years, the ministry has been investigating numerous 
cases of alleged fraud and misuse of OSAP funds, with 902 investigations last year, up from 862 the year before. 
At the time, the minister's office did not provide additional details on the outcomes of those investigations but 
provided the Globe with links to online videos and posts in which students appeared to claim using OSAP funds for 
Blue Jays tickets and Ray-Ban sunglasses.
"Any misuse of government funding through a program like OSAP is concerning because you want that financial 
assistance to go to students who need it the most," said New Democrat MPP Peggy Sattler, her party's critic for 
colleges and universities.
But, she posited, "Why is the premier making these suggestions that abuse of OSAP is rampant ... this data does 
not support that.
"They're using these allegations as a way to justify gutting the financial assistance that so many low- and moderate-
income students in Ontario rely on to be able to fund their post-secondary education."
Data obtained by the Star shows there were 909 cases investigated by the province in 2025; 751 were closed and 
151 remain open. In 2024, there were 879 investigations; 39 remain open.
Over those two years, 530 cases were deemed the most egregious, and, according to the ministry, would have 
required immediate repayment of ineligible funds and restricted access to OSAP until the debt was repaid. 
Penalties in other cases vary depending on the seriousness and can include a hold on funding, a warning, an 
adjustment to entitlement and a requirement to repay overpayments.
The ministry draws a clear line between misuse, misrepresentation and fraud with only the latter constituting a 
criminal offence and the focus of police investigations, of which none were reported. 
The documents note that OSAP investigations are becoming increasingly complex, particularly in verifying the 
identity and eligibility of applicants with complicated immigration or residency status. They also point to challenges

wrongly granted to students later found to be ineligible, with no cases referred to police, raising questions about the 
scale of alleged abuse Premier Doug Ford cited, in part, to justify overhauling OSAP.

statuses, participation in non-bona fide studies or other discrepancies," according to records obtained by the 
Toronto Star through a freedom-of-information request. In 2024, the amount was $4,719,310.

473,000 students. Based on these figures and the new data, the payments found to be ineligible represent less 
than one per cent of total disbursements and number of students affected. (The proportions of ineligible aid may in 
fact be overstated as the wrongly granted aid covers two whole years as opposed to one fiscal year.)

body:
The movies first came to Toronto in the late summer of 1896, as the Lumière Cinématographe flickered away 
under a tent at the Industrial Exhibition (now the CNE). In the 130 years since, scores of cinemas have lined 
Toronto's streets, some closing down, others resurrected thanks to the repertory and art-house scenes of the 1960s 
and '70s. Unlike multiplexes, these screens weren't chasing opening-weekend grosses. They were showing Ingmar 
Bergman and Bruce Lee, experimental films and cult classics, restored prints and midnight horror - all of which gave 
the city a unique movie culture.
Some of these theatres - including the Paradise, Fox and Revue (which I briefly ran) - have survived every 
supposed death knell: corporate consolidation, multiplex creep, cable television, home video, streaming, the COVID 
pandemic. And despite Cineplex recently shuttering its Beaches location and posting a fourth-quarter profit of 
$369,000, down from $3.3 million a year earlier, Toronto's independent and repertory houses are not in retreat, 
they're thriving.
Talking about movie theatres really lights people up. Mention a long-gone neighbourhood cinema and suddenly 
someone's telling you about the sticky floors and velvet curtains of their childhood. And if the venue is still standing, 
brace yourself for the diehards, fiercely loyal to their screen of choice. It's part nostalgia, part civic pride, part deeply 
personal memory.
Frequent filmgoer Gregory Dalgetty sees lines around the block at various venues on a weekly basis. "There's a 
huge renaissance happening right now," he told the Star. "People are clearly starved for this kind of experience. 
Repertory cinemas feel like they're in a boom, and I think it's partly a reaction to streaming - which a lot of people 
don't want."
Film critic, programmer and Star contributor Saffron Maeve said, "I enjoy hearing other people's reactions. There's 
something phenomenal about sitting beside someone, breathing beside them, while you're watching the same 
movie."
As a programmer herself - she curates the "Contours" series at the Paradise (films about art) and "Apparatus 
Theory" at the Revue (films about filmmaking) - she's struck by how varied audiences are. 
Page 2 of 6

repertory theatres have created a vast community of c....
"The megaplex and the rep cinema are different cultural products," Sonya William, executive director of the Network 
of Independent Cinema Exhibitors, told the Star. "They are both important. The megaplex can show the big new 
movie that is in the zeitgeist. Whereas the rep cinema is a place that values cinema as art and offers its audience a 
personalized touch."
Beyond inventive programming, these cinemas sometimes offer custom posters designed by local artists and 
specialty zines. Some series, like the Revue's "Black Belt Cinema" and "Neon Dreams," sell their own branded 
merch.
Sure, you may be able to stream a particular vintage or cult movie at home. But you can't stream a sold-out 35-mm 
restoration, a filmmaker Q&A or a drag-hosted screening - many of which can be had at the following cinemas (as 
well as TIFF Lightbox, Hot Docs Ted Rogers Cinema and Innis Town Hall).
Fox Theatre
2236 Queen St. E.
Origin story
The Fox opened in 1914 as The Theatre Without a Name, was once affectionately known as "The Morgue," and 
more than a century later remains one of the city's last neighbourhood picture houses east of the Don Valley. Once 
you've passed the street-facing box office, its doors open beneath a glowing stained-glass panel featuring one of 
the theatre's former names, "Prince Edward," casting warm light over red carpets and framed posters. Past the 
spacious lobby, where the snack bar gleams under soft bulbs, a long, patterned corridor guides moviegoers toward 
the auditorium.
Andy Willick and Daniel Demois bought the theatre in 2007. "It's not a very glamorous business," Willick said. 
"There's this perception that it's all fun and games and you get to watch movies all the time, but it's kind of 
relentless. You're constantly programming for the future and there's a lot more marketing work required these 
days."
Still, Willick is optimistic about the road ahead for independent cinemas. "COVID was such a terrifying time, and I 
felt like it was over for us. But we've rebuilt the business and the audience supported us - there was a genuine 
outpouring of love for the theatre, and that feels really good."
Shirley Hughes, a resident of the Beach, considers the Fox her go-to and plans her monthly movie-going around 
the cinema's calendar.
"It's an incredibly important space," she told the Star. "I'm starting to see regulars in the line all the time. It feels a 
little family-like. They're also doing some new and interesting things with their programming."
What's new
 Over the past year, The Fox has expanded its slate of new independent and international films. Willick grew up 
seeing foreign-language titles at the now-closed Cumberland in Yorkville and believes those films are underserved 
in Toronto. "It's been such a strong year overall for international films," he said, "and they're breaking into the 
mainstream in a bigger way."
Coming attractions
 "Romy and Michele's High School Reunion," with live BoylesqueTO show (March 6); "Jesus Christ Superstar" 
singalong (April 5).
Carlton Cinemas
20 Carlton St.

repertory theatres have created a vast community of c....
Origin story
 The Carlton opened in 1981 as part of Cineplex's expanding multiplex empire. At first, its screens focused on 
action films because of its proximity to Maple Leaf Gardens, but it quickly shifted to art-house and foreign films 
because of neighbouring Toronto Metropolitan University (then known as Ryerson) and the Village. The art-house 
strategy continues to this day under the Imagine Cinemas banner, offering many Canadian films their only 
theatrical venue.
Stefan Kern, operations manager for Imagine Cinemas, said the narrative that theatrical exhibition is on life support 
doesn't square with what he's seeing. Imagine Cinemas, which also operates the six-screen Market Square on 
Front Street, as well as theatres in Windsor and Timmins, is "on pace with pre-COVID numbers," he said.
When the Hollywood pipeline was disrupted by the pandemic and strikes, the Carlton leaned harder into repertory 
programming and international and indie releases. At first, it was experimentation - "throwing everything at the wall 
and seeing what stuck." Now, he said, those screenings - and the discounted "Rewind and Replay" throwback 
series of nostalgic '80s and '90s fare - are doing very well.
The audience has shifted, too. With TMU next door, Kern said, the repertory crowd skews heavily Gen Z - and, 
notably, young women.
The audience speaks
 When Alison Lang first moved to Toronto, she gravitated toward the Carlton Cinemas.
"I grew up with multiplexes around me - I was in the suburbs - and I just thought the cinema experience was like 
that: cookie-cutter," she said. "The Carlton was amazing because it was so affordable." The nine screens, which 
show a mix of Hollywood fare and independent and older titles, offer five-dollar admission on Tuesdays.
An author and editor of the zine Movies Men Ruined for Me, Lang still visits the Carlton monthly. What keeps her 
coming back, she said, is the atmosphere. "It has a distinct esthetic. The velvet rope. Everything feels so warmly 
antiquated. The staff are always amazing."
Coming attractions
 "Enter the Dragon" (March 6-12); "There Will Be Blood" (March 20-26).
Paradise Theatre
1006 Bloor St. W.
Origin story
 After shutting down in 2006, the Paradise Theatre sat dark for 13 years. Built in 1937, the theatre was revived in 
2019 by winery magnate Moray Tawse, who wanted to see his childhood cinema flicker back to life. It reopened 
three months before the pandemic closed cinemas across the country.
Today, the Paradise boasts some of the most imaginative programming in the city. There's the Canada-focused 
"Desire in Motion" series; the Queer Cinema Club, a communal living room for Toronto's LGBTQ audiences; 
"Eastern Promises," showing the best of East Asian cinema; and programming director Lucy Walker's monthly 
spotlights on themes ranging from working class-struggles to the telephone as a dramatic motif. It is also home to 
the Toronto Film Society, established in 1948, which screens classic films from the 1920s to the '70s.
The Paradise has cycled through multiple identities. It screened Italian films throughout the '60s and '70s, and in the 
'80s became Toronto's last outpost of the national Eve chain of adult cinemas.
Film fans

repertory theatres have created a vast community of c....
Burak Batu Tunçel, who co-programs the Free Friday Films series at Innis Town Hall, moved to Toronto from 
Istanbul three years ago. "When I first came here, I was so overwhelmed by the amount of films I could see," 
Tunçel said. "Every month I look at what the cinemas are offering, and sometimes they shed a light on films you've 
never heard of."
He attends the Paradise regularly. "I love the old-school marquee and billboards that light up after dark. I find 
myself so distracted these days, and going to the Paradise, I'm immersed."
Local filmmaker Kire Paputts recently premiered his new movie, "Junkie Run," at the Paradise. "Some of my 
favourite film screening experiences have been at Toronto rep cinemas," he said. While promoting the screening, 
Paputts evoked the spirit of the east end's late Roxy Theatre (now a Circle K and Tim Hortons), which became a 
hotbed of counterculture in the '70s, introducing Toronto moviegoers to the films of trash auteur John Waters. "I've 
always gravitated toward counterculture cinema," Paputts said, "and you just don't find that at Cineplex."
Coming attractions
 "Bridget Jones's Diary" screening and "Definitely Thriving" book launch (March 5); "In the Movies: The Music 
Videos of Sloan," with Jay Ferguson and Chris Murphy (March 22).
Revue Cinema
400 Roncesvalles Ave.
Origin story
On a recent cold Sunday afternoon, the 504 streetcar stopped in front of the 114-year-old Revue Cinema. Riders 
disembarked and got in line for a free community screening of the Oscar-winning 1942 drama "Casablanca." Inside 
the auditorium, Roncesvalles resident Jennifer Taylor, who first attended the Revue in 1998, found her regular seat 
- close to the screen, to the left of the middle section. "I grew up in a really small village in Eastern Canada and 
there was no movie theatre to go to," she said. "I've always thought the movie theatre experience was a bit of a 
magical treasure."
Toronto's oldest operating movie theatre, which survived a lease dispute in 2024, is now a registered charity and 
recently installed a 70-mm projector - one of the few places in the city to offer what was once a common movie-
going experience. But the Roncesvalles institution started off on shaky ground, as civic groups opposed its 
construction in 1911 because of its proximity to a school, concerned about the supposed moral corruption of the 
movies.
In the 1960s, the Revue screened German films, at a time when many neighbourhood cinemas catered to the 
cultural diversity of its residents. (The Brighton, a few blocks south, screened Polish films, and is now a 
convenience store.) Cemented as a go-to art-house destination in the '70s, thanks to former managers Paul Ennis 
and Bob Huber, the Revue was revived as a not-for-profit in 2006, and is an electric space many nights of the week, 
with queues curving around the corner onto Howard Park Avenue.
Inside, the concession line spills out of the modest lobby, snaking its way down to the front of the auditorium. The 
green reclining seats, installed in the '90s, are overdue for renewal, but the energy in the cinema on a busy night is 
a shared pulse that makes the worn upholstery beside the point.
Get with the programming
 Established series like "Dumpster Raccoon," "Designing the Movies," "Black Belt Cinema," "Drunken Cinema" and 
"Nightmare Alley" have dedicated audiences. New series like "Apparatus Theory" and "Psych-Out Cinema" are 
gathering their own devoted crowds.
Page 5 of 6
Let's go to the movies By screening stone-cold classics, cult favourites and avant-garde greats, Toronto's 
repertory theatres have created a vast community of c....
Programming director Serena Whitney balances the busy roster of monthly curated series with her own savvy picks 
(series like "Dead of Winter" and "The Perfect Date").
Whitney took over programming in 2020, steered the cinema through the pandemic, and isn't too worried about the 
existential threat of a potential Warner Bros. merger with Netflix or Paramount. Indie cinemas are creatures of 
survival, she said.
"It can be challenging when you don't have access to certain catalogues or titles, but indie theatres have always 
found ways to be creative and get past that."
She did note, however, that programming a theatre is exhausting. "Most people aren't aware of how much work 
goes into programming and running a theatre. So much planning, way in advance, to make sure we can build up 
the excitement for movies people want to see," Whitney said. "I'm really proud of the community we built."
Coming attractions
"Friday the 13th Part III" in 3D, with live performance by Blood Opera (March 13); "Wicked" and "Wicked for Good" 
singalong (March 28).
Micro-cinemas
Toronto's earliest film exhibitions in the 1890s were pop-ups - storefronts, makeshift screening rooms with wooden 
planks for seating.
Now, micro-cinemas, vital to the city's film culture, are thriving alongside their repertory counterparts. Intimate DIY 
spaces like CineCycle, tucked behind 401 Richmond St.; Eyesore Cinema, one of Toronto's few remaining video 
rental shops, which operates a 40-seat screening room in the back; Killer B Cinema, at Junction bar See-Scape, 
which screens public-domain oddities to its regulars; Market Video, located in Kensington Market; and Reg Hartt's 
long-running Cineforum at his Bathurst Avenue home, whose black-and-white flyers advertising screenings of 
"Nosferatu" are permanently affixed into the city's utilities poles.
Some screenings don't even require a roof - the renegade They Might Be Movies series presents films in thematic 
public spaces, including the parking lot of a McDonald's and outside the Brickworks.

- close to the screen, to the left of the middle section. "I grew up in a really small village in Eastern Canada and 
there was no movie theatre to go to," she said. "I've always thought the movie theatre experience was a bit of a 
magical treasure."
Toronto's oldest operating movie theatre, which survived a lease dispute in 2024, is now a registered charity and 
recently installed a 70-mm projector - one of the few places in the city to offer what was once a common movie-
going experience. But the Roncesvalles institution started off on shaky ground, as civic groups opposed its 
construction in 1911 because of its proximity to a school, concerned about the supposed moral corruption of the 
movies.
In the 1960s, the Revue screened German films, at a time when many neighbourhood cinemas catered to the 
cultural diversity of its residents. (The Brighton, a few blocks south, screened Polish films, and is now a 
convenience store.) Cemented as a go-to art-house destination in the '70s, thanks to former managers Paul Ennis 
and Bob Huber, the Revue was revived as a not-for-profit in 2006, and is an electric space many nights of the week, 
with queues curving around the corner onto Howard Park Avenue.
Inside, the concession line spills out of the modest lobby, snaking its way down to the front of the auditorium. The 
green reclining seats, installed in the '90s, are overdue for renewal, but the energy in the cinema on a busy night is 
a shared pulse that makes the worn upholstery beside the point.
Get with the programming

gathering their own devoted crowds.

Let's go to the movies By screening stone-cold classics, cult favourites and avant-garde greats, Toronto's 
repertory theatres have created a vast community of c....

found ways to be creative and get past that."

goes into programming and running a theatre. So much planning, way in advance, to make sure we can build up 
the excitement for movies people want to see," Whitney said. "I'm really proud of the community we built."

singalong (March 28).

Toronto's earliest film exhibitions in the 1890s were pop-ups - storefronts, makeshift screening rooms with wooden

spaces like CineCycle, tucked behind 401 Richmond St.; Eyesore Cinema, one of Toronto's few remaining video 
rental shops, which operates a 40-seat screening room in the back; Killer B Cinema, at Junction bar See-Scape, 
which screens public-domain oddities to its regulars; Market Video, located in Kensington Market; and Reg Hartt's 
long-running Cineforum at his Bathurst Avenue home, whose black-and-white flyers advertising screenings of 
"Nosferatu" are permanently affixed into the city's utilities poles.
Some screenings don't even require a roof - the renegade They Might Be Movies series presents films in thematic 
public spaces, including the parking lot of a McDonald's and outside the Brickworks.

title: Liberal MPs should be defending city's stake in Billy Bishop
body:
Lately I've been thinking of the desperate words uttered by Princess Leia in "Star Wars": "Help me, Obi-Wan 
Kenobi. You're my only hope." However the "me" is Toronto, Obi-Wan is the federal Liberal government and the 
reason we need help is Billy Bishop airport expansion.
Liberals could shut down Doug Ford's jet airplane ambitions today if they wanted to. One reason they should be 
speaking up is that the Ford government is changing the rules of the game and the Liberals are the only player with 
the power to say "stop."
The "rules" are the tripartite agreement governing the airport, mandating shared responsibility and oversight 
between federal, provincial and municipal governments. The potential rule change is the "Building Billy Bishop 
Airport Act" the Ford government tabled last week that would formalize the takeover of Toronto's role in the 
agreement, breaking the spirit, if not the law itself, of that agreement. A hijacked Toronto is not what the federal 
government agreed to so it should put the brakes on jet expansion on that basis alone.
Changing the rules midgame is a classic Ford move, like the cut to Toronto city council midway through the 2018 
election. The most recent dubious rule change altered Ontario's freedom of information laws making government 
activity far more secret and - as the Trillium reported this week - will "likely" retroactively quash two Greenbelt legal 
battles by preventing the release of scandal-related documents. This is anti-democratic and, to borrow a phrase 
usually applied to rogue states, "illiberal."
The Building Billy Bishop Airport Act puts local Liberal MPs in an awkward position in another way too. So far they 
and their government have walked a high-wire act, neither supporting nor opposing airport expansion, though 
federal Transportation Minister Steve MacKinnon has indicated they're open to "modernizing arrangements at the 
airport." Vague enough to mean everything and nothing at the same time.
Local MPs, while largely maintaining fidelity to that vague sentiment, have often stressed that local views must be 
taken into account and the community must be consulted. Ford's new legislation would remove Toronto's local 
voices so the city's Liberal MPs, who have long had a reputation for taking safe-seat Toronto for granted, should at 
the very least be robustly defending constituents more than they are.
Those MPs are surely hearing an earful from their constituents, and there are petitions that have garnered 
signatures in the tens of thousands. Even resident groups in south Etobicoke are discussing the implications jets 
will have on their community.
Page 2 of 3
Liberal MPs should be defending city's stake in Billy Bishop
 That's pretty close to Ford's home turf, so it isn't just a downtown concern.
On Thursday, Chi Nguyen, the MP whose riding includes the airport, said on CBC "Metro Morning" that she's also 
hearing from residents and has questions herself, but "doesn't have an official position" about the province's 
takeover, saying there "isn't a proposed plan in front of us to react to."
Ah, but there's yet another way local Liberals are implicated, deeper than simply being part of a tripartite 
agreement: the airport is owned and operated by the Toronto Port Authority, a federally regulated agency (the 
passenger terminal itself is owned and operated by Nieuport Aviation, an investment group run by J.P. Morgan). It 
appears an agency Liberals oversee is indeed literally making concrete plans.
In an interview this week with the Globe and Mail, TPA president Roelof-Jan "RJ" Steenstra outlined some details of 
their expansion plans that could involve adding 900 metres of land for a longer runway - nearly a kilometre - into 
Lake Ontario - far more than previous expansion proposals.
With much of it jutting into the lake to the west of the airport, that's a runway aimed directly at south Etobicoke and 
is breathtakingly close to Ontario Place. 
Folks enjoying a theoretical relaxing day at Ford's Therme spa will surely be able to read plane tail numbers and 
smell jet fuel. 
Even though Torontonians themselves are largely in the dark, the city's own Liberal MPs have a direct connection 
to and authority over plans their own government agency is cooking up right now. They can't play passive, coy or 
cagey anymore: they are in a unique position to give real answers to their constituents and take a clear position. 
Actually, with the port authority plans, they already have.
So while the Liberal government has a tripartite duty to speak up and defend Toronto's legitimate stake in the future 
of Billy Bishop, they're also directly connected to plans already being made.
It's a mess. A mess of jurisdictional sleight-of-hand and shadowy plans we can't wholly see, only glimpsed here, 
there and in 900-metre chunks. All that leaves Toronto residents with a lot of uncertainty and turmoil.
What would Obi-Wan Kenobi do if he was a Liberal Toronto MP?
Maybe Torontonians should let them know what they think he'd do. I'd bet he'd be loyal and stand up for the people 
he represented.

title: Liberals against women; Ottawa doesn't seem too happy about IOC decision to limit women's categories to
body:
As the world slowly comes to terms with restoring the rights of women, the Carney government seems intent on 
perpetuating discrimination against females.
The International Olympic Committee, once steadfast in its bizarre commitment to opening up the female sporting 
category to all and sundry, is the latest organization to see the light.
A statement last week from the IOC was headlined "on the Protection of the Female (Women's) Category in 
Olympic Sport."
The IOC's new policy is that only "biological females" will be able to compete in the women's category.
It's a sensible, if long-awaited, decision although the left will rail and fulminate against it - in its coverage of the 
decision, the CBC described "biological females" as a "problematic term."
The CBC's offensive posturing is part of the continuing effort to erase women from the lexicon altogether so that we 
are left with "pregnant persons" or the even more dehumanizing "menstruators."
Last year, the United Nations even recognized that the words women and girls were in danger of being erased from 
the language with Reem Alsalem, the UN special rapporteur on violence against women and girls, feeling obliged to 
write a special report in support of biological women.
"I never imagined the day would come where my mandate would deem it necessary to prepare a report affirming 
that the words women and girls refer to distinct biological and legal categories," she said in a speech.
The IOC's new policy rests on a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test that would ensure only females compete in the female 
category. It would essentially ban transgender women and those with differences in sexual develop- ment 
conditions. From the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic Games onward, the IOC will administer a saliva, cheek swab or a 
blood sample test checking for the SRY gene.
The IOC said "the presence of the SRY gene is fixed throughout life and represents highly accurate evidence that 
an athlete has experienced male sex development."
Page 2 of 3
Liberals against women; Ottawa doesn't seem too happy about IOC decision to limit women's categories to 
females
Kirsty Coventry, a former Olympic gold-medal swimmer who was elected IOC president last June, said in the 
statement, "At the Olympic Games, even the smallest margins can be the difference between victory and defeat. 
So, it is absolutely clear that it would not be fair for biological males to compete in the female category. In addition, 
in some sports it would simply not be safe."
The new policy mirrors the approach taken by the World Athletics organization last year when they introduced gene 
testing in the female category.
In a statement, World Athletics president Seb Coe, said, "We are saying, at elite level, for you to compete in the 
female category, you have to be biologically female. It was always very clear to me and the World Athletics Council 
that gender cannot trump biology." The 2024 Paris Olympics were engulfed in controversy, particularly over 
Algerian Imane Khelif who won the women's welterweight gold medal for boxing. A leaked DNA test later revealed 
Khelif was a biological male with XY chromosomes.
But restoring the women's category to only females doesn't appear to sit well with the federal government.
A statement from Adam van Koeverden, the sports minister, while not outright denouncing the IOC policy, seemed 
to imply that the government was not happy with the ban on transgender athletes. "Our government believes in a 
sport system that provides opportunities for all Canadians, including the transgender community, to participate in 
sport and excel without discrimination," he said.
The government was reviewing "the impact of this decision on Canadian athletes," he added.
Meanwhile, Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre seemed happy to back the IOC.
Poilievre reposted a statement from author J.K. Rowling that called the IOC decision a "welcome return to fair sport 
for women and girls, but I'll never forget the scandal of Paris 2024, when people who consider themselves virtuous 
and progressive publicly cheered on men punching women."
Poilievre commented on Rowling's tweet, "What she said."
The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) on the other hand was clear in its condemnation of the IOC.
"The introduction of new rules restricting participation in women's sport categories to 'biological females', 
determined through mandatory genetic screening and testing, imposes exclusionary criteria," it said in a statement.
But that's the point: it's way past time to exclude people from the female category who don't qualify as "biological 
women."
The CCLA insisted that the policy was discriminatory in that it banned transgender women. But if transgender 
women take the test - which World Athletics called "a reliable proxy for determining biological sex" - and they fail it, 
indicating male sex development, what are they doing in the female category in the first place?
The new IOC policy is welcome in that restores the right of women to compete in their own category, will make it 
safer for them in their individual sports and because it's the right thing to do.
The headline on Koeverden's statement said it concerned the IOC's "decision regarding transgender women 
athletes." It talked about "integrity and fairness" in sport; "equal opportunities and respecting human rights" and 
"empathy, respect and care" for all Canadians.
But tellingly, Koeverden never used the word women in his statement, another example of erasing women from the 
public space.

title: Liberals move to reset committees Motion gives party more power to push through legislation
body:
The Liberals are flexing their majority muscle to change House of Commons committees, giving themselves more 
seats and the power to shut down investigations and push legislation through Parliament.
Government House Leader Steven MacKinnon introduced a motion in the Commons on Wednesday to boost the 
number of MPs on most committees to 12, with the Liberals getting seven seats, the Conservatives four and the 
Bloc Québécois one. The current 10-member makeup of the legislative committees - five Liberals, four 
Conservatives and one Bloc - gives the opposition the majority of votes, because committee chairs only vote in 
cases of a tie. 
Mackinnon said with the government's new majority standing it is time for the committee rosters to change. He said 
the government wants committees to study legislation and make changes, but is tired of partisanship that slows 
legislation.
"We do not want to play silly partisan games that waste the time and the money of taxpayers in this place. We want 
to work together to achieve big things for the Canadians we all represent," he said outside the House of Commons 
chamber.
He said it only makes sense for the government that holds a majority of seats in Parliament have a majority of seats 
on committees.
"Our democracy is built on the pillars of the House of Commons being reflected in all of the institutions of 
Parliament and notably house committees," he said. 
Committees in Parliament study legislation, and can summon witnesses and request documents in investigations of 
the government. 
Most recently, opposition members demanded Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne appear before a 
committee to speak to a possible conflict of interest over his partner's employment with the high-speed rail 
agency Alto. Liberal members of that committee filibustered for days to prevent a vote on summoning Champagne 
before they finally relented. 
MacKinnon said the Liberal filibuster was not a "silly partisan game" because the opposition was simply trying to 
attack Champagne.
Page 2 of 3
Liberals move to reset committees Motion gives party more power to push through legislation
"This felt like a deeply partisan and vexatious series of attacks on the finance minister that were completely 
unwarranted," he said. 
The Liberals secured a majority government this month after MP Marilyn Gladu crossed the floor from the 
Conservatives and Liberal candidates won in three byelections.
Conservative House Leader Andrew Scheer said the government had seized the majority through floor-crossings 
and was giving itself power that voters had denied it in last year's general election. 
"The very first thing this Liberal government has done is to make life easier for themselves, to avoid scrutiny on 
their legislation, and to avoid transparency on their decisions," he said. 
The changes are slightly different for four committees which provide oversight: ethics, public accounts, government 
operations and status of women. They currently have nine members, four from the government and five from the 
opposition. The government will gain one MP on each, giving it five to the opposition's combined five. That will 
effectively give the government majorities, because the chairs - who are usually opposition MPs - only vote in the 
case of a tie.
Scheer said the Tories would offer an amendment to MacKinnon's motion to have the oversight committees 
maintain a clear majority of opposition members as a basic symbol of transparency.
"These are important committees where the opposition does the work on behalf of Canadian taxpayers and voters, 
to shine a light, to go through line-by-line spending, to find out who got contracts and how decisions were made," he 
said. 
Scheer said those committees played central roles in investigating past Liberal scandals and should be left alone. 
"The only reason to stack the deck on these oversight committees is so that the government can sweep these types 
of investigations under the rug," he charged.
In a statement late Wednesday afternoon, MacKinnon rejected the Conservative amendment, saying all committees 
should reflect the new composition of Parliament. 
"There are not two tiers of committees in Parliament. They are all the same and the principle applies to them 
equally," he said. 
Scheer's view did not appear unanimous within his own party. On Wednesday, Conservative MP Greg McClean 
suggested that MacKinnon's move is within bounds. Asked what he made of claims the Liberals were contravening 
parliamentary tradition, McLean said they were disputes over "technicalities."
"The way Parliament runs seems to change all the time here, well, the rules of committee. We'll see what happens," 
McLean said.
B.C. Conservative MP Bob Zimmer said it would be "normal" for a majority government to have more seats on a 
committee than the opposition, but called the Liberals' success in courting floor-crossers "stacking the deck" in their 
favour.
It's unclear when the government will bring MacKinnon's motion for a vote, as the three MPs who won this month's 
byelections have not yet taken their seats in Parliament.

"The only reason to stack the deck on these oversight committees is so that the government can sweep these types 
of investigations under the rug," he charged.
In a statement late Wednesday afternoon, MacKinnon rejected the Conservative amendment, saying all committees 
should reflect the new composition of Parliament.

equally," he said. 
Scheer's view did not appear unanimous within his own party. On Wednesday, Conservative MP Greg McClean

parliamentary tradition, McLean said they were disputes over "technicalities."
"The way Parliament runs seems to change all the time here, well, the rules of committee. We'll see what happens," 
McLean said.
B.C. Conservative MP Bob Zimmer said it would be "normal" for a majority government to have more seats on a 
committee than the opposition, but called the Liberals' success in courting floor-crossers "stacking the deck" in their 
favour.
It's unclear when the government will bring MacKinnon's motion for a vote, as the three MPs who won this month's 
byelections have not yet taken their seats in Parliament.

title: Liberals move to take control of House committees now that they've secured majority
body:
OTTAWA - The Liberals are moving to take control of House of Commons committees now that they've secured a 
majority government.
House leader Steven MacKinnon said in a social media post Tuesday that the Liberals will seek to change the 
standing orders, the rules that govern the Commons, to ensure they have the most votes on committees.
"Prime Minister Mark Carney and his government are determined to work constructively both in the House and in 
parliamentary committees," he said. 
Majority governments traditionally hold a majority of seats on House committees.
Because the Liberals won a minority in last April's election, MPs agreed to form committees with four Liberals, four 
Conservatives and one member from the Bloc Québécois.
MacKinnon is proposing that most committees will now have seven Liberals, four Conservatives and one Bloc 
member.
The standing orders are typically agreed upon unanimously, but MacKinnon's proposed change will require a vote 
in the House. He said he intends to give notice of a motion in the coming days.
Committees are a key step in examining legislation and holding the government to account through studies.
Carney's Liberal government was granted a majority earlier this month through a set of byelection wins.
The governing party swept three byelections in the Toronto area and the Montreal suburb Terrebonne, giving them 
174 seats in the House of Commons. Carney's federal government is the first in Canada's history to switch from a 
minority to a majority between elections.
The byelection results, combined with five opposition MPs who crossed the floor to the Liberals in recent months, 
have pushed Carney's party over a threshold it could not reach in last year's election.
The Liberals won 169 seats last April, shy of the 172 needed for a bare-bones majority.

Page 2 of 3

Conservatives sent supporters a fundraising email Tuesday evening arguing that Carney is "going to use his 
majority powers to make life easier for his government."
The email asked for donations to help Conservatives "stop Carney from stacking the deck and continuing his 
cynical power grab."
"He’s going to stack the deck on committees to shut down investigations into his scandals, conflicts, and waste, 
because he thinks no one can stop him," said the email. "Since 1867, the founding of our country, committees have 
reflected the results of the ballot box, not a manufactured majority. But now, Carney is trying to reset the balance of 
power on committees to limit his opposition."
"We will not stand by quietly while Liberals and their insiders rig the system."
Canada hadn't had a majority government since 2019, when former prime minister Justin Trudeau's Liberals were 
reduced to a minority in an election.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published April 21, 2026.

title: Liberals' C-3 gives millions a door pass; A potential flood of undesirables Comment
body:
In December, the Liberals extended Canadian citizenship to everyone in the world over the age of three months 
who can prove that one of their ancestors was born here, no matter how far back.
This was the result of Bill C-3. It means that potentially millions of people with no natural democratic right to 
intervene in our politics will soon be able to vote in our elections. Millions who haven't contributed a cent to our 
economy will become eligible for our social safety net. Among them will be organized criminals, terrorists spawned 
from parents who left Canada to engage in barbarism overseas, people who can't speak English or French, 
scammers, drug dealers, and many more undesirables.
And, as most of this newly enfranchised population is American, many Trumpfugees. Some 1,480 people became 
citizens via C-3 in its first month and a half of life, according to Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. In 
that time, 6,280 applications have been processed. The Liberals won't give their estimate for how high these 
numbers can go.
You can get a rough snapshot of who's taking advantage of this new immigration loophole and how it works by 
snooping on the relevant corners of Reddit. On r/Canadiancitizenship, people help each other with applications, 
assuring each other that they are just as Canadian as anyone else up there, and congratulating each other on 
getting approved. Users worry about having insufficient documentation, only to be assured that Ancestry.com 
records are good enough, and that certified copies of records aren't necessary.
For them, it's great; for us, we have to wonder what fraud safeguards are in place at the immigration department ... 
and what it even means to be a Canadian anymore.
One user reported that their children became citizens by way of a great-greatgreat-grandparent born in Ontario, 
who died in the United States in 1922. Another person, five generations down from someone born in New 
Brunswick, claimed they were approved in one week without submitting baptism or birth records for that original 
ancestor.
Anecdotes by people with more Canadian ancestry are more common, but it's not unusual to see victory posts by 
people whose family was last in "Canada" before it became a country with that name.
While we don't have demographic statistics of the immigrants who are getting waved through under C-3, it does 
seem to be the case that some are using this new pathway to flee what they perceive as persecution in the United 
Page 2 of 3
Liberals' C-3 gives millions a door pass; A potential flood of undesirables Comment
States. A number of users identifying as trans, or parents of trans children, have stated that their applications were 
processed with urgency, taking anywhere from a few weeks to 10 days. The department notes that the estimated 
processing time for new applications is 10 months.
People seeking to "avoid situations of potential harm or hardship" relating to race, gender, religion, nationality, 
sexuality, or otherwise being part of "particular groups," can get fast processing. Which is a low bar given the 
"potential" part.
It's obvious enough that the C-3 loophole will be attractive to U.S. progressives, especially those who are radical 
enough to want to leave their home country for Canada. The Liberals would have made that assessment when they 
were making the rules, too: despite their anti-American rhetoric, they've been more than happy to create a rule that, 
fully realized, would bring Canada closer to 51st-state status than President Donald Trump could ever achieve.
Indeed, the descendants of French Canadians in the U.S. are estimated to number at least 10 million. If they were 
all suddenly given citizenship, they'd comprise about a quarter of the nation, as Canada counted only 33 million 
citizens in the past census.
And remember: C-3 considers everyone eligible to be born a citizen, thus, criminal records don't matter. Nor does it 
assess whether someone will be a net-negative contributor to Canada, indeed, the immigration department offers 
speedy processing for those in need of health care and pension money.
The benefits only flow in one direction here: Canada's population is at risk of being overwhelmed by foreign 
interests, and its people - its actual people, the ones who have always lived herehave been saddled with the 
responsibility of providing for unknown numbers of new civic dependants capitalizing on their family tree. The U.S. 
will not be submitting to Canadian interests in turn, nor will it be extending its welfare net to a significant portion of 
our people.
These problems don't even end at the U.S. For example, Indian descendants of Canada's early population of Sikh 
nationalists could use this route; so could the offspring of anyone in the history of Canada who ever left to join a 
terrorism group overseas.
There were 40,000 Canadians living in Lebanon in 2006, and who knows how many descendants; that could 
translate into thousands of eligible citizens today - it's hard to know. There is, of course, a risk that there are 
Hezbollah members today who could take advantage of the new doors-open policy, especially since the Liberals 
insisted on keeping security checks out of the process.
The only flimsy guardrail the Liberals put on Bill C-3 is that anyone born to a Canadian who was born abroad after 
Dec. 15, 2025 has a slightly higher barrier to citizenship eligibility. Their parent has to spend 1,095 days in Canada 
to pass citizenship down to their kids. That's all. It's a joke.
Prime Minister Mark Carney boasted in February that he had "taken back control of immigration," pointing to a 
reduction in new asylum applications and foreign workers. And it's true that those taps have been turned down. But 
a new one has been opened, and it's poised to flood the country in a way that is much more difficult to deal with.
Visas are easy to reduce and revoke; citizenship, less so. That's going to change if things keep going the way they 
are.

title: LLRIB sets March 13 nomination meetings for chief, council
body:
LA RONGE — The Lac La Ronge Indian Band (LLRIB) has announced nomination meetings for its upcoming band 
election, with candidates for chief and councillor positions to be nominated March 13.
According to a public notice from the band, nomination meetings will take place from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. across six 
electoral sections within the LLRIB.
The meetings will allow electors to nominate candidates for one chief position and 12 councillor positions 
representing communities throughout the band’s territory.
Nomination meetings will be held at the following locations:
• Electoral Section 1: White Hall, Little Red River Reserve (#106C and #106D) — two councillor positions
• Electoral Section 2: Band Hall, Grandmother’s Bay Reserve (#219) — one councillor position
• Electoral Section 3: Charlie Halkett Memorial Band Hall, Morin Lake Reserve (#217) — one councillor 
position
• Electoral Section 4: Sucker River Band Hall, Sucker River Reserve (#156C) — one councillor position
• Electoral Section 5: Rhonda Hardlotte Band Hall, Stanley Mission Reserve (#157) — three councillor 
positions
• Electoral Section 6: Jonas Roberts Memorial Community Centre, Lac La Ronge Reserve (#156) and 
Kitsaki Reserve (#156B) — four councillor positions
In the post from LLRIB, candidates seeking the position of chief or councillor must meet several requirements 
under the Lac La Ronge Indian Band Election Act.
Among the eligibility criteria, candidates must:
• Be at least 18 years old and eligible to vote under the Act
• Provide a criminal record check and vulnerable sector check issued within the past six months
• Have no more than $1,000 in outstanding debt to the Lac La Ronge Indian Band or its affiliated entities
• Not have been convicted of corrupt election practices

Page 2 of 2
LLRIB sets March 13 nomination meetings for chief, council
Councillor candidates must also meet any residency requirements tied to the electoral section they intend to 
represent.
LLRIB said eligible electors may nominate and second candidates during the nomination meeting. If more 
candidates are nominated than positions available, an election will be held in accordance with band election 
regulations.
Candidates may also speak in support of their nomination during the meeting.
Copies of the Lac La Ronge Indian Band Election Act and Election Regulations are available from the band 
administration office or through the LLRIB website.
The nomination process is being overseen by Chief Electoral Officer Randy Clarke, with the election office based in 
La Ronge.
Residents seeking additional information can contact the election office by email at llrib.elections@llrib.ca or by 
phone at 306-420-7385.
