title: Report raises red flags on procurement; Questions surround efficacy of program aimed at increasing
body:
The federal government may be overestimating how much procurement spending ends up in Indigenous hands by 
hundreds of millions of dollars, a recent study finds.
The peer-reviewed research paper, published in the journal Studies in Political Economy, found that up to $839 
million in government spending under the Procurement Strategy for Indigenous Business (PSIB) went to 
organizations that appeared to have few Indigenous employees or limited capacity to carry out the work.
Of that total, the study found $699 million was awarded to "red flag" suppliers, or those that qualified as Indigenous 
under current federal rules, but, according to the study, seemed to offer little to no added value to a given 
government contract.
"It puts into question the effectiveness of PSIB in bringing dollars to Indigenous peoples," said Noah Fry, a post-
doctoral fellow in political science at Dalhousie University and the study's author.
"They (the government) are going to come up with figures saying they've awarded billions of dollars to Indigenous 
peoples and firms, and the reality is a lot of those dollars aren't going to Indigenous peoples and firms."
The study, published online at the end of February, put a dollar figure on an issue thrust into the spotlight during the 
ArriveCan scandal and the ensuing federal hearings and reports released in the aftermath.
ARRIVECAN SCANDAL RAISED QUESTIONS ABOUT PROCUREMENT The PSIB is meant to increase the 
number of federal contracts awarded to Indigenous-owned and -operated businesses.
The strategy has been around in some form since 1996, but government spending under the PSIB has increased 
substantially since 2021, when then prime minister Justin Trudeau's government set a target that would see five 
per cent of total federal procurement spending go to Indigenous businesses.
"Under the Trudeau government, they ramped up the ambition of the strategy," Fry said. "It has been ramping up to 
include more and more departments."
Page 2 of 5
Report raises red flags on procurement; Questions surround efficacy of program aimed at increasing 
Indigenous capacity
Progress toward the five per cent target is achieved through "set-asides," or restrictions on some federal contracts 
that limit competition to Indigenous suppliers. Suppliers are required to be at least 51 per cent Indigenous owned 
and conduct at least 33 per cent of the total value of work performed on the contract.
The approach came under scrutiny during the ArriveCAN scandal, a series of revelations over the mismanaged 
procurement process behind an app developed during the COVID-19 pandemic to help travellers share their 
vaccination status before entering the country. The fallout led to scrutiny of Dalian Enterprises, an Indigenous IT 
firm awarded several set-asides for work on the app.
Dalian, which was part of a joint venture with a non-Indigenous firm, received nearly $8 million in federal 
procurement value while subcontracting the work to other non-Indigenous firms.
Several Indigenous organizations have voiced concerns both at parliamentary committees and in the media about 
potential abuses of the system.
Dawn Madahbee Leach, member of the First Nation Procurement Authority (FNPA) board, said Fry's study pointed 
to a "major problem."
Using two government data sets - the Indigenous Business Directory (IBD) and a government database for 
proactive disclosure of government contracts - Fry searched for businesses with a similar setup to Dalian.
'RED FLAG SUPPLIERS' By combing the databases for organizations with "no evident added value to their work as 
suppliers beyond contract management," Fry flagged 44 distinct organizations representing 1,192 contracts worth 
up to $839 million.
The contracts he included date back to 2014, though most were awarded after 2021 when the "ambition" of the 
strategy started to grow, Fry said.
Fry labelled 26 of the 44 firms as "red flag suppliers" that "often have no products, limited internal capacity (i.e. staff 
) to deliver the contracts they receive, and vague company descriptions." Many of these firms were IT suppliers, Fry 
found.
While these firms illustrate government loopholes, Fry stressed that they worked within legal parameters.
"Nothing in this research note suggests that these groups are conducting immoral or illicit work," Fry wrote.
In one example, the study cited Adirondack Information, which was listed as receiving contracts worth up to a total 
of $220 million and had just four employees, according to the IBD. The consulting firm had several contracts with a 
non-Indigenous businesses, according to the study.
Adirondack Information's website said that it was "a pre-approved vendor to the Federal Government (... that) has 
access to a variety of Aboriginal set-aside and non-Aboriginal procurement vehicles."
Adirondack Information did not respond to requests for comment.
In another example, Tato Recruiting - an Indigenous-owned IT professional services firm - was listed as the primary 
contractor for up to 33 contracts worth $42.9 million, despite having one staff member, according to the IBD.
According to the study, 30 of those contracts were joint ventures with S.i. Systems, a non-Indigenous IT company 
with a workforce large enough it lists 14 vice-presidents on its website.
"Contracts may not be going to Indigenous people at all because they don't have the in-house capacity to do those 
contracts," Fry said.
Page 3 of 5
Report raises red flags on procurement; Questions surround efficacy of program aimed at increasing 
Indigenous capacity
Reached by the Ottawa Citizen for comment, president of Tato Recruiting John Beaupré said he was a proud First 
Nation entrepreneur and member of Timiskaming First Nation, with more than 15 years of experience in industry 
and strong ties to his community.
"I am aware of the study in question which has significant factual inaccuracies and many of its assertions are 
patently false. I will note that at no time was I ever contacted for comment or fact-checking prior to publication," he 
said.
"Tato Recruiting has already returned more than $200,000 to Indigenous communities through direct support and 
community initiatives, from supporting youth sports teams and friendship centres to funding academic 
scholarships."
Beaupré added that the majority of Tato Recruiting's team was Indigenous.
"Tato Recruiting has followed all rules and regulations of the Procurement for Indigenous Business Strategy (PSIB) 
... This has been confirmed through government audits, as well as most recently through an Indigenous Business 
Directory audit," he said.
Beaupré said the study was based on an "erroneous conception of how the industry operates," and that firms in the 
space provided significant value beyond contract management. Further, he said, Tato was a "staffing firm" and not 
a recruiting agency, as the study suggested. The company, he said, conducts its own recruiting and, in cases where 
it works with third parties, they are Indigenous partners.
An organization called Setaside Solutions was another example cited in Fry's research. The study said that the 
business management consultancy was named to five contracts worth up to a total of $519,043 and it had just three 
listed employees, according to its IBD registration.
Setaside Solutions did not respond to a request for comment.
INDIGENOUS FIRMS, SUPPLIERS NOT TO BLAME, RESEARCHER SAYS Fry emphasized that nothing in his 
research suggested these Indigenous firms or suppliers were to blame.
Instead, he said, the federal government "has created a procurement landscape in which departments (and) 
procuring officers are incentivized to flag firms and suppliers as Indigenous without much consideration to whether 
those dollars are going to Indigenous people at all."
In an email, Indigenous Services Canada spokesperson Anispiragas Piragasanathar said safeguards were in place, 
such as ensuring businesses listed in the IBD are at least 51 per cent Indigenous-owned and have Indigenous 
partners who were actively involved in strategic and operational decision-making and receive financial benefits 
proportional to their ownership and role.
In 2025, the department strengthened the integrity of the directory by standardizing internal processes and audits, 
enhancing training materials and strengthening verification guidelines for staff, Piragasanathar said.
He also pointed to a federal government web page that aimed to "set the record straight, dispeling common 
misconceptions" about the PSIB and defended the strategy as an effective way to create fair and equitable 
opportunities for Indigenous businesses.
"PSIB reduces barriers, advances reconciliation, and supports the growth of Indigenous businesses," the website 
reads.
"In 2023-24, the Government of Canada awarded over $1.24 billion in contracts to Indigenous businesses, 
surpassing the 5 per cent minimum target and repre- senting 6.1 per cent of all eligible government contracts, of 
which about 40 per cent were awarded through set-aside opportunities specific to Indigenous businesses under the 
PSIB."
Page 4 of 5
Report raises red flags on procurement; Questions surround efficacy of program aimed at increasing 
Indigenous capacity
Responding to a followup question, another spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada Jacinthe Goulet said 
the study "appears to make conclusions" that do not fully reflect policies and practices under the PSIB.
Goulet said most PSIB contracts were competitively tendered and awarded to firms delivering needed services.
"As well, business eligibility to be listed on the Indigenous Business Directory and/or capacity to participate in PSIB 
contracts cannot be judged solely from publicly available information," she said.
The government said it was working to transfer administration of the IBD to an Indigenous organization to allow 
Indigenous peoples to set their own criteria for which businesses qualify.
INDIGENOUS ORGANIZATION SAYS STUDY POINTS TO 'MAJOR PROBLEM' The task of developing an 
Indigenous-led national First Nations business directory will fall to the First Nation Procurement Authority (FNPA), 
established by the Assembly of First Nations.
Madahbee Leach is a board member.
"It concerns me that some opportunities may be taken by others who aren't experienced or are using non-
Indigenous suppliers to meet the need when we do have Indigenous suppliers able and ready and willing to take on 
some of these contracts," said Madahbee Leach, who has worked for nearly 40 years on financing Indigenous 
businesses.
"I think there's a lot of opportunities that legitimate Indigenous businesses are missing when we don't have the 
proper requirements in place."
Madahbee Leach said she favoured a system that would verify whether applicants had the necessary credentials to 
carry out the work for the contract on offer.
"If it's a mechanic's garage, they have to have the mechanic's licence," she said. "We always have to make sure 
that the individual has the expertise and the credentials ... We've brought that into the Indigenous business 
directory, too."
Madahbee Leach said any issues occurring in public contracting were likely found in the private sector, too.
"There's lost opportunity in the private sector as well," she said.
And Canada isn't the only place grappling with the problem, Fry said, listing Australia as another country with an 
Indigenous procurement target and similar loopholes.
"If you don't design the program right, then what's going to happen is you're going to have these firms who are 
effectively using the program to further the ends of those who have long been advantaged by public procurement 
anyway," he said. !@COPYRIGHT=© 2026 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Requests 'stale to the point of being useless' when released Bike lane FOI filing in 2024 one example of
body:
In November 2024, the Star first filed a freedom of information request with Ontario's Ministry of Transportation for 
communications sent or received by the minister and five ministry officials, containing the words "bike lanes."
The request followed Prabmeet Sarkaria's announcement that his government would force the removal of some 
Toronto bike lanes - legislation that sparked intense public debate, a legal challenge now being deliberated by 
Ontario's Court of Appeal and, finally, a compromise with the city of Toronto to preserve the Bloor Street bike lane 
while resurrecting a vehicle lane.
Sixteen months later, the Star has not received any internal emails, reports or other records from Sarkaria's 
ministry. Nor has it received a ministry decision about which records it considers releasable and which it will try to 
keep secret under Ontario's government transparency laws. 
Last week, the province's information and privacy commissioner - which ordered the Transportation Ministry in 
August to give the Star its decision no later than last Sept. 18 - said the ministry "has advised that it is actively 
working on responding to your request." The ministry has provided the Star with such assurances since late 2024.
The timeline doesn't surprise government transparency advocates. Although Premier Doug Ford's government has 
come under fire for moving to retroactively shield records from public scrutiny, they say the Ontario government 
was already dragging out the current freedom-of-information (FOI) process - potentially making records no longer 
relevant to public debate or decision-making.
"The FOI system in Ontario is barely adequate" now, said James Turk, director of the Centre for Free Expression 
at Toronto Metropolitan University, with little to stop the province from delaying release until records are "stale to 
the point of being useless.
"And instead of dramatically increasing access to records, for which people have a right, Ford is moving to 
dramatically reduce public access."

title: Robert Mueller, ex-FBI chief who led Trump-Russia inquiry, dead at 81
body:
Robert Mueller, the former FBI director who led a politically explosive investigation into Donald Trump, has died 
aged 81, triggering a gloating response Saturday from the U.S. president.
U.S. media reported that Mueller died late Friday, citing a family statement, but did not specify a location or cause.
Trump responded quickly on Truth Social, writing: "Robert Mueller just died. Good, I'm glad he's dead. He can no 
longer hurt innocent people!"
Mueller led the FBI for 12 years, starting just days before the September 11, 2001 Al-Qaeda attacks on the United 
States, during which time he built up the bureau's counterterror mission.
After his tenure at the FBI, he was tapped as a special counsel for the Justice Department to lead an investigation 
into whether Trump's presidential campaign conspired with Russia to get him elected.
Starting in 2017, Mueller operated for two years quietly behind the scenes, emerging in July 2019 to testify before 
Congress about the probe that Trump regularly denounced as a "witch hunt."
For many Americans, the nationally televised hearing was the first close look at the patrician, grey-haired former 
FBI director.
What many saw was a cautious career prosecutor who was forced to testify under duress and who deflected 
questions from both Democrats and Republicans by referring repeatedly to his voluminous report.
Mueller said his report did not exonerate Trump but he mostly deflected questions from lawmakers seeking to score 
political points for their sides.
A straight shooter
That was in keeping with the career of a public servant who had spent four decades serving both Democratic and 
Republican presidents.
Before taking on the politically sensitive Russia investigation, Mueller, a former marine who was wounded and 
decorated for heroism in Vietnam, enjoyed a sterling reputation in Washington.
Page 2 of 3
Robert Mueller, ex-FBI chief who led Trump-Russia inquiry, dead at 81
Mueller is a "consummate professional and a straight shooter," then-FBI chief Christopher Wray, a Trump 
appointee, said in July 2019.
As a young prosecutor in San Francisco and Boston, Mueller took on cases involving grisly murders, organized 
crime, fraud by powerful banks and terror attacks - winning some, losing some, but rarely drawing serious criticism 
for his work.
At the FBI, he gained a reputation of being an exacting taskmaster and, despite his early Republican political 
alignment, someone who was appreciated by politicians of both political parties.
Two of his most heralded prosecutions involved New York mobster John Gotti and General Manuel Noriega of 
Panama.
After retiring in 2013, he joined a private Washington law practice where he handled official arbiter missions.
Trump's May 2017 firing of Mueller's successor at the FBI, James Comey, resulted in Mueller being recalled to 
public service to lead the investigation into suspected Russia meddling.
Over 22 months, his investigators issued charges against 34 individuals, including six Trump associates, and three 
companies.
Born August 7, 1944, in New York City, Mueller grew up on Manhattan's tony upper East Side. He attended the 
elite, and at the time all-male, Princeton University where he earned his bachelor's degree in 1966.
After college, Mueller enlisted in the US Marines, and after one year as an enlisted man, entered officer candidate 
school. As a marine, Mueller earned a Bronze Star for valor and a Purple Heart for wounds received in combat.
In 2001, he took over an FBI beset by scandals, including the years-long deception by FBI mole Robert Hanssen 
and the agency's failure to turn over thousands of pages of investigative documents to Oklahoma City bomber 
Timothy McVeigh's attorneys.
Then-president George W. Bush and legislators agreed that Mueller was the person to set the bureau right. "His 
skills should be a perfect match for the challenge," Republican Senator Jeff Sessions said at the time.
Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, heartily agreed. "Bob Mueller," he said, "will give the FBI a major boost that will help it 
get back on its feet."

title: Serbian ex-officer faces ouster; Citizenship Case Man allegedly involved in war crimes in 1990s
body:
Alleged Serbian war criminal Goran Pavic has failed to derail the federal government's attempt to prove he obtained 
Canadian citizenship by fraudulent means and that he should be deemed inadmissible to this country.
Immigration Minister Lena Diab and Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree are alleging Pavic "made false 
statements on his application for permanent residence, which allowed him to obtain permanent residence in 
Canada in 1997 and Canadian citizenship in 2002," according to a recent Federal Court decision.
They're also claiming Pavic "is inadmissible to Canada because he was involved in the commission of, or was 
complicit in, crimes against humanity committed in the village of Sotin, now in Croatia," said the Feb. 19 decision.
"Specifically, the plaintiffs claim the defendant was involved in crimes of imprisonment, forcible transfer and murder. 
The factual allegations in the statement of claim concern (Pavic's) time as part of the Serbian Territorial Defence 
Forces and the Sotin Police in 1991."
In his defence, Pavic "advised that in September 1991, he was involuntarily conscripted into what became the 
Serbian Territorial Defence Forces and that in October 1991, was assigned to the Sotin Police. The statement of 
defence makes detailed pleadings, including about the defendant's actions in 1991 and his lack of knowledge of 
any of the alleged crimes."
Pavic, 60, was born in Vukovar in the Socialist Republic of Croatia, part of the former Yugoslavia, and currently the 
Republic of Croatia, according to the federal government's statement of claim.
Pavic has "a Serb ethnic background," it said.
"In response to the question: 'in periods of either peace or war, have you ever been involved in the commission of a 
war crime or a crime against humanity?' he answered 'no,' " said the claim.
"These assertions were false. (Pavic) was a member of the Serbian Territorial Defence Forces from June 1991 until 
the fall of 1991, when he became a member of the Sotin Police in or about the month of October 1991. He also 
failed to declare that he had resided in Sotin as of about October 1991. Finally, he was involved in the commission 
of - or was complicit by making a voluntary, significant and knowing contribution to - crimes against humanity 
committed in Sotin between October 1991 and at least December 1991."
Page 2 of 3
Serbian ex-officer faces ouster; Citizenship Case Man allegedly involved in war crimes in 1990s
Pavic wrote to the Serbian Prosecutor for War Crimes in December 2010 indicating "he was in Sotin during the war 
days and in particular in September-October 1991; everything he did was 'on someone's orders,' " said the federal 
government's claim.
In late 2007, while he was working as a truck driver, Pavic was detained by U.S. authorities after crossing the 
Ambassador Bridge to Detroit "based on an Interpol warrant issued by Croatia," according to a briefing note from 
the Zagreb office of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE).
"Pavic was subsequently released from detention and returned to Canada," according to the OSCE, after a "United 
States federal prosecutor in Michigan cited expiration of the statute of limitations as the reason for abandoning a 
request to extradite Goran Pavic, a Canadian citizen of Serb national origin, to Croatia to stand trial on war crimes 
charges."
According to the federal government's statement of claim, "in late 1991/early 1992, Serb armed forces carried out a 
widespread and/or systematic attack against the non-Serb civilian population in the Vukovar area generally and the 
village of Sotin in particular."
Pavic "alongside other members of the Sotin police and the Sotin (Territorial Defence Forces) transported 13 non-
Serb detainees from the Sotin police station to a vineyard outside of the village where they were executed. He 
thereby committed or was complicit in the crime against humanity of murder," said the claim.
Pavic was unable to convince a Federal Court judge to toss the case out recently, arguing the statute of limitations 
had run out because the events in question were more than six years in the past.
In order to revoke his Canadian citizenship, the federal government is looking for a declaration from the court that 
Pavic obtained it by fraud. Same goes for his permanent resident status.
But Pavic still has refugee status here, his lawyer, Jared Will, said Friday. "He has refugee status in addition to 
having permanent residence and citizenship, so further steps would have to be taken to remove him if he were to 
lose his citizenship and permanent residence." !@COPYRIGHT=© 2026 Postmedia Network Inc. All rights

title: Sim Ducks queries after attacking ORR; News conference on false accusations against political foes lasts just 5
body:
After days of dodging questions about a bizarre scandal of his own creation, Vancouver Mayor Ken Sim appeared 
to want to clear the air on Tuesday afternoon.
Unfortunately, he didn't really do that.
Sim's office invited the media to city hall for a media conference on Tuesday. It was short notice, but at least the 
invitation offered an opportunity for reporters to ask the mayor about a false public accusation he recently made 
against a fellow Vancouver council member, which came to light last week.
If it was meant as an effort at accountability, it did not land that way. Five minutes after the mayor took the stage, he 
was rushing out of the room, leaving behind a mystified group of journalists with unasked and unanswered 
questions.
The saga began last Tuesday, when the four Vancouver city councillors from outside the mayor's ABC party held a 
joint news conference, responding to what they described as "inflammatory and harmful misinformation" from ABC 
Coun. Lenny Zhou. The week before, Zhou had posted a Mandarin-language video on the Chinese social media 
platform WeChat, describing non-ABC councillors as drug-users and dealers.
Within hours of the non-ABC councillors' public statement, Zhou retracted the comments and apologized, and Sim 
applauded his ABC colleague "for acknowledging his mistake and taking responsibility for sharing information that 
was not accurate."
Two days later, the story took a twist when it was revealed Sim himself had publicly made a similar, but more 
specific, claim several days before Zhou. The Canadian Press reported last Thursday that Sim, during an on-the-
record briefing to Chinese-language media at city hall on Feb. 6, had accused Coun. Sean Orr of "handing out 
illegal drugs on Christmas Day to people on the streets."
Orr said the accusation was categorically false, and while he supports harm reduction and a regulated supply of 
hard drugs, he said he had never distributed illegal drugs.
Page 2 of 3
Sim Ducks queries after attacking ORR; News conference on false accusations against political foes lasts just 5 
minutes
Sim declined to publicly answer questions about the false accusation, including after being confronted by reporters 
on Friday. Then on Tuesday afternoon, when the mayor assembled dozens of reporters and camera operators at 
city hall, he appeared on stage to read a prepared speech, which lasted one minute and 25 seconds.
Sim's remarks included one new detail not publicly known before: His comments about Orr were apparently based 
on "a picture that had been shown to me regarding Coun. Orr distributing drugs," he said. "I didn't verify what I 
thought I saw, and frankly, I should have never repeated it," Sim said, adding that he apologized to Orr, his council 
colleagues, and Vancouverites.
With that, Sim's staff opened it up to questions. Reporters had many.
As journalists queued up behind the microphone, the first question was about why Sim did not report the image to 
the police if he believed he had seen evidence of a municipal politician breaking the law. The mayor did not answer 
the question.
Asked whether he would offer an apology, explanation, and retraction to Chinese-language media, where Sim 
originally spread the misinformation, he said he would.
Then a reporter asked how the mayor would, in the future, attempt to verify images and online content. If Sim does 
intend to start using some verification methods, he did not share them, instead calling this a "unique situation," and 
saying he will hold himself to a higher standard.
And that was it. Sim's director of communications Zoë Frankcom abruptly informed the reporters waiting in line at 
the microphone that the event was over, while Sim bolted out of the room.
The news conference began at 2 p.m., and by 2:05 p.m., the mayor had disappeared.
Journalists and other observers present were baffled.
ABC has now faced a full week of negative news, starting with Zhou's misinformation coming to light last Tuesday, 
and intensifying when the conduct of Sim, the party leader, became the focus.
But even if one disregards the partisan shots from ABC's political rivals - which are to be expected - what's not 
clear, from the outside, is how this episode is playing out inside Sim's own party.
Does the ABC party leadership have any concerns about Sim's judgment or his fitness to lead? Or do they consider 
the matter resolved, and fully support the mayor (and Zhou)? ABC Vancouver president Stephen Molnar and party 
spokesperson Sarah Kanakos declined to answer those questions by email on Monday or Tuesday this week.
None of ABC's six elected councillors, including Zhou, responded to Postmedia's text messages and emails on 
Monday or Tuesday, asking whether they still supported the mayor or had any concerns about his conduct. It does 
not seem as though any of them have made a public statement supporting Sim since the story broke last week. Not 
one of ABC's elected officials appeared on stage with him Tuesday, as they usually do at news conferences.
None of ABC's three park board commissioners, or three school board trustees replied to Postmedia's emails.
If ABC's leaders and elected officials have any concerns about Sim's conduct, they are opting not to reveal them 
outside the party at this time.
But if they still support their party leader, they also don't seem to want to make that known publicly either.

Within hours of the non-ABC councillors' public statement, Zhou retracted the comments and apologized, and Sim 
applauded his ABC colleague "for acknowledging his mistake and taking responsibility for sharing information that 
was not accurate."
Two days later, the story took a twist when it was revealed Sim himself had publicly made a similar, but more 
specific, claim several days before Zhou. The Canadian Press reported last Thursday that Sim, during an on-the-
record briefing to Chinese-language media at city hall on Feb. 6, had accused Coun. Sean Orr of "handing out 
illegal drugs on Christmas Day to people on the streets."
Orr said the accusation was categorically false, and while he supports harm reduction and a regulated supply of 
hard drugs, he said he had never distributed illegal drugs.
Page 2 of 3
Sim Ducks queries after attacking ORR; News conference on false accusations against political foes lasts just 5 
minutes
Sim declined to publicly answer questions about the false accusation, including after being confronted by reporters 
on Friday. Then on Tuesday afternoon, when the mayor assembled dozens of reporters and camera operators at 
city hall, he appeared on stage to read a prepared speech, which lasted one minute and 25 seconds.
Sim's remarks included one new detail not publicly known before: His comments about Orr were apparently based 
on "a picture that had been shown to me regarding Coun. Orr distributing drugs," he said. "I didn't verify what I 
thought I saw, and frankly, I should have never repeated it," Sim said, adding that he apologized to Orr, his council 
colleagues, and Vancouverites.
With that, Sim's staff opened it up to questions. Reporters had many.
As journalists queued up behind the microphone, the first question was about why Sim did not report the image to 
the police if he believed he had seen evidence of a municipal politician breaking the law. The mayor did not answer 
the question.
Asked whether he would offer an apology, explanation, and retraction to Chinese-language media, where Sim 
originally spread the misinformation, he said he would.
Then a reporter asked how the mayor would, in the future, attempt to verify images and online content. If Sim does 
intend to start using some verification methods, he did not share them, instead calling this a "unique situation," and 
saying he will hold himself to a higher standard.
And that was it. Sim's director of communications Zoë Frankcom abruptly informed the reporters waiting in line at 
the microphone that the event was over, while Sim bolted out of the room.
The news conference began at 2 p.m., and by 2:05 p.m., the mayor had disappeared.
Journalists and other observers present were baffled.
ABC has now faced a full week of negative news, starting with Zhou's misinformation coming to light last Tuesday, 
and intensifying when the conduct of Sim, the party leader, became the focus.
But even if one disregards the partisan shots from ABC's political rivals - which are to be expected - what's not 
clear, from the outside, is how this episode is playing out inside Sim's own party.
Does the ABC party leadership have any concerns about Sim's judgment or his fitness to lead? Or do they consider 
the matter resolved, and fully support the mayor (and Zhou)? ABC Vancouver president Stephen Molnar and party 
spokesperson Sarah Kanakos declined to answer those questions by email on Monday or Tuesday this week.
None of ABC's six elected councillors, including Zhou, responded to Postmedia's text messages and emails on 
Monday or Tuesday, asking whether they still supported the mayor or had any concerns about his conduct. It does 
not seem as though any of them have made a public statement supporting Sim since the story broke last week. Not 
one of ABC's elected officials appeared on stage with him Tuesday, as they usually do at news conferences.
None of ABC's three park board commissioners, or three school board trustees replied to Postmedia's emails.
If ABC's leaders and elected officials have any concerns about Sim's conduct, they are opting not to reveal them 
outside the party at this time.
But if they still support their party leader, they also don't seem to want to make that known publicly either.

title: Smart policy overshadowed by unforced errors
body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford got something big right in the last few weeks, though he's distracted from his own 
accomplishment by focusing on pet projects and self-serving new rules.
Ford has done just the right thing to boost Ontario's stagnant housing industry and sharply increase new home 
affordability. His good work was amplified by getting Prime Minister Mark Carney on board.
Ford and Carney's decision to eliminate the HST on new homes valued up to $1 million will save buyers $130,000. 
Homes up to $1.5 million will also get a tax break on a sliding scale. The two leaders are also reducing municipal 
development charges by 50 per cent, although details of how it would work are a bit vague.
Combined, the two moves would save buyers of new homes up to $200,000, an incentive that's sure to boost 
Ontario's stagnant housing industry and produce more homes. This is a real solution to a significant problem, just 
the sort of thing people ought to expect from government.
Unfortunately, at a time when voters are looking for more stability in a world of disruption, the premier who has 
made a career out of being in sync with the mood of Ontarians has also seemed tone deaf. The war in the Middle 
East, rapidly rising fuel prices and the broader wave of inflation to follow are all bad news for people just trying to 
lead a normal life and live within their budgets. Many are concerned about the costs of their mortgage renewals.
Given the financial uncertainty and pressures taxpayers face, it hardly seems the time to propose a new convention 
centre for Toronto, five times as big as the one there now. Ford says the new centre will create "shock and awe." 
Taxpayers will more likely be shocked than awed by Ford's plan, which comes without a business case or an 
estimated cost.
It's not like the Ford government has the money for this whimsical project. The province's projected deficit this year 
is $13.8 billion, up from $12.3 billion last year.
Ford has also dug himself into an unnecessary hole with his attempt to impose new restrictions on freedom of 
information requests that will exclude any communication on personal devices by him, his ministers, or their staff. 
Ford has tried to justify the plan as necessary to protect the privacy of citizens he communicates with and even 
suggested that the rule change is necessary to protect Ontario from being to open to Chinese surveillance. He 
responded to a well-crafted critique from the information and privacy commissioner by saying her argument was 
"political." Ford dismissed criticism from opposition parties by saying he "kicked their asses three times in a row" 
and was ahead in the polls.
Page 2 of 3
Smart policy overshadowed by unforced errors
Ford's plan to give his own government added protection from the public is exactly the wrong thing to do. It creates 
the impression that he has something to hide. His government has already dragged its heels on releasing emails 
about its costly fight to eliminate some Toronto bike lanes. The new law would be applied retroactively to cover up 
whatever they're hoping to hide.
People evidently aren't impressed. A new Abacus Data poll this week shows PC support is at its lowest level in two 
years and Abacus reports that Ford's own popularity is down, though both he and his party are still ahead of the 
opposition. The poll finds "widespread opposition to proposed changes to freedom of information rules."
One of Ford's strengths has been admitting when he's made a mistake and changing course. It's time to do that 
again, instead of arrogantly dismissing opposition MPPs elected by Ontario voters. He's even lately been picking 
on the hapless Bonnie Crombie, his Liberal opponent in the last election, saying he'd "send an army" to prevent her 
from being elected as mayor of Mississauga this fall. It makes him sound like a bully.
The Abacus poll shows that 51 per cent of Ontarians think it's time for a change of government and an additional 19 
per cent think it would be nice.
Fortunately for Ford, he doesn't have to worry about going to the voters any time soon. His "protect Ontario" 
election last year insured that there will be no vote required until at least 2029. That's not an appealing prospect if 
he doesn't start spending his time and the public's money better.
Ontarians are sending Ford a message about how he's doing his job. The premier would be wise to listen.

title: Smith says caucus executive director didn't report voter list meeting to higher-ups
body:
EDMONTON - Premier Danielle Smith says the buck stops with her caucus when it comes to questions over why 
Smith didn’t know sooner about a massive breach of private information on Albertans.
Smith’s United Conservative caucus has previously said one of their staffers was at an April 16 meeting in which 
private information on Albertans was shown on an app.
Smith confirmed Monday the caucus staffer then briefed Tricia Velthuizen, the executive director of caucus, on the 
meeting but that Velthuizen did not pass any information on to Smith's office.
"(Velthuizen) said there was nothing that was presented that was out of the ordinary that would have required her to 
report up," Smith said. "No one was saying that this list was illegal -- that was not on anybody's radar."
The UCP caucus is made up of all the elected party members in the legislature. Smith said her caucus staff is 
managed separately from her office, adding that chief government whip Justin Wright oversees caucus staff, and 
didn't flag anything to cabinet.
Rakhi Pancholi, deputy leader of the Opposition NDP, told reporters Smith was making a staffer take the fall for 
something that ultimately falls to her.
"The buck stops with the premier," Pancholi said.
"It would be laughable if it didn't speak to the culture that this premier has instilled in her caucus and the lack of 
responsibility and accountability.”
The April 16 meeting is a key date in what has become a three-headed investigation into the breach of names and 
home addresses of nearly three million Alberta voters.
Elections Alberta, the provincial privacy commissioner and the RCMP are each investigating.
The NDP said last week it knew about the April 16 meeting and informed the RCMP about it a day later, on April 17.

Page 2 of 3
Smith says caucus executive director didn't report voter list meeting to higher-ups
The issue, though, did not become public for two weeks after that when, on April 30, Elections Alberta went to court 
to shut down the public-facing app containing the private information.
The controversy has prompted Smith to say they may make changes to rules to safeguard voter information, but 
added that will come after the investigations run their course.
Later Monday, Smith's office, when asked if there will be any changes or consequences for caucus staff, deferred 
the issue to caucus spokesperson Shanna Schulhauser.
Schulhauser declined to comment, citing the fact it concerns internal issues and personnel, but reiterated, "Staff 
observing the meeting had no reason to believe the website in question was unlawful."
In recent days, Smith’s government has tried to get the Speaker of the legislature to formally reprimand the NDP for 
not telling her government sooner about the breach.
Last week, government house leader Joseph Schow argued NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi's decision to not divulge 
put public officials at risk. Nenshi said he acted responsibly and didn't trust Smith on the issue given her prior ties to 
David Parker, the founder of the group tied to the app.
On Monday, Speaker Ric McIver said there is no evidence that members of the legislature had their rights 
compromised or parliamentary duties interfered with.
The app was organized by the Centurion Project, a group seeking support for separatism ahead of a fall 
referendum.
Lawyers for Elections Alberta have said they traced the database back to an official voter list legally provided to the 
pro-independence Republican Party of Alberta. How the list changed hands is under investigation.
Also Monday, chief electoral officer Gordon McClure told reporters he thinks there needs to be stronger rules in 
place guarding the voter list and until that happens, the list shouldn't be distributed to any political party.
"Our technology experts are monitoring the dark web (to) determine how far the information has gone at this time,” 
McClure said.
He couldn't provide a timeline for his investigation, but said it's "evolving very quickly."
This report by The Canadian Press was first published May 11, 2026.
-- With files from Jack Farrell

title: So you want to run for council in Almaguin ? Here are 5 things to know
body:
On Thursday, April 16, the Almaguin Clerks Group hosted a candidate information session for anyone thinking 
about throwing their name in the ring for local office.
Whether you're passionate about your community or just curious about the process, here are five things you need 
to know from the session before you hit the campaign trail.
1. It's a bigger commitment than you think
Serving on municipal council isn't a side quest, it's closer to a second job. Councillors are expected to review 
agendas, reports, bylaws and legislation before meetings, and those meetings happen during business hours and 
evenings. Appointments to external boards and committees add even more to the plate. The role, as the clerks 
group put it, doesn't have an on/off switch.
2. You're one voice, not a one-person show
There are no political parties at the municipal level. Every councillor sits as an independently elected 
representative, which means you'll need to make your case, persuade colleagues and accept that decisions are 
made collectively by majority vote. Coming in with a single issue and expecting to steamroll it through? The 
Almaguin Clerks group wants you to know that's a recipe for frustration.
3. Municipal government has real limits
Councils in Ontario draw their authority from provincial legislation, primarily the Municipal Act 2001 and the 
Planning Act. That matters because many of the issues — cost of living, gas prices at the pump, housing — fall 
under provincial or federal jurisdiction, not the township's. Further than that: roughly 25 per cent of budgeted 
property taxes flow to nondirect services like the Ontario Provincial Police, Parry Sound District Paramedic Service 
and the District of Parry Sound Social Services, costs that municipalities have no control over. During the 2022-26 
term of council alone, those costs have climbed nearly 20 per cent.
4. Everything you say is on the record
The moment you announce you're running, you're a public figure. Under the Municipal Freedom of Information and 
Privacy Act, the public has the right to access council members' correspondence, including email. The clerks 

Page 2 of 2
So you want to run for council in Almaguin ? Here are 5 things to know
group's advice: don't say or write anything you wouldn't say out loud in a public meeting. That goes double for 
social media, where the guiding principle is simple: when in doubt, don't post.
5. Conflict of interest rules are serious business
Every councillor swears a Declaration of Office and is bound by the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act. If you have 
a pecuniary interest — direct or indirect — in a matter before council, you must declare it, stay out of the discussion 
and not vote. Failing to do so can end in court. An Integrity Commissioner is available to provide guidance and 
investigate complaints.

title: Spy games prove costly in England Playoff expulsion ends Southampton shot at promotion
body:
Southampton was expelled from English soccer's Championship playoffs on Tuesday after admitting to repeatedly 
spying on opponents.
As a result, the English Football League reinstated Middlesbrough to play in Saturday's Wembley final - the richest 
game in soccer - against Hull City. The winner gets promoted to the Premier League with a windfall of at least $270 
million (U.S.) in future earnings from rights deals and ticket sales.
Southampton, which by Tuesday night had not announced any plans to appeal the ruling, was charged with the 
unauthorized filming of Middlesbrough's practice sessions ahead of their playoff semifinal and went on to win the 
two-leg series. The league said the southcoast club, which was demoted from the Premier League after a last-
place finish last season, admitted further breaches this season involving games against Oxford United and Ipswich. 
Four points were also deducted for next season.
In 2019, Leeds was fined $259,000 for spying on Derby training sessions ahead of a game.
 Spying has proven costly in several other high-profile sports cases:
 Patriots spygate
In 2007, the NFL's New England Patriots were caught using video to record New York Jets signals during a game. 
Coach Bill Belichick was fined $500,000, while the Patriots were docked $250,000 and a first-round draft pick. 
Twelve years later, the team acknowledged that a crew filmed the Cincinnati Bengals sideline during a game 
against the Cleveland Browns, a week before the Bengals hosted the Patriots. The Patriots were fined $1.1 million 
in that case and had a third-round pick taken away in 2021.
Canadian drone scandal
At the 2024 Paris Olympics, the defending champion Canadian women's soccer team flew drones over New 
Zealand's closed practice sessions in violation of several rules. Coach Bev Priestman was suspended and removed 
from the team, while two staffers members were sent home. FIFA fined Canada Soccer $228,000 and docked the 
team six points in the tournament. Canada still advanced before losing in the quarterfinal. Priestman and the 
staffers were suspended for a year. 
Page 2 of 3
Spy games prove costly in England Playoff expulsion ends Southampton shot at promotion
Astros sign stealing
The Houston Astros used more basic technology in a sign-stealing scandal that rocked MLB in 2020: a camera, a 
TV monitor and, most famously, a trash can. MLB's investigation found the Astros had used a scheme during their 
2017 World Series title run to steal signs relayed between opposing catchers and pitchers. A camera in centre field 
zoomed in on the catcher and fed a monitor near Houston's dugout during home games. Teammates would study 
the signs on the monitor, then bang on a trash can to indicate to the batter if the next pitch was a fastball or off-
speed. Manager A.J. Hinch and GM Jeff Luhnow were fired, as was former bench coach Alex Cora from his job as 
the Boston Red Sox manager. 
McLaren vs. Ferrari
While McLaren and Ferrari drivers battled for the Formula One title on the track in 2007, details emerged of 
McLaren staff obtaining confidential technical information about Ferrari's car design. A British copy shop manager 
informed Ferrari when he spotted a customer, who turned out to be a McLaren engineer's wife, making copies of 
the documents. McLaren was eventually fined $100 million and stripped of all points in that year's constructors 
championship.
The Associated Press

title: Student allowed to stay in Canada despite crime; 'A dupe' in attempted auto theft
body:
An international student who was kicked out of college but remained in Canada on an expired student permit has 
been allowed to stay in the country after it was determined that, although he had participated in a crime, it was not 
an organized crime and he was merely "a dupe."
The case involved a man who came to Canada from India on a study permit in 2022 when he was 21.
"He was enrolled in a college but after two semesters ended up homeless, jobless and, by his own admission, 
addicted to weed," case documents said. "The study permit expired on July 30, 2024 so he was also without status 
in Canada when the relevant events took place."
Those events involved the attempted theft of a BMW from a dealership in Vancouver. The man said he had become 
acquainted with someone who offered to help him get a job in construction and arranged a flight from Ontario to 
Vancouver.
"The Respondent traveled to Vancouver and was taken to a basement apartment by a person he did not know and 
whose face he could not see behind a breathing mask," according to court documents. "The next day, September 
21, 2024, that person gave the Respondent better clothes to wear, and said a favour was needed before going to 
the promised job."
"He took the Respondent to an auto dealership and explained along the way how to transact with a fake ID and 
credit card for a previously arranged purchase of a 2019 BMW 330 priced at $37,252. Everything did not go as 
hoped. The fake ID was detected, the dealer staff called police, the acquaintance disappeared, and the Respondent 
got arrested."
Local police investigated, but the Crown did not pursue a criminal charge and the man was referred to Canada 
Border Services Agency, which prepared a report that alleged he was inadmissible to Canada for participating in 
organized crime.
However, the Immigration Division rejected the allegation. The Minister of Public Safety then appealed.
In her ruling, tribunal member Maryanne Kingma wrote: "The Respondent was a dupe whose personal 
circumstances led him into trouble. It was trouble that a local prosecutor did not consider worth pursuing."

"He was not a member of a criminal organization or a group that planned and organized criminal activity. He did not 
knowingly participate in organized criminal activity. He was coerced into domestic criminal actions that did not even 
lead to a criminal charge."
Kingma concluded: "There are reasonable grounds to believe the Respondent committed the domestic crimes 
described by the Minister as attempted theft of a vehicle, identity fraud and forgery. However, committing a 
domestic crime is not the same as having knowledge and involvement in a criminal organization."

title: Sun columnist Palmer receives major honour; Getting the Michener-Baxter Award left veteran journalist 'kind of
body:
Vaughn Palmer has received many awards over his five-decade career at The Vancouver Sun.
But he was dumbfounded when he received a call that he was one of two recipients of the 2026 Michener-Baxter 
Award "for exceptional service to Canadian journalism."
"I was genuinely awed when they called me to tell me that Bruce (Mackinnon) and I were going to be the winners," 
said Palmer.
"I'm not known for modesty. In fact, people tell you even my false modesty is fake. But on this one, I was kind of 
knocked over."
The Michener-Baxter Award "recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to Canadian 
journalism and public service through a career dedicated to integrity, excellence, and the public good."
The ceremony is to be held at Rideau Hall in Ottawa on June 18.
The award is not awarded annually. It has been handed out only 14 times to 13 individuals and one organization 
since it was established in 1983.
Global TV's Keith Baldrey said the honour is well-deserved, because Palmer is like "an encyclopedia of B.C. 
political history."
"We sit next to each other in budget lockups, deliberately," said Baldrey.
"He is the one person in the entire room who will know the history of everything, in terms of the government's 
budget history and spending habits and misuse and missteps, in an instant."
Former premier Mike Harcourt joked that, "They should download (Palmer's) brain before he retires."
"The stories he could tell," said Harcourt.
As a politician, Harcourt doesn't always agree with Palmer. But he said his column is a must-read.
Page 2 of 3
Sun columnist Palmer receives major honour; Getting the Michener-Baxter Award left veteran journalist 'kind of 
knocked over'
"I enjoy reading him, even though I think he's over the top in anti-Eby stuff," he said with a laugh. "He was mentored 
by Bruce Hutchison. He comes from great lineage at The Sun."
Hutchison was a B.C. journalism legend who was close with Palmer. Palmer points out that Hutchison's first photo 
in the B.C. legislative press gallery was in 1919, and Hutchison's last column was in 1992, the year be died.
Palmer's career hasn't been quite that long, but he is still going strong after 53 years at the newspaper.
Born in Gaspe, Que., Vaughn Wilson Palmer arrived in Nanaimo at 15, when his father moved west to become a 
B.C. Ferries captain in 1967. He got into journalism at the University of B.C. and started working at The Sun part-
time in 1973.
He was The Sun's "rock 'n' roll" critic and city editor before becoming the legislative columnist.
"I've been on the political beat since 1984. So that's 11 premiers and counting, as Baldrey and I put it," said 
Palmer.
Other journalists have come and gone as well, but Palmer still loves covering provincial politics.
"B.C. politics is generous in terms of material," he said.
"You're writing every day, and they're doing something every day. The other thing that has been fruitful in terms of 
material is the dramatic contrast between the way (Premier David) Eby runs the government and the way (former 
premier John) Horgan did.
"That's a lot of what we write about. You don't need to go back to the B.C. Liberals to see the difference."
Palmer points out there was also a dramatic contrast between two Social Credit premiers, Bill Bennett and Bill 
Vander Zalm.
"Vander Zalm was God's gift to B.C. political writers," Palmer said in 2023. "Whatever you think about what kind of 
premier he was, he generated staggering amounts of material and unbelievable storylines. After that, I was 
established as a columnist. And I've sort of done OK ever since."
Palmer, Baldrey and Les Leyne of the Victoria Times Colonist have become such fixtures in the B.C. legislature that 
they now give talks to the interns on that beat.
"We used to tell them Vander Zalm stories, until we realized that none of them were born when he was premier," 
deadpans Palmer. "So we've kind of had to retire some of that material."
Palmer is legendary for digging nuggets out of government reports. His first major scoop was when he pored 
through Highway Ministry reports and found that construction of the Coquihalla Highway had cost much, much more 
than what the government claimed.
"When Vander Zalm became premier, he ordered a public inquiry into the overrun on the Coquihalla (in 1987), 
which was advertised at $250 million, but ended up costing a billion dollars. And that was real money."
Palmer will turn 74 on May 26. Others might retire and kick back to enjoy life with their family (wife Dale 
Ketcheson, daughter Elise and grandson Reid), but retirement doesn't seem imminent.
"I talk to (Sun/Province editor) Harold (Munro) every year on my birthday, and I say I'd like to stay another year," he 
said.
"And he says, 'Fine.' My birthday is coming up in a couple of weeks. ... I'm going to ask him if I can stay another."

title: Survey finds FOI moves hurting PCs Poll suggests Ford government has lowest level of support in two years
body:
Premier Doug Ford's controversial changes to access to information laws appear to be hurting his government's 
popularity, a new poll suggests.
Abacus Data's monthly tracking survey found Ford's Progressive Conservatives at 39 per cent - down from 44 per 
cent in March. That's their lowest level of support in almost two years.
Abacus president David Coletto noted it was his firm's first poll since Ford announced he would exclude records of 
the premier, ministers, parliamentary assistants and aides from being released under the Freedom of Information 
and Protection of Privacy Act.
That decision has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum, including all three opposition parties at 
Queen's Park and the Canadian Taxpayers Federation.
"It undermines his brand. The Ford brand is built around being accessible, being a man who connects with the 
average person, who answers phone calls, who always shares his cellphone (number) with every audience he goes 
to," Coletto said Wednesday.
Ironically, Ford's move comes against the backdrop of an ongoing legal challenge to gain access to the records of 
his personal cellphone that he uses to conduct public business.
The premier has insisted he is "not going to release personal, confidential information about people's lives" 
because Ontarians routinely share their private health information with him.
"Every personal problem people have, they call me, I feel like a psychologist every day trying to solve everyone's 
personal issues," Ford said last month.
But Coletto said the policy changes "reinforces some of the weaknesses the party and the premier had around the 
Greenbelt (land swap) scandal and these controversies that have hung over them."
Abacus surveyed 2,185 Ontarians from last Thursday through Monday using online panels based on the 
PureSpectrum platform. While opt-in polls cannot be assigned a margin of error, for comparison purposes, a 
random sample of this size would have one of plus or minus 2.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. 
Page 2 of 2
Survey finds FOI moves hurting PCs Poll suggests Ford government has lowest level of support in two years
The poll found that 51 per cent of respondents feel it's time for a change in government at Queen's Park. "It's the 
highest we've had it, but it's not the danger zone. Sixty is where you really get in trouble. But it's still up nine points 
since the first time we asked it, so that is not a good sign," said Coletto. 
In terms of personal popularity, Ford was at 33 per cent positive, 41 per cent negative for a minus eight per cent 
favourability rating, with 22 per cent of respondents neutral and one per cent unsure.

title: Suspected arson attempt at Macclesfield stadium under investigation
body:
MACCLESFIELD, England (AP) — English sixth-tier club Macclesfield claimed someone tried to burn down its 
stadium on Tuesday, two months after it pulled off the biggest upset in FA Cup history by knocking out titleholder 
Crystal Palace.
The “suspected arson attempt” on Leasing.com Stadium took place overnight and there were no casualties, the 
club said.
“Emergency services have responded immediately and are on site tackling the blaze in the affected areas,” 
Macclesfield said in a statement.
It still urged “anyone nearby to keep windows shut and not to approach the stadium.”
Authorities were investigating the cause of the fire and the club said it was not commenting further for now. The 
stadium dates to 1891. It has a capacity of 6,355 spectators.
Led by the younger brother of England and Manchester United icon Wayne Rooney, the tiny club from England’s 
northwest stunned Premier League 's Palace 2-1 on Jan. 11 in Macclesfield and created one of the most iconic 
moments in soccer’s oldest knockout competition.
With 117 places separating National League North team Macclesfield and Palace when they played, it was the 
biggest upset in the FA Cup’s 155-year history. Macclesfield was knocked out in the next round — the fourth — by 
the Premier League's Brentford.

title: Suspended cop will co-operate with probe Deputy chief accused of using 'offensive' language during meeting
body:
Durham police Deputy Chief Chris Kirkpatrick says he will fully co-operate with an independent investigation 
launched by the service into his alleged use of a "racially inappropriate term" during an internal meeting last week.
"As (the incident) is under investigation, I am ready to fully co-operate in that process but would decline making a 
statement to the media at this time," Kirkpatrick told the Star in a written statement on Monday.
Kirkpatrick, a 29-year veteran, was suspended following Wednesday's meeting, which was attended by both civilian 
and uniformed members of DRPS as part of the service's Afro-Caribbean Canadian Internal Support Network 
(ACC-ISN). In a statement released the next day, Chief Peter Moreira said he'd notified the Durham police board of 
the incident, which made the decision to suspend Kirkpatrick with pay. The board later said an independent third 
party would investigate the incident "with the firm objective of ensuring accountability and demonstrating the board's 
unwavering commitment to the importance of equity, diversity and inclusion."
Sterling Lee, the regional councillor for Ajax Ward 2, said in a statement Kirkpatrick had used the N-word during 
the meeting.
"Let's be precise, because precision matters here," Lee said in a Thursday evening post to X. "He didn't misspeak. 
He didn't immediately apologize. He casually weaponized it as a superior, from a position of power, in a room full of 
Black subordinates who had no safe recourse in that moment."
In his statement, Lee demanded change for what he called a "racially toxic workforce."
While the comment was "offensive" and "inconsistent" with Durham police values, Moreira said in his statement that 
it was not directed at anyone individually.
"DRPS is committed to transparency to foster trust with our community," Moreira said.
Kirkpatrick made headlines in 2024, after getting caught speeding in his police-issued vehicle twice in two days, 
once while travelling through a school zone. Peel police were tapped to investigate the allegations, clearing 
Kirkpatrick of wrongdoing by October.

title: Teachers who created hostile environment at Montreal school have licences revoked
body:
MONTRÉAL - Quebec's Education Department has revoked the teaching licences for all 11 staff members accused 
of creating a toxic climate at a Montreal elementary school, in a scandal that led the province to strengthen its 
secularism rules.
Education Minister Sonia LeBel said Tuesday no further details could be released because the teachers are 
appealing the government's decision.
In 2024, a government investigation concluded that a group of teachers, many of North African descent, created a 
hostile environment by yelling at, humiliating, and imposing their religious views on students and staff at Bedford 
school. At the time, former premier François Legault claimed the teachers were trying to “introduce Islamist 
religious concepts into a public school.”
The investigation revealed that the teachers, who were allegedly influenced by the local mosque, subjected children 
to physical and psychological abuse. There were incidents of prayers in the classroom, and some teachers 
allegedly refused to teach — or paid little attention to — the science and sex education curriculum.
Eleven teachers — a mix of men and women — were suspended from the school in the city's Côte-des-Neiges 
district.
At a news conference in Quebec City on Tuesday, Michelle Setlakwe, a Liberal member of the legislature whose 
riding includes Bedford school, said she was relieved by the outcome. 
“I find it appalling what was done to young girls. I find it appalling that we didn’t provide all the necessary services to 
students who were vulnerable.... Their (licences) were permanently revoked? Perfect.”
As a result of the events at Bedford, the government investigated 17 other schools over alleged breaches of the 
province’s secularism law, known as Bill 21, but no violations were ultimately found. The 17 schools are all in the 
French system, with 11 in and around Montreal, three in Quebec City, one in Gatineau and two in the Saguenay 
region north of the capital.

Page 2 of 3
Teachers who created hostile environment at Montreal school have licences revoked
Simultaneously, two independent administrators appointed by the province produced an action plan aimed at 
preventing similar situations to the one at Bedford school. It included 24 recommendations specific to Bedford and 
10 broader recommendations for the education system.
The plan says schools should be required to evaluate their teachers every two years, with support from an expert 
as needed. It also says the government should consider enshrining in law the obligation to speak French anywhere 
that students are present in schools, including classrooms, hallways and common areas. The Bedford report found 
that staff often spoke in languages other than French.
Another recommendation says the government should modify Quebec's law on public education to ban all religious 
activities in schools, during and after school hours.
In 2025, Quebec adopted legislation extending the province's ban on religious symbols to include all staff who 
interact with students inside schools. Before the expansion of the law only teachers were affected. In 2026, the 
Quebec government introduced another secularism law, restricting prayer in certain public spaces and expanding 
the ban on religious symbols to include daycare workers.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published May 12, 2026.

title: The complicated legacy of Otto Schaefer and Canada 's Indigenous people
body:
From the 1950s to the 1970s, a doctor educated under and possibly indoctrinated by the Nazis wielded 
tremendous authority over Canadian Indigenous people and their health care. "Otto Schaefer had a very interesting 
history, which he tried very hard to cover up," the late writer Elaine Dewar observed. "He studied under the leaders 
of Hitler's hygiene program, which was their science of race." And he had a passion for studying the Inuit. What 
about caring for them? That, as her new posthumously published book "Oblivious" suggests, is a more complicated 
question.
 When he arrived in Aklavik, N.W.T., by plane in January 1953, dressed in European clothes that were next to 
useless in the -45 C weather, he ran to get out of the cold. He was a fast-moving small man, and the Inuit who saw 
him dash for cover gave him a nickname: shik shik - ground squirrel.
Two years later, he and his family were posted to Pangnirtung, on the east side of Baffin Island, in what is now 
Nunavut. This was where he'd always wanted to be. Apparently, he and his wife absolutely loved their time there, 
though by then she had two children to care for, and he was often away with his guide and dog team taking care of 
people scattered around the island. Their little house was not up to the weather and frost would bloom all over the 
interior walls. Two years later he was posted to Whitehorse.
He began to publish about the Indigenous people he cared for in 1957, after he left Pangnirtung. 
 He referred to the Inuit as Eskimos, though he must have known that was not what they called themselves: he 
described how his Inuk guide refused to speak to him in English so he had to learn Inuktitut. He displayed the same 
combination of admiration and disgust I'd seen in earlier papers by other doctors who'd studied the Inuit and 
northern First Nations people. He described delivering babies in smoky tents without much more than an oil lamp 
for light. He wrote of a medicine woman who dealt with difficult deliveries involving recalcitrant placentas by 
reaching into the patient's uterus and scraping the placenta off the uterine wall with her bare hands. He described 
the fingernails on those hands as blackened with dirt, but the woman assured him she bit her nails off before 
reaching inside her patient. But he also described medical methods used by Indigenous people that worked better 
than the ones he employed. Using spruce gum to close a nasty wound, for example, worked better than his sutures.
These early articles were rife with the racist tropes of the period and hinted that he'd bought into Hitler's version of 
race theory. Hitler had insisted that the original Aryans from whom Germans were said to descend, who invented all 
Page 2 of 4
The complicated legacy of Otto Schaefer and Canada 's Indigenous people
of civilization, were from somewhere in the far north and west - some place like Iceland or possibly the Eastern 
Arctic - that the ancients called Thule. Schaefer certainly believed in the existence of racial types. He also believed 
that civilization was destroying the noble savages of the North.
After his time in Whitehorse, he went back to Edmonton and qualified as an internal medicine specialist. 
 At the Charles Camsell Indian Hospital, he focused on the North, doing various experiments and studies. He 
sometimes worked on his own, sometimes with others such as Jack Hildes, a doctor whom he'd met on the medical 
survey ship C.D. Howe and asked for help getting the articles he wrote into publishable shape.
By 1964 when Schaefer became director of Health and Welfare's Northern Research Medical Unit, he was 
convinced that the imposition of southern lifestyles was destroying the health of the Inuit. This was a theme he 
wrote about for years. By 1968 he was both a part of and the facilitator for the International Biological Program's 
Project D experiments on human adaptability in the North. Some 450 Inuit people of Igloolik and about 160 more 
from Hall Beach were roped into Project D as study subjects over the course of six years, everyone from babies to 
school children to the most elderly. From what I could tell from the papers and reports I reviewed, all the 
experiments done for Project D in Igloolik and Hall Beach were unethical: consent was not informed, nor was it 
given by individuals, and because the federal government which funded the project also provided housing, 
schooling, and medical care to the community, it was coercive.
As I learned to my surprise working through his documents, Schaefer and Hildes had not published some important 
results of their research for the IBP in a timely way. As part of the medical survey they did of all the inhabitants of 
Igloolik, Schaefer and Hildes collected hair and blood samples and tested them for mercury and cadmium. Some 
contained high levels of both, which have serious neurological impacts. The deleterious impact of methylmercury 
was in the news at the time. The Indigenous population of Grassy Narrows First Nation and the Whitedog and 
Islington bands in Ontario were exposed to methylmercury in the English and Wabigoon River systems, dumped by 
a paper company in Dryden in 1962. The methylmercury bioaccumulated up the food chain into the fish they relied 
on, and some displayed early signs of Minamata disease, a severe neurological condition. Those facts had become 
public while the IBP experiments were conducted. My husband Stephen helped reveal them on CTV's "W5," which 
is no doubt why Schaefer and Hildes collected the hair samples in Igloolik. Yet that information was not included in 
the first group of papers Schaefer and Hildes published on Project D.
Letters show that Schaefer's colleagues at Health and Welfare at first thought the problem stemmed from industrial 
pollution drifting around the North. Then they came to believe that cadmium and mercury had bioaccumulated 
naturally in seal livers and trout. Some at Health and Welfare wanted to warn the Inuit to stop eating these foods. 
Schaefer argued against it: he feared that would exacerbate their already poor nutritional condition. The Inuit were 
very careful about how they ate animals with known parasites, like walrus and fish, he said.
The internal argument continued for years. And it stayed internal. In 1977, Paul Grescoe reported on the disastrous 
health circumstances of Indigenous people. By then methylmercury poisoning had also been discovered in Cree 
people in northern Quebec. But it wasn't the governments of Canada or Quebec that informed the public. It was 
neurologist Dr André Barbeau, director of the Clinical Research Institute of Montreal. He told Grescoe that 
knowledge of methylmercury poisoning of Native people was treated by government "as a state secret."
Telling the public through an academic journal that the Inuit in Igloolik had been exposed to mercury and cadmium - 
even if from a natural source - would have brought a lot of unwelcome media attention to the federal government. 
The Grassy Narrows situation caused a significant fuss, but federal politicians could brush it aside as a provincial 
environmental problem. But cadmium and mercury pollution in the North fell under federal responsibility and would 
have caused a ruckus that politicians would certainly have wanted to smother.
 In January 1977, for an article on the women's movement, I'd interviewed Marc Lalonde, who was then the 
minister of the status of women but also minister of health and welfare. After the interview, as I was packing up 
my notebooks to leave, his political assistant leaned in and whispered, "The minister would like to have lunch with 
you." "I'm sorry," I said. "Thank you for the invitation, but I have another appointment."
Page 3 of 4
The complicated legacy of Otto Schaefer and Canada 's Indigenous people
I walked from his inner office to the outer office. The outer office was jammed with reporters who wanted to ask the 
minister what he knew and when he knew that arsenic from the Giant Mine outside Yellowknife had contaminated 
Indigenous children and mine workers and infiltrated the sediments of Great Slave Lake. The National Indian 
Brotherhood and the steelworkers union had done independent tests, which showed the contamination was very 
significant. A government study in 1975 had also shown arsenic contamination in Indigenous children near the 
mine, but Lalonde downplayed those results to the point of suppression. I concluded I was asked to lunch to keep 
him out of the line of fire.
In 1976, Schaefer, like Jack Hildes later was inducted into the Order of Canada. After reading his correspondence 
on mercury and cadmium, I began to wonder if Schaefer received the honour because he'd kept his mouth shut in 
public about what they found in the hair of people from Igloolik and Hall Beach.
That March, Schaefer agitated to maintain the Camsell as a segregated treatment centre, even as the federal 
government took steps to shut it down . I found internal letters he wrote protesting the government's plan. It seemed 
to me clear evidence that Schaefer was worried that he'd lose access to a patient population he wanted to study.
I read file after file of the reports he'd compiled from autopsies and from the studies he did on the northern 
Indigenous people in his care - files that frequently included names and details of the medical conditions his 
subjects suffered from. Some of the resulting papers, published in journals, included images of those patients' 
faces. He should not have used the medical information he gathered for those studies without getting informed 
consent from his patients. Even if he got it, those studies would still have been ethically dicey because he was 
working for the government that ran their lives.
And yet I also read clippings of the many articles he wrote to local newspapers, advocating on behalf of Indigenous 
people who by the 1960s, he claimed, were suffering more from alcohol and accidents than from TB and other 
infectious diseases. 
In the 1980s he'd also written letters protesting the collapse of a clinical trial, to test a flu vaccine called Praxis. It 
was to be given with the diphtheria vaccine to see if it would protect babies in the North under thirty months of age 
from a form of meningitis. There was an incidence of that form of meningitis of 25 cases per 100,000 among Inuit 
children versus 1.5 cases per 100,000 among Whites. The after-effects of meningitis include retardation, seizures, 
and deafness; the mortality rate is five to eight per cent. All infants under 30 months across the entire Arctic were to 
be enrolled. The control group would receive a normal diphtheria vaccine plus placebo. The government of the 
Northwest Territories pulled the plug.
By the time I staggered out of the archive, I had four contradictory versions of Schaefer whirling in my head: a 
goodhearted advocate of Indigenous peoples' health who saw himself as their protector; a man who did grossly 
unethical studies and helped others to do the same; a man who might have exiled himself to the North in search of 
support for the weird Nazi theory of German origin; and a man seeking personal redemption.
I was still asking: who was Otto Schaefer?
From "Oblivious: Residential Schools, Segregated Hospitals, and the use of Indigenous Peoples as Slaves of Race 
Science" by Elaine Dewar. Copyright © 2026 by Elaine Dewar. Published by Biblioasis. Reproduced by 
arrangement with the publisher. All rights reserved.
